items.title: Smashing Security podcast #488: How a ransomware negotiator ended up arrested at his own conference
items.summary: A ransomware negotiator attended a cybersecurity conference, only to be arrested by the FBI in connection with its investigation into the ShinyHunters gang. Meanwhile, hackers get the keys to ASOS's app and the chance to message every single customer. What did they say? And how did the company respond? We have thoughts. All this and more is discussed in episode 488 of the "Smashing Security" podcast with cybersecurity expert and keynote speaker Graham Cluley, and special guest Paul Ducklin.

That is why we provide in-depth blogposts, tools, trainings, weekly internal conferences (called Fridaycon, guess when they are), we teach in universities and schools and write articles in tech magazines. Sharing is caring, but sharing is also learning. We provide the environment for that and the rest relies on you. Intern package in France: Salary: €1800 gross per month (approximately €1550 net); "Tickets restaurant" (restaurant coupons); In-depth and challenging topics. Internships Topics 🟢 Vulnerability assessment and exploitation of a Telematic Control Unit Description Since 2016, every new model of vehicle sold in Europe should be equiped with an eCall module, that provides voice and data connectivity for emergency services. This was an important milestone in the connectivity of road vehicles, as manufacturer are using this data capability to enhance the driver experience, with live information, remote control, ... Therefore, the telematic control module (TCU) is a key element in the security of a car, with a permanent 3GPP connectivity. From this perspective, questions arise: Are these modules secure enough to prevent an attacker to get a remote access to a vehicle ? What kind of data are transmitted to backend server, brokers, and what could be the impact from a privacy point of view ? During this internship you'll focus on one or two telematic control unit, to get an understanding on how they work, analyze communications and evaluate the maturity of their security features. Required Skills ARM reverse engineering (intermediate) Fuzzing (basic to intermediate) Programming: Python, C What you will do The goals of this internship are: Extract and analyse the operating system of a telematic control unit Reverse-engineer targeted binary to understand how the device communicate with the backend Analyze the TCU baseband Assignment Download the assignment.zip file and follow the instructions in assignment.md . Duration 6 months Location Paris, France 🟢 Vulnerability assessment and exploitation of satellite communication systems Description This internship focuses on the practical security analysis of satellite communication systems, starting from the completion and operation of an existing ground station project . The first objective will be to finalize the ground station setup and validate its ability to receive and process satellite signals. The intern will then use the station to capture and analyze real satellite communications , identify the protocols and implementations in use, and understand the different layers involved in the communication chain. From these observations, the intern will study the security properties of the identified protocols and software implementations, map potential attack surfaces, and investigate possible weaknesses or vulnerabilities. Depending on the results, the project may include reproducing known vulnerabilities, analyzing protocol weaknesses, developing test or fuzzing environments, and experimenting with potential attacks in a controlled environment. The overall objective is to follow the complete path from signal acquisition to security research , combining radio communications, protocol analysis, reverse engineering and vulnerability research. Required Skills Programming: Proficiency in Python, C/C++, or similar languages. Cybersecurity: Understanding of vulnerability research, reverse engineering, and security assessment techniques. Networking & Protocols: Familiarity with communication protocols and packet analysis. Research: Ability to investigate unfamiliar technologies, read technical specifications, and independently formulate hypotheses. Radio/SDR knowledge: Familiarity with SDR or digital communications is appreciated but not mandatory. Assignment Choose a publicly documented vulnerability from 2022 or later affecting a space-related protocol, software component, ground station, or satellite communication system. Rather than simply summarizing the CVE: Analyze it: Explain where the vulnerable component fits within a realistic satellite communication architecture, the root cause, and what an attacker would realistically need to exploit it. Investigate it: Perform a small technical experiment: analyze the vulnerable code and its patch, reproduce the behavior, build a test harness, craft an input reaching the vulnerable code path, or propose another relevant experiment. Go beyond the documentation: Identify one question or hypothesis that is not answered by the CVE/advisory and explain how you would investigate it. A successful exploit is not required . We are more interested in your technical reasoning, methodology, observations, and ability to investigate an unfamiliar system. You may use AI tools during the assignment. Briefly indicate how you used them and describe at least one AI-generated suggestion or conclusion that you verified, corrected, or rejected , and explain why. Duration 6 months Location Paris, France. 🟢 Protections against dynamic attacks for firmware Description If you like playing cat and mouse and getting your hands dirty, this internship is for you! At Quarkslab, we have been developing application protection tools since 2014, featuring obfuscation and runtime application self-protection (RASP). One of these tools (QShield App Protection) relies on a compiler framework, LLVM, and comes as a replacement for the regular compiler used by our customers. While desktop and mobile targets have been supported for several years, supporting embedded targets is more challenging, due to the variety of situations. The goal of this internship is to ~~help the QShield team~~ improve ~~both~~ the level of protection for the IoT/embedded domain by developing sensors to detect dynamic attacks. For that you will need to reproduce the setup of attackers, analyze the weaknesses of the tooling they use, and develop proof of concepts to detect them or prevent their usage. You will then integrate them in our software protection tooling. Required Skills Have an experience in building a firmware or a static library for an embedded device, and playing with compiler options. Have some familiarity with either Arm32 or AArch64 instruction sets. Be able to demonstrate experience developing in C. Have an interest in compilers and software protection or security (you don't need to be an expert in compilation ;) ). What you will do During this internship, you will: research and develop detection or counter measures for dynamic tools/techniques used to reverse-engineer embedded software such as JTAG/SWD debugging, emulation with QEMU, dynamic instrumentation, etc.; integrate them into our coverage testing infrastructure which ensures that the sensors behave as expected in different environments; work on the integration in the development toolchains to improve the user experience. For that you will work with people with various skills, such as reverse-engineering, software development with huge code bases and testing them. Assignment Write a small bare-metal firmware for the Arm Cortex-M3 emulated by QEMU ( qemu-system-arm -M mps2-an385 ). You don't need any hardware. Use any Arm toolchain (e.g. Arm Toolchain for Embedded or the GNU Arm toolchain), but no vendor SDK, HAL, IDE or RTOS. The firmware must: use your own linker script and startup code (vector table, reset handler); print its output through the board's UART (not semihosting); determine whether it runs on an emulator or on real silicon , using at least two independent checks , and print the verdict and the raw values it observed. Send us a zip containing: the sources; a Makefile (or CMake) where make run builds and runs everything; the ELF; a report of 2 pages at most that: explains the boot sequence of your firmware, from reset to main ; for each check: what it reads, the value seen under QEMU, the value you expect on a real Cortex-M3 with a reference to the Arm documentation , and how an attacker could get around it; describes at least one check that did not work , and why; lists the tools you used, LLMs included, and what you checked yourself. This should take 3 to 4 hours. We don't expect a perfect detector: a check that fails, with a good explanation, is worth more than a long list of checks you can't explain. If you're selected, you'll run the firmware during the interview and we'll change it together, look at the binary, and discuss how to bypass your checks. Duration 6 months Location Paris, France 🟢 Development of tooling for fuzzing infrastructure Description Fuzzers produce a lot of output data and it can sometimes be hard to sift through the results. Furthermore, different fuzzing targets require different sets of tools which might not share output formats. To face this, you will implement an aggregator that defines a common format for integrating fuzzing results into a unified dashboard. On top of displaying fuzzing campaign results, the goal of this aggregator is to triage bugs for efficient vulnerability research. The methodology will be different for each bug class and target, so the system shall be modular to allow for the integration of different types of fuzzers on different platforms. Required Skills Proficient in C, C++ for analyzing code, experienced in python, js, or others for development work Deep understanding of fundamental bug classes in binary exploitation (buffer overflow, use-after-free, race condition, ...) Good communication skills Proficient in French and/or English What you will do Most of your work will be programming the dashboard with the help of LLMs when applicable. Alongside that, you will come up with ad-hoc strategies for automatically analyzing certain bug classes in a specific context and producing actionable insights. Assignment This assignment is mostly theoretical.and consists of two write ups: A 5 page (maximum) document describing the state of the art of binary fuzzers. In this report, include a comparison of the different fuzzing methodologies available and their use-cases. Pick any Android application that uses a native library to parse user-provided data, and write a small document on how you would fuzz that library. Duration 6 months Location Paris, France 🟢 Fighting Dynamic Binary Instrumentation Description If you like playing cat and mouse and getting your hands dirty, this internship is for you! At Quarkslab, we have been developing application protection tools (QShield) since 2014, featuring protections against static attacks (obfuscation) and dynamic ones. Among the latter, Dynamic Binary Instrumentation (DBI) frameworks such as QBDI , Intel Pin , DynamoRIO , WinDBG TTD and Frida have become foundational tools in software security, enabling fine-grained runtime analysis, tracing, and modification of program execution without requiring source code. While invaluable for legitimate purposes such as vulnerability research, malware analysis, and software testing, these same capabilities make DBI a powerful vector for reverse engineering, intellectual property extraction, and license or DRM circumvention when turned against commercial or sensitive software. As a result, anti-DBI techniques have become a critical component of software protection strategies. However, developing robust anti-DBI protections faces substantial technical barriers. DBI frameworks operate at a privileged level close to the CPU and OS, making their artifacts (timing anomalies, memory layout changes, code cache behavior) subtle and inconsistent across platforms and versions. The goal of this internship is to help the QShield team improve their current protections and develop new anti-DBI sensors. For that you will need to reproduce the setup of attackers, analyze the weaknesses of several DBI frameworks, and develop proofs of concept to detect them or prevent their usage. You will then integrate them into our software protection tooling. Required Skills Be familiar with reverse-engineering. Be able to demonstrate experience developing in C. Have an interest in software protection or security. What you will do During this internship, you will: research and develop detection or counter measures for DBI frameworks; integrate them into our coverage testing infrastructure which ensures that the sensors behave as expected in different environments. For that you will work with people with various skills, such as reverse-engineers, and the developers of huge code bases and their testing infrastructure. Assignment As a first step, you will develop a "hello world" Linux x64 binary that detects when it is being executed under this tracer . As a second step, you will assess whether your solution still works if the tracer is modified to hide or alter the artifacts you rely on (for example a string identification), and propose a more resilient detection mechanism. Expected outputs : A PoC in source code form (feel free to use the language you want), that builds cleanly on a standard Linux environment (dockerfile accepted), with no manual tweaking required. A write-up in Markdown explaining the choices made for the PoC and detailing the second part of the assignment. Duration 6 months Location Rennes, France

items.title: The Threat Hunting Flywheel: Why Threat Hunting Isn’t About Finding Bad Things
items.summary: Here’s a counterintuitive truth: the ultimate goal of threat hunting isn’t to find more security incidents—it’s to drive continuous improvement across your entire security program. We’re not hunting merely to find present bad; we’re hunting to decrease the probability of future bad. Think of it like debugging. You don’t debug just to find bugs—you debug to build better software. Each bug you find teaches you something about your system, improves your testing, and makes future bugs less likely. Threat hunting works the same way. The Cyclical Nature of Threat Hunting Every threat hunting framework can be thought of as a cycle that improves with every revolution. Step 1: Determine Your Focus The biggest challenge in threat hunting? Answering this question: “Where do we even start?” You can’t just randomly poke around in logs hoping to find something interesting. You need a method to focus your efforts. The good news is that there are several effective approaches, and you don’t have to pick just one. In fact, most mature programs blend approaches over time. Hypothesis-driven hunting starts with an educated guess, perhaps informed by the latest threat intelligence. Maybe something like, “I bet adversaries are using scheduled tasks for persistence on our web servers.” Baseline hunting flips the question entirely: instead of rooting around for specific threats, you map what “normal” looks like in your environment, then investigate anything that doesn’t fit the pattern. Statistical analysis tools like RITA let you approach those patterns from yet another angle. They surface statistically weird behaviors and connections, giving you a prioritized list of anomalies to consider and maybe investigate. Machine learning models can highlight specific events that deviate from learned baselines, essentially saying “start here” with confidence scores attached. Step 2: Investigation The real detective work happens here. Investigation is iterative and rarely linear. You start broad, progressively narrow your focus by filtering out known-good activity, and follow interesting patterns wherever they lead. One scheduled task leads to a user account, which leads to authentication logs, which leads to source IPs, which leads to ... you get it. The “art” is knowing which threads to pull and which to drop. Something can be technically anomalous but contextually benign, like a DBA running weird queries at 2 AM because production is on fire. Step 3: Discovery and Analysis Eventually you reach a conclusion. Maybe you found a threat. Awesome! Now hand it to incident response. But maybe, or most likely in fact, you found nothing… Here’s the critical mindset shift: finding nothing isn’t failure. It’s validation—discovery of a different kind, even. A thorough hunt might confirm that your defenses are working and that an attack isn’t happening (win!). Or it might reveal that a detection you thought existed doesn’t, or that it’s misconfigured and wouldn’t fire even if the attack happened (also a win because now you know what to fix). Approached with this mindset, any outcome is a win, and every hunt ultimately makes you more secure. Step 4: Knowledge Refinement and Improvement This is where threat hunting transforms from investigation into force multiplication. Everything you’ve learned feeds back into your security program: Create detection rules so you don’t have to manually hunt for the same thing again. Document baselines about normal behavior in your environment. Share knowledge with your team and the wider community (Document!). Generate new hypotheses for the next hunt (Back to Step 1...). Close visibility gaps you discovered. Measure and communicate your program’s value. This phase is what makes hunting a continuous improvement engine. Remember: You’re not just looking for today’s threats. You’re building tomorrow’s defenses. Every rotation improves your skills, the program, and the rotations themselves. items.title: Yandex outage: Data shows that instead of going dark, malicious bots went on the move
items.summary: Following reported strikes on Yandex data centers, claims circulated on the Internet that Russian bot farms and influence operations had been knocked offline. HTTP traffic charts showed steep drops, fueling speculation that the infrastructure damage had stopped these malicious actors. However, aggregate traffic metrics can easily mislead. There are two autonomous system numbers ( ASNs ) associated with Yandex: AS13238 is used by Yandex’s search engine, while AS200350 runs its cloud services. Using Cloudflare Radar and Bot Management data, we analyzed how these two ASNs were affected — and while both saw drops in traffic, they saw differing impact. Yandex Search (AS13238) : The drop in traffic consisted almost entirely of verified search crawlers indexing web pages, images, and site resources. Yandex.Cloud (AS200350): There was a decline in malicious activities like vulnerability scanning and probing, but high-volume automation did not vanish — it simply migrated to other hosting providers. While malicious traffic may originate from a particular provider, it does not necessarily tell us who is responsible for the traffic. Understanding why the strikes had little lasting effect on malicious traffic requires analyzing request behavior, rather than just overall traffic patterns. What happened: the effect of the strikes and pre-event baseline Between October 7 and 11, reported Ukrainian drone strikes hit three Yandex facilities in Russia, progressively knocking data centers and network capacity offline. As seen on Cloudflare Radar , this culminated in a near-total collapse of the Yandex network on October 11 when traffic plummeted to 99% below baseline for Yandex Search (AS13238) and 90% for Yandex.Cloud (AS200350). Despite a brief partial recovery, both networks remained disrupted through October 13, settling at 86-90% below normal baselines. (As of October 14 at 18:00 UTC, traffic is at 85% of normal.) A drop in overall HTTP traffic only confirms that the network went down. It does not reveal whether malicious or evasive bots were disrupted. Looking at the pre-event automation baseline, we can see that before the strikes, automated requests accounted for 36.1% of all HTTP traffic observed globally across Cloudflare's network, and 35.8% of traffic from Russian IP addresses . The outage had different effects on automated activity on the two affected ASNs because they served different roles. Yandex Search ASN (AS13238) is used for search index crawling. Cloudflare classified 99.5% of its requests as automated, and 93.6% of its bot requests as Verified . Our analysis showed that traffic from this ASN indexed pages, rendered pages, and rendered images, which is consistent behavior for a search crawler. The Yandex Search ASN supplied about 7% of Russia-origin bot requests, and just 0.05% of the global total. Yandex.Cloud ASN (AS200350) is a cloud-hosting network and carries a very different mix of automation. Approximately 95.0% of its scored requests were bots, but none of its observed bot requests were verified by Cloudflare. Yandex.Cloud’s bots looked more like software apps: nearly two-thirds of their requests sent data to websites, some identified themselves as JavaScript, Python, or Go programs, and a larger share went to software companies than Yandex’s search bots. The Yandex.Cloud ASN supplied about 2% of Russia-origin bot requests, and just 0.01% of the global total. Impact of the event on overall bot traffic "Bot traffic" refers to automated requests to websites on Cloudflare's network, such as crawlers and scripts, not necessarily activity on social media platforms. As Yandex’s networks lost capacity, their bot requests fell too. That was expected: nearly all traffic from Yandex Search and Yandex.Cloud was automated. While we saw the obvious drop in total traffic, we did not see any evidence linking a global disruption in malicious traffic to the drop in traffic from Yandex. Russia-origin bot requests fell roughly in proportion to the Yandex traffic that went offline, since most requests from those networks were automated. Date UTC+3 Global bot requests (% of all HTTP requests)* Russia-origin bot requests (% of Russia-origin HTTP requests) October 1–6: pre-event baseline 39.4% 50.4% October 7–8: drone strike on Sasovo 39.2% (−0.2%) 48% (-2.4%) October 9: drone strike on Kaluga 39.4% (+0%) 42.5% (-7.9%) October 11: drone strike on Vladimir 39.5% (+0.1%) 42.2% (−8.2%) October 12 39.6% (+0.2%) 43.6% (−6.8%) October 13 39.5% (+0.1%) 42.1% (−8.3%) * Radar reports global traffic by both total HTTP requests, and by HTML requests (an approximation of a page view). The above table reflects total request volume. Impact on Yandex Search ASN (AS13238): less search crawling The decline on Yandex Search ASN was almost entirely search crawling. Sampled requests showed that 78.1% belonged to verified YandexBot, 11.5% to YandexRenderResourcesBot, and 1.9% to YandexImages. Among websites and services, the industry segment that saw the steepest drop was Publishing and Newspapers, where traffic from Yandex networks fell 44%. Approximately 90% of pre-event traffic to news sites from this ASN was YandexBot indexing articles, with 40.5% of Cloudflare customers returning HTTP 403 Forbidden responses because the site owner blocked the crawler. When the Yandex Search ASN went offline, customers simply saw less indexing from Yandex. Impact on Yandex.Cloud ASN (AS200350): legitimate use and migrating malicious traffic Yandex.Cloud displayed a completely different profile. Following the reported strikes, bot traffic from Yandex.Cloud fell about 40%. Several attack-like categories showed especially sharp declines. For example, WordPress plugin probing fell 90% and scanner-identified requests fell 93%. Interestingly (and tellingly), Cloudflare customer blocks on Yandex.Cloud traffic also fell 70% during the event period, suggesting that proportionately less malicious traffic was even hitting the Cloudflare WAF from this ASN. Impact on business verticals Yandex.Cloud’s bot traffic is also interesting when segmented by top request destination industries: Destination industry Bot traffic pre-event Bot traffic during event (Oct 7-13) Change 4xx (client error) HTTP response status share: pre → event Computer software 24.24M 15.18M −37.4% 18.5% → 15.9% Gambling 23.01M 18.80M −18.3% 99.1% → 99.3% Media incl. adult 1.33M 223.1K −83.3% 82.0% → 61.8% Internet and telecom 524.2K 206.5K −60.6% 71.4% → 51.1% Travel / tourism 363.9K 158.1K −56.6% 27.0% → 12.3% Retail / wholesale 316.0K 167.7K −46.9% 71.0% → 55.9% Gaming / computer games 226.3K 63.2K −72.1% 51.4% → 9.2% Publishing / newspapers 90.8K 8.8K −90.3% 90.2% → 61.4% The majority of traffic from the Yandex.Cloud ASN fell into two industry buckets: computer software and gambling. The computer software bucket was predictable for an ASN meant to host third-party applications and software integrations. In fact, we even saw that api.cloudflare.com is a top hostname for Yandex.Cloud request traffic. An overall majority of that traffic succeeded (requests returned 200s) both before and during the event, pointing to legitimate usage. The gambling sector offers the clearest evidence that malicious automation relocated rather than disappeared. Nearly all of Yandex.Cloud’s bot requests were targeted at one gambling customer account, with traffic shifting among its hostnames. Immediately following the October 8 disruption, bot requests from Yandex.Cloud to this account dropped to zero. Simultaneously, identical requests began appearing from other Russian hosting ASNs, including Radist and Selectel. The incoming traffic maintained an identical fingerprint across providers: The same JA4 TLS client fingerprint The same uncommon request paths and HTTP headers The same custom User-Agent strings Overall, Russian bot traffic targeting gambling accounts remained essentially flat over the week, moving from 167.7 million to 170.1 million requests (+1.4%). The automation never stopped running; the operators simply migrated their workloads to alternate cloud providers once Yandex.Cloud became unavailable. Across most industries, the share of bot requests from Yandex.Cloud returning any HTTP 4xx response fell. This is largely due to a drop off in the attack-like traffic mentioned above. This, in combination with the gambling customer analysis, shows that malicious traffic that was sending requests through Yandex.Cloud simply shifted its “services” to other providers after the service disruption. Finally, when we analyzed social media traffic, we found no unexpected changes in traffic either from Russian-origin IPs (0.6% decrease in total traffic over the event period) or globally (1.2% increase in total traffic over the event period). We repeated the analysis on bot traffic hitting the “post”, “reply”, and “like” endpoints for a specific social media platform and similarly did not find an unexpected shift before or during the event period from either Russian-origin IPs (5.7% decrease in total traffic over the event period) or globally (1.1% increase in total traffic over the event period). Based on our assessment, the data does not appear to support the claims that the strikes crippled social media manipulation, though without further analysis with data outside of Cloudflare, we cannot conclusively say there is no connection. What the data told us — and what it didn’t When traffic from Yandex networks collapsed, speculation spread across the Internet that Russian influence operations and malicious botnets had suffered a crippling blow. Cloudflare data tells a different story: across Cloudflare's network, there was no evidence that the strikes knocked social media manipulation offline or otherwise disrupted malicious activity on the Internet. Instead, the data demonstrated: Search indexing dropped. The overwhelming majority of the traffic that dropped from Yandex Search ASN consisted of verified YandexBot crawlers fetching news articles and web assets. The main impact was reduced content discovery in Yandex Search. Malicious automation migrated instead of stopping. While vulnerability scanning and plugin probing temporarily dropped on Yandex.Cloud, high-volume operations quickly moved to alternative hosting networks. A network disruption means that specific servers stopped sending requests, but it does not mean an automated threat disappeared. Cloud workloads are portable, so when a data center goes dark or an IP prefix gets blocked, operators can migrate their scripts to another provider in hours. Our analysis here is a reminder that client ASN traffic volume is an unreliable proxy for interpreting automated bot behavior. Defending against automated threats requires inspecting request behavior, such as identifying shared JA4 fingerprints, monitoring anomalous request rates, and applying WAF rules to sensitive endpoints, regardless of which network the request originates from. Physical infrastructure is static, but malicious automation is built to move.

items.title: Penetration testing every deployment with AWS Continuum
items.summary: Most security tooling that fits into a CI/CD pipeline—static analysis (SAST), software composition analysis (SCA), and dynamic scanners (DAST)—flags potential issues from patterns and signatures. A flagged pattern shows you where to look; penetration testing is what confirms whether something is actually exploitable. That confirmation has traditionally come from a periodic, out-of-band engagement that runs on a schedule rather than on a deploy, so deploys between engagements reach production with that confirmation still pending. AWS Continuum for penetration testing (formerly AWS Security Agent) is a service that uses AI agents to find and confirm exploitable vulnerabilities in your running applications. In this post, we walk you through making it a post-deployment gate in your pipeline. The gate runs a penetration test that is automatically scoped to the change you just deployed , and it can block promotion to production when a finding is at or above a severity threshold you choose. Because each run tests only the change since the last passing gate rather than the whole application, it is fast and economical enough to run on every deploy. We give a high-level overview of the pattern, which can be applied on four major CI/CD platforms: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI/CD, Bitbucket Pipelines, and Azure DevOps Pipelines. We then provide a specific worked example for GitHub Actions. By the end, you will have a pipeline that deploys a change to a staging environment, runs a scoped penetration test against the deployed change, and promotes the change to production only when the gate passes. The following diagram shows the end-to-end flow. Your CI/CD pipeline deploys to staging, then the pentest gate step authenticates to your AWS account through OpenID Connect (OIDC) and calls Continuum for penetration testing, which runs the scoped test against the staging environment. The gate waits for the result, reports the outcome back to your pipeline, and conditionally blocks promotion to production. All testing runs server-side in your AWS account, so no penetration testing logic runs on your CI/CD runner. Figure 1: Pipeline gate architecture: Your CI/CD pipeline deploys to staging, the pentest gate authenticates via OIDC and calls Continuum for penetration testing, which returns a scope decision that gates promotion to production. Why scoping to the change matters What makes the gate practical to run on every deploy is that it scopes each test to the change you just deployed. Continuum for penetration testing determines the commit range—the head is the commit being gated, and the base is the previous commit the gate already cleared—and tests only what changed. Testing the change instead of the whole application is what keeps a per-deploy penetration test fast and cheap enough to belong in a pipeline rather than on a quarterly calendar. Each run returns one of three scope decisions: in scope (the change modified the attack surface—findings are evaluated against your threshold), scoped out (the change was within scope but nothing security-relevant changed—the pipeline passes), or scope conflict (the change fell outside the configured scope and was not tested—you choose whether that blocks). The Continuum for penetration testing console records the decision and the commit range on the Scoping tab of each run. When a gate blocks, you can see exactly why. For the full mechanics of how the commit range is computed and validated, see How the pipeline integration scopes the test . Because the gate blocks on findings that Continuum for penetration testing validated as exploitable rather than on pattern matches, a red pipeline carries a clear meaning: a reproducible vulnerability in the change, waiting to be fixed before promotion. Setting up the gate The gate takes three steps to set up: configure a penetration test, create an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that your pipeline can assume, and add the gate step to your pipeline. Before you start, you need an AWS account with permission to create both an IAM OIDC identity provider and an IAM role, and a staging environment the penetration test can reach. Step 1: Configure the penetration test Complete the one-time setup described in Before you start : verify your target domain, create a penetration test in your Agent Space, enable CI/CD mode, and connect your repository. Note the Agent Space ID (as-…) and penetration test ID (pt-…), because you pass both to the gate step in Step 3. The pipeline tests whatever this penetration test is configured to test, so its target and scope set what the gate covers. Step 2: Create the IAM role Authentication uses OIDC federation rather than stored keys. Your CI/CD provider issues a short-lived token identifying the pipeline, and AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) exchanges it for temporary credentials when the pipeline assumes an IAM role you create. There are no long-lived AWS access keys to store as CI/CD variables, which removes the credential most often leaked from a pipeline. The security of the gate rests on two policies: the IAM role’s trust policy (which pipelines can assume the role) and its permissions policy (what the pipeline can do once the role is assumed). For the exact policy JSON, the provider-specific OIDC URLs and audience values, and the sub claim format for each CI/CD platform, follow the reference in Scope the trust policy to your pipeline and Grant least-privilege permissions . The following judgment calls help you decide how to scope these policies. How tightly to scope the trust policy is the first decision. Pinning the sub claim to a single branch (for example, main ) is the right default when a branch is the only one that deploys through this pipeline. If several branches or environments legitimately run the gate, scope to the environment instead of the branch where your provider’s claim supports it—and remember that not every provider carries a branch in the claim at all. On Bitbucket, the repository (and optionally a deployment environment) is as tight as it gets. Start as narrow as your deployment reality allows and widen only when a real branch or environment needs it. Note that GitHub repositories created or renamed on or after July 15, 2026 emit an immutable sub claim with numeric IDs—confirm the exact sub your pipeline emits before you write the policy. Step 3: Add the gate step to your pipeline The step is the same idea on every provider—the syntax differs. Pin the integration to an immutable version (a release tag, commit SHA, or pinned component version) so an upstream change can’t alter what runs in your pipeline. For the full settings reference and defaults table, see Defaults the integration ships with . Before relying on the gate, run it once in dry-run mode . A dry run checks authentication, the Region, and that your repository resolves—without starting a scoped penetration test job. If validation fails, the step fails regardless of your error-handling settings, so a misconfiguration surfaces immediately. A worked example: GitHub Actions The following workflow shows the three-job topology that makes the gate work: deploy deploys to staging, security-pentest runs the gate, and deploy-prod promotes to production. Because deploy-prod declares needs: [security-pentest] , GitHub skips production whenever the gate fails. Note: The tutorials use an application with a deliberate SQL injection so the gate has a real finding to block on. Deploy it only to an isolated, non-production environment and remove it when you finish. jobs: deploy: runs-on: ubuntu-latest environment: staging steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 with: persist-credentials: false - run: ./deploy.sh staging security-pentest: needs: [deploy] runs-on: ubuntu-latest permissions: id-token: write contents: write actions: read deployments: read steps: - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4 with: role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/my-pentest-gate-role aws-region: us-west-2 role-duration-seconds: 7200 - uses: aws-actions/aws-continuum-run-pentest@v1 with: agent-space-id: as-xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx pentest-id: pt-xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx severity-threshold: HIGH on-scope-conflict: block timeout-minutes: "45" deploy-prod: needs: [security-pentest] runs-on: ubuntu-latest environment: production steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 with: persist-credentials: false - run: ./deploy.sh production Replace the account ID, role name, Region, and the as-/pt- identifiers with your own values. Two things in this example deserve attention. First, the contents: write permission lets the gate advance the baseline marker it keeps as a ref in your repository—without write access, every run would test a wider range than intended. Second, the role-duration-seconds: 7200 on the credential step must outlast the penetration test; AWS STS rejects a request for more than the role allows rather than reducing it, so set the role’s maximum session duration to at least (timeout + 10) x 60 seconds. A credential that expires partway through makes an otherwise-healthy run fail as though the service were at fault and leaves the cleanup unable to stop the abandoned, still-running job. The full step-by-step tutorials for all four providers are linked at the end of this post. Rolling out the gate: from report-only to blocking The single most important detail before you roll this out. Three independent settings decide whether the step fails, and each covers a different outcome: severity-threshold (what happens to findings), on-scope-conflict (what happens when the change wasn’t tested), and fail-on-infrastructure-error (what happens when the job couldn’t run). They are independent—relaxing one does not affect the others. Most teams introduce the gate in report-only mode first—set threshold to NONE so the test runs and publishes findings without blocking anyone’s pipeline. Watch what it finds for a release or two, then tighten the threshold to HIGH . This staged rollout is sound, with one critical caveat: A run that passes—including a report-only run—advances the baseline. The commits in that run’s range are then recorded as cleared and will not be re-tested when you later tighten the threshold. If you run report-only for a month and then switch to HIGH , the gate only assesses commits after the last report-only run—it does not go back and recheck what it already reported on. This is by design: relaxing a setting is you accepting the outcome it allows. But if you want a stricter setting to reassess a range an earlier run cleared, override the head and base commit SHAs by setting base-commit-sha and head-commit-sha . Where the marker lives differs by provider; see What advances the baseline, and why that matters for the full matrix. One default also deserves attention: fail-on-infrastructure-error ships as false (fail-open) . For pipelines where promotion requires security sign-off, set it to true from the start. GitLab: your committed settings are defaults, not a contract On GitLab CI/CD, a pipeline variable overrides the value a job sets in its own variables: block. That means anyone who can run a pipeline could supply a variable that lowers the threshold, turns on dry-run, or relaxes error handling—and the gate does what the variable says, not what your .gitlab-ci.yml says. Restrict who may override variables in your project’s CI/CD settings before you rely on the gate to hold a release. Protecting credentials on the runner The temporary credentials and OIDC token are sensitive for the duration of the step. Three practices matter: Keep debug and verbose tracing off for steps that handle credentials—shell-trace modes (for example, GitLab CI’s CI_DEBUG_TRACE ) echo command arguments to the job log in plaintext. Don’t persist source control credentials in the workspace —set persist-credentials: false on the checkout step so a token isn’t written to the runner’s .git configuration where a later step could read it. Don’t expose the token to untrusted steps —grant OIDC-token permission only to the jobs that need it, and don’t run untrusted code (such as a fork build) in a job that can read the token. Taking this to production and multiple accounts The example uses one account for clarity. In practice, your staging and production environments are often separate AWS accounts. The pattern extends cleanly: Create the pentest-gate IAM role in the account where the penetration test and Agent Space live—the security account. Your pipeline assumes that role via OIDC regardless of which workload account it deploys to, so you keep one well-scoped gate role rather than a copy or a set of long-lived keys in every account. Run the gate against each pre-production environment you promote through, and gate promotion to the next stage on its result. Because the baseline advances only on a passing gate, coverage stays continuous across deploys. Set fail-on-infrastructure-error to true and restrict who can override pipeline variables once the gate is holding real releases. Pin the integration version so upstream changes are reviewed before they run. For broader guidance of AWS Security Agent—testing against non-production environments, validating AI-generated findings, and IAM—see Security best practices for AWS Continuum . Cleanup If you followed one of the provider tutorials to try the gate, complete its Clean up section to remove everything it had you create: the sample application’s staging environment, the IAM role and OIDC identity provider, and—if you created one specifically for the walkthrough—the penetration test (and dedicated Agent Spaces) in the Continuum for penetration testing console. Removing them avoids ongoing charges and takes the intentionally vulnerable sample application offline. Conclusion Scoping penetration tests to the deployed change is what makes them practical as a per-deploy gate rather than a quarterly exercise. The key decisions you now have are: How strict : Start report-only ( NONE ), but know the baseline advances—delete the marker when you tighten. How to fail : Set fail-on-infrastructure-error to true for anything that requires security sign-off. How to scope trust : Pin the sub claim as narrowly as your deployment reality allows. Where to put the role : One role in a security account, assumed from workloads pipeline via OIDC. To build the gate end to end on your platform, follow the worked tutorial for your provider: Tutorial: Gate a GitHub Actions deployment with a scoped penetration test Tutorial: Gate a GitLab CI/CD deployment with a scoped penetration test Tutorial: Gate a Bitbucket Pipelines deployment with a scoped penetration test Tutorial: Gate an Azure DevOps deployment with a scoped penetration test For the concepts and full reference, see Run penetration tests from your CI/CD pipeline . Before joining the AI security space, Jigar spent several years building developer tools on AWS CodeBuild. He holds a Master of Engineering in Software Systems from BITS Pilani, India. items.summary_html:
Most security tooling that fits into a CI/CD pipeline—static analysis (SAST), software composition analysis (SCA), and dynamic scanners (DAST)—flags potential issues from patterns and signatures. A flagged pattern shows you where to look; penetration testing is what confirms whether something is actually exploitable. That confirmation has traditionally come from a periodic, out-of-band engagement that runs on a schedule rather than on a deploy, so deploys between engagements reach production with that confirmation still pending.

AWS Continuum for penetration testing (formerly AWS Security Agent) is a service that uses AI agents to find and confirm exploitable vulnerabilities in your running applications. In this post, we walk you through making it a post-deployment gate in your pipeline. The gate runs a penetration test that is automatically scoped to the change you just deployed, and it can block promotion to production when a finding is at or above a severity threshold you choose. Because each run tests only the change since the last passing gate rather than the whole application, it is fast and economical enough to run on every deploy. We give a high-level overview of the pattern, which can be applied on four major CI/CD platforms: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI/CD, Bitbucket Pipelines, and Azure DevOps Pipelines. We then provide a specific worked example for GitHub Actions.

By the end, you will have a pipeline that deploys a change to a staging environment, runs a scoped penetration test against the deployed change, and promotes the change to production only when the gate passes.

The following diagram shows the end-to-end flow. Your CI/CD pipeline deploys to staging, then the pentest gate step authenticates to your AWS account through OpenID Connect (OIDC) and calls Continuum for penetration testing, which runs the scoped test against the staging environment. The gate waits for the result, reports the outcome back to your pipeline, and conditionally blocks promotion to production. All testing runs server-side in your AWS account, so no penetration testing logic runs on your CI/CD runner.

Figure 1: Pipeline gate architecture: Your CI/CD pipeline deploys to staging, the pentest gate authenticates via OIDC and calls Continuum for penetration testing, which returns a scope decision that gates promotion to production.

Why scoping to the change matters

What makes the gate practical to run on every deploy is that it scopes each test to the change you just deployed. Continuum for penetration testing determines the commit range—the head is the commit being gated, and the base is the previous commit the gate already cleared—and tests only what changed. Testing the change instead of the whole application is what keeps a per-deploy penetration test fast and cheap enough to belong in a pipeline rather than on a quarterly calendar.

Each run returns one of three scope decisions: in scope (the change modified the attack surface—findings are evaluated against your threshold), scoped out (the change was within scope but nothing security-relevant changed—the pipeline passes), or scope conflict (the change fell outside the configured scope and was not tested—you choose whether that blocks). The Continuum for penetration testing console records the decision and the commit range on the Scoping tab of each run. When a gate blocks, you can see exactly why. For the full mechanics of how the commit range is computed and validated, see How the pipeline integration scopes the test.

Because the gate blocks on findings that Continuum for penetration testing validated as exploitable rather than on pattern matches, a red pipeline carries a clear meaning: a reproducible vulnerability in the change, waiting to be fixed before promotion.

Setting up the gate

The gate takes three steps to set up: configure a penetration test, create an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that your pipeline can assume, and add the gate step to your pipeline.

Before you start, you need an AWS account with permission to create both an IAM OIDC identity provider and an IAM role, and a staging environment the penetration test can reach.

Step 1: Configure the penetration test

Complete the one-time setup described in Before you start: verify your target domain, create a penetration test in your Agent Space, enable CI/CD mode, and connect your repository. Note the Agent Space ID (as-…) and penetration test ID (pt-…), because you pass both to the gate step in Step 3. The pipeline tests whatever this penetration test is configured to test, so its target and scope set what the gate covers.

Step 2: Create the IAM role

Authentication uses OIDC federation rather than stored keys. Your CI/CD provider issues a short-lived token identifying the pipeline, and AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) exchanges it for temporary credentials when the pipeline assumes an IAM role you create. There are no long-lived AWS access keys to store as CI/CD variables, which removes the credential most often leaked from a pipeline.

The security of the gate rests on two policies: the IAM role’s trust policy (which pipelines can assume the role) and its permissions policy (what the pipeline can do once the role is assumed). For the exact policy JSON, the provider-specific OIDC URLs and audience values, and the sub claim format for each CI/CD platform, follow the reference in Scope the trust policy to your pipeline and Grant least-privilege permissions.

The following judgment calls help you decide how to scope these policies.

How tightly to scope the trust policy is the first decision. Pinning the sub claim to a single branch (for example, main) is the right default when a branch is the only one that deploys through this pipeline. If several branches or environments legitimately run the gate, scope to the environment instead of the branch where your provider’s claim supports it—and remember that not every provider carries a branch in the claim at all. On Bitbucket, the repository (and optionally a deployment environment) is as tight as it gets. Start as narrow as your deployment reality allows and widen only when a real branch or environment needs it. Note that GitHub repositories created or renamed on or after July 15, 2026 emit an immutable sub claim with numeric IDs—confirm the exact sub your pipeline emits before you write the policy.

Step 3: Add the gate step to your pipeline

The step is the same idea on every provider—the syntax differs. Pin the integration to an immutable version (a release tag, commit SHA, or pinned component version) so an upstream change can’t alter what runs in your pipeline. For the full settings reference and defaults table, see Defaults the integration ships with.

Before relying on the gate, run it once in dry-run mode. A dry run checks authentication, the Region, and that your repository resolves—without starting a scoped penetration test job. If validation fails, the step fails regardless of your error-handling settings, so a misconfiguration surfaces immediately.

A worked example: GitHub Actions

The following workflow shows the three-job topology that makes the gate work: deploy deploys to staging, security-pentest runs the gate, and deploy-prod promotes to production. Because deploy-prod declares needs: [security-pentest], GitHub skips production whenever the gate fails.

Note: The tutorials use an application with a deliberate SQL injection so the gate has a real finding to block on. Deploy it only to an isolated, non-production environment and remove it when you finish.

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: staging
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - run: ./deploy.sh staging

  security-pentest:
    needs: [deploy]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      id-token: write
      contents: write
      actions: read
      deployments: read
    steps:
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/my-pentest-gate-role
          aws-region: us-west-2
          role-duration-seconds: 7200
      - uses: aws-actions/aws-continuum-run-pentest@v1
        with:
          agent-space-id: as-xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx
          pentest-id: pt-xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx
          severity-threshold: HIGH
          on-scope-conflict: block
          timeout-minutes: "45"

  deploy-prod:
    needs: [security-pentest]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - run: ./deploy.sh production

Replace the account ID, role name, Region, and the as-/pt- identifiers with your own values.

Two things in this example deserve attention. First, the contents: write permission lets the gate advance the baseline marker it keeps as a ref in your repository—without write access, every run would test a wider range than intended. Second, the role-duration-seconds: 7200 on the credential step must outlast the penetration test; AWS STS rejects a request for more than the role allows rather than reducing it, so set the role’s maximum session duration to at least (timeout + 10) x 60 seconds. A credential that expires partway through makes an otherwise-healthy run fail as though the service were at fault and leaves the cleanup unable to stop the abandoned, still-running job.

The full step-by-step tutorials for all four providers are linked at the end of this post.

Rolling out the gate: from report-only to blocking

The single most important detail before you roll this out.

Three independent settings decide whether the step fails, and each covers a different outcome: severity-threshold (what happens to findings), on-scope-conflict (what happens when the change wasn’t tested), and fail-on-infrastructure-error (what happens when the job couldn’t run). They are independent—relaxing one does not affect the others.

Most teams introduce the gate in report-only mode first—set threshold to NONE so the test runs and publishes findings without blocking anyone’s pipeline. Watch what it finds for a release or two, then tighten the threshold to HIGH. This staged rollout is sound, with one critical caveat:

A run that passes—including a report-only run—advances the baseline. The commits in that run’s range are then recorded as cleared and will not be re-tested when you later tighten the threshold. If you run report-only for a month and then switch to HIGH, the gate only assesses commits after the last report-only run—it does not go back and recheck what it already reported on.

This is by design: relaxing a setting is you accepting the outcome it allows. But if you want a stricter setting to reassess a range an earlier run cleared, override the head and base commit SHAs by setting base-commit-sha and head-commit-sha. Where the marker lives differs by provider; see What advances the baseline, and why that matters for the full matrix.

One default also deserves attention: fail-on-infrastructure-error ships as false (fail-open). For pipelines where promotion requires security sign-off, set it to true from the start.

GitLab: your committed settings are defaults, not a contract

On GitLab CI/CD, a pipeline variable overrides the value a job sets in its own variables: block. That means anyone who can run a pipeline could supply a variable that lowers the threshold, turns on dry-run, or relaxes error handling—and the gate does what the variable says, not what your .gitlab-ci.yml says. Restrict who may override variables in your project’s CI/CD settings before you rely on the gate to hold a release.

Protecting credentials on the runner

The temporary credentials and OIDC token are sensitive for the duration of the step. Three practices matter:

  • Keep debug and verbose tracing off for steps that handle credentials—shell-trace modes (for example, GitLab CI’s CI_DEBUG_TRACE) echo command arguments to the job log in plaintext.
  • Don’t persist source control credentials in the workspace—set persist-credentials: false on the checkout step so a token isn’t written to the runner’s .git configuration where a later step could read it.
  • Don’t expose the token to untrusted steps—grant OIDC-token permission only to the jobs that need it, and don’t run untrusted code (such as a fork build) in a job that can read the token.
Taking this to production and multiple accounts

The example uses one account for clarity. In practice, your staging and production environments are often separate AWS accounts. The pattern extends cleanly:

  • Create the pentest-gate IAM role in the account where the penetration test and Agent Space live—the security account. Your pipeline assumes that role via OIDC regardless of which workload account it deploys to, so you keep one well-scoped gate role rather than a copy or a set of long-lived keys in every account.
  • Run the gate against each pre-production environment you promote through, and gate promotion to the next stage on its result. Because the baseline advances only on a passing gate, coverage stays continuous across deploys.
  • Set fail-on-infrastructure-error to true and restrict who can override pipeline variables once the gate is holding real releases.
  • Pin the integration version so upstream changes are reviewed before they run.

For broader guidance of AWS Security Agent—testing against non-production environments, validating AI-generated findings, and IAM—see Security best practices for AWS Continuum.

Cleanup

If you followed one of the provider tutorials to try the gate, complete its Clean up section to remove everything it had you create: the sample application’s staging environment, the IAM role and OIDC identity provider, and—if you created one specifically for the walkthrough—the penetration test (and dedicated Agent Spaces) in the Continuum for penetration testing console. Removing them avoids ongoing charges and takes the intentionally vulnerable sample application offline.

Conclusion

Scoping penetration tests to the deployed change is what makes them practical as a per-deploy gate rather than a quarterly exercise. The key decisions you now have are:

  1. How strict: Start report-only (NONE), but know the baseline advances—delete the marker when you tighten.
  2. How to fail: Set fail-on-infrastructure-error to true for anything that requires security sign-off.
  3. How to scope trust: Pin the sub claim as narrowly as your deployment reality allows.
  4. Where to put the role: One role in a security account, assumed from workloads pipeline via OIDC.

To build the gate end to end on your platform, follow the worked tutorial for your provider:

  • Tutorial: Gate a GitHub Actions deployment with a scoped penetration test
  • Tutorial: Gate a GitLab CI/CD deployment with a scoped penetration test
  • Tutorial: Gate a Bitbucket Pipelines deployment with a scoped penetration test
  • Tutorial: Gate an Azure DevOps deployment with a scoped penetration test

items.title: CVE-2026-104935: Ivanti Connect Secure Zero-Day Exploited for Unauthenticated Code Execution
items.summary: Ivanti has disclosed CVE-2026-104935, a high-severity vulnerability in Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) that is being actively exploited in real-world attacks. The flaw carries a CVSS score of 8.6 and enables unauthenticated attackers to bypass authentication and execute arbitrary commands on vulnerable VPN appliances. The vulnerability came to light after Volexity investigated a compromised Ivanti Connect Secure appliance that was fully patched at the time. The previously unknown threat actor, tracked as UTA0576, chained the authentication bypass and remote code execution covered by CVE-2026-104935 with a separate privilege-escalation zero-day to achieve unauthenticated root-level command execution. The observed campaign demonstrates the security risks associated with vulnerabilities in internet-facing VPN infrastructure. After gaining root privileges, the attackers targeted credentials, Active Directory data, LAPS passwords, BitLocker recovery keys, and other sensitive information that could support lateral movement deeper into the victim environment. Ivanti confirmed on October 13, 2026 that it was aware of limited exploitation in the wild and urged organizations running impacted releases to act immediately. CISA subsequently added the vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Security teams can leverage SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to accelerate investigation of emerging threats and operationalize detection content across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments. Prime Architect can further assist detection engineers by transforming emerging threat intelligence into detection logic, hunting queries, and environment-specific rules, while Prime Hunt enables retrospective investigation across organizational telemetry. Contact Sales CVE-2026-104935 Analysis CVE-2026-104935 affects specific versions of Ivanti Connect Secure and combines two weaknesses used by attackers to move from an unauthenticated web request to arbitrary code execution in the context of the cgi-server account. The vulnerability is categorized as an authentication bypass by spoofing under CWE-290. According to Ivanti, the issue can be exploited remotely without credentials or user interaction and has a CVSS score of 8.6. Volexity reconstructed the exploitation chain while investigating an appliance running Ivanti Connect Secure 22.8R2.4, Build 19097. The device was considered fully patched when malicious activity began on October 3, 2026. Researchers started investigating the incident on October 5 and subsequently worked with Ivanti to analyze memory, disk images, and core dumps from the affected system. The first stage abuses request-routing behavior associated with the publicly accessible /dana-na/auth/url_default/welcome.cgi endpoint. Attackers can supply an X-DSCGI-PATH HTTP header pointing to a CGI resource that would normally require authentication. The security decision is based on the public URL while the header controls the actual script receiving the request. This discrepancy allows an attacker to route unauthenticated requests to protected CGI functionality. UTA0576 used this mechanism to reach wu.cgi, an upload handler containing the second vulnerability. The attacker submitted a malicious Perl script disguised with a .zip extension. The handler temporarily wrote the uploaded content to /home/runtime/tmp/ before checking whether the file was a valid ZIP archive. Although an invalid file was subsequently deleted, attackers exploited the short period between file creation and removal. Parallel requests referencing the temporary file through X-DSCGI-PATH allowed the Perl payload to execute before deletion. The initial payload launched Bash and then an encoded Python stage that existed primarily in memory. At this point, the attacker obtained code execution as the lower-privileged cgi-server account. To escalate privileges, UTA0576 chained a separate zero-day involving the privileged dsinvoked service and the DSCache configuration store. The attackers modified the in-memory copy of an Ivanti library, changed the configuration of a privileged maintenance task, and caused dsinvoked to execute attacker-controlled Perl code as root. After achieving root access, the exploit restored the modified in-memory configuration and library state. It also removed relevant entries from Ivanti debug logs and Linux audit logs, significantly reducing the forensic artifacts available on disk. This behavior is especially significant because Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool focuses on identifying unexpected file changes. Since portions of this exploit modify code only in memory and restore temporary configuration changes afterward, Volexity found that the attack could evade detection by the tool. The attackers also did not install a conventional persistent web shell or first-stage backdoor. Instead, UTA0576 repeatedly executed the complete exploitation chain whenever another command needed to run and returned command output directly through the exploit’s HTTPS traffic. Post-exploitation activity focused heavily on credentials and Active Directory. Volexity observed the attackers extracting credentials stored on the VPN appliance, querying Active Directory, searching for Windows LAPS passwords and BitLocker recovery keys, performing password spraying, inspecting authentication logs, and collecting LDAP traffic. The threat actor also used custom Python and Kerberos tooling to test credentials and access sensitive directory attributes. Files associated with reconnaissance and credential collection were temporarily staged under /tmp/ before exfiltration and cleanup. Attribution remains uncertain. Volexity tracks the actor as UTA0576 and assesses with low confidence that its motivation may be criminal rather than espionage. The researchers also assessed with medium confidence that the actor may have used large language models to assist with exploit development or post-exploitation activity, based on operational characteristics of the intrusion. No broadly available, validated CVE-2026-104935 PoC was identified in the primary sources reviewed at publication time. However, Volexity has published substantial technical detail about the attack chain, meaning organizations should assume that additional actors may attempt to reproduce the technique. For CVE-2026-104935 detection, defenders should monitor for high volumes of requests to /dana-na/auth/url_default/welcome.cgi, especially when the X-DSCGI-PATH header references another CGI resource or a temporary file. CVE-2026-104935 Mitigation Ivanti has released fixes for the authentication bypass and RCE components covered by the CVE. Organizations running affected Connect Secure releases should update immediately rather than relying solely on integrity checks. Ivanti’s October security guidance identifies fixed releases across supported branches, including 22.8R2.5, 25.1.1.2, 25.1.3.0, and 25.1.3.1 , depending on the deployed code line. Ivanti recommends moving to the 25.x branch as soon as practical because the 22.x code line is approaching end of life. The separate privilege-escalation vulnerability used in the observed three-zero-day chain was not yet fixed when Volexity published its analysis on October 13. Ivanti was preparing a patch for a future release. This makes installation of the CVE-2026-104935 fixes especially important because blocking the initial authentication bypass and RCE prevents attackers from reaching the stage required to exploit the local privilege escalation. Organizations should also continue running Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool, as recommended by the vendor, but should not treat a clean result as definitive evidence that exploitation has not occurred. Ivanti itself recommends combining updates and integrity checks with network monitoring, log review, access controls, and ongoing appliance validation. To Detect CVE-2026-104935 exploitation, defenders should inspect HTTP telemetry for mismatches between the requested URL and the value of the X-DSCGI-PATH header. Particularly suspicious values observed by Volexity include paths referencing wu.cgi or files under /home/runtime/tmp/. Security teams should also inspect /tmp/ for unexplained scripts or reconnaissance artifacts and investigate unexpected activity originating from the VPN appliance toward Active Directory, LDAP services, DNS infrastructure, or internal authentication systems. Known CVE-2026-104935 IOCs from the investigated incident include the attacker-controlled IP address 108.165.147[.]64, suspicious activity involving /data/.icscap/, and repeated requests targeting the exposed welcome CGI path. These indicators should be used alongside behavioral detection because attackers can easily rotate infrastructure or alter temporary filenames. Organizations that identify signs of compromise should conduct network and memory forensics rather than relying exclusively on disk-based examination. Credentials stored or accessible through the appliance should be considered potentially exposed, including LDAP service credentials, and should be rotated following containment. Defenders should additionally investigate Active Directory for suspicious LDAP queries, password spraying, access to LAPS or BitLocker recovery attributes, anomalous Kerberos activity, and lateral movement originating from the VPN appliance. Ivanti has disclosed CVE-2026-104935, a high-severity vulnerability in Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) that is being actively exploited in real-world attacks. The flaw carries a CVSS score of 8.6 and enables unauthenticated attackers to bypass authentication and execute arbitrary commands on vulnerable VPN appliances.

The vulnerability came to light after Volexity investigated a compromised Ivanti Connect Secure appliance that was fully patched at the time. The previously unknown threat actor, tracked as UTA0576, chained the authentication bypass and remote code execution covered by CVE-2026-104935 with a separate privilege-escalation zero-day to achieve unauthenticated root-level command execution.

The observed campaign demonstrates the security risks associated with vulnerabilities in internet-facing VPN infrastructure. After gaining root privileges, the attackers targeted credentials, Active Directory data, LAPS passwords, BitLocker recovery keys, and other sensitive information that could support lateral movement deeper into the victim environment.

Ivanti confirmed on October 13, 2026 that it was aware of limited exploitation in the wild and urged organizations running impacted releases to act immediately. CISA subsequently added the vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

Security teams can leverage SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to accelerate investigation of emerging threats and operationalize detection content across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments.

Prime Architect can further assist detection engineers by transforming emerging threat intelligence into detection logic, hunting queries, and environment-specific rules, while Prime Hunt enables retrospective investigation across organizational telemetry.

Contact Sales

CVE-2026-104935 Analysis

CVE-2026-104935 affects specific versions of Ivanti Connect Secure and combines two weaknesses used by attackers to move from an unauthenticated web request to arbitrary code execution in the context of the cgi-server account.

The vulnerability is categorized as an authentication bypass by spoofing under CWE-290. According to Ivanti, the issue can be exploited remotely without credentials or user interaction and has a CVSS score of 8.6.

Volexity reconstructed the exploitation chain while investigating an appliance running Ivanti Connect Secure 22.8R2.4, Build 19097. The device was considered fully patched when malicious activity began on October 3, 2026. Researchers started investigating the incident on October 5 and subsequently worked with Ivanti to analyze memory, disk images, and core dumps from the affected system.

The first stage abuses request-routing behavior associated with the publicly accessible /dana-na/auth/url_default/welcome.cgi endpoint. Attackers can supply an X-DSCGI-PATH HTTP header pointing to a CGI resource that would normally require authentication.

The security decision is based on the public URL while the header controls the actual script receiving the request. This discrepancy allows an attacker to route unauthenticated requests to protected CGI functionality.

UTA0576 used this mechanism to reach wu.cgi, an upload handler containing the second vulnerability. The attacker submitted a malicious Perl script disguised with a .zip extension. The handler temporarily wrote the uploaded content to /home/runtime/tmp/ before checking whether the file was a valid ZIP archive.

Although an invalid file was subsequently deleted, attackers exploited the short period between file creation and removal. Parallel requests referencing the temporary file through X-DSCGI-PATH allowed the Perl payload to execute before deletion.

The initial payload launched Bash and then an encoded Python stage that existed primarily in memory. At this point, the attacker obtained code execution as the lower-privileged cgi-server account.

To escalate privileges, UTA0576 chained a separate zero-day involving the privileged dsinvoked service and the DSCache configuration store. The attackers modified the in-memory copy of an Ivanti library, changed the configuration of a privileged maintenance task, and caused dsinvoked to execute attacker-controlled Perl code as root.

After achieving root access, the exploit restored the modified in-memory configuration and library state. It also removed relevant entries from Ivanti debug logs and Linux audit logs, significantly reducing the forensic artifacts available on disk.

This behavior is especially significant because Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool focuses on identifying unexpected file changes. Since portions of this exploit modify code only in memory and restore temporary configuration changes afterward, Volexity found that the attack could evade detection by the tool.

The attackers also did not install a conventional persistent web shell or first-stage backdoor. Instead, UTA0576 repeatedly executed the complete exploitation chain whenever another command needed to run and returned command output directly through the exploit’s HTTPS traffic.

Post-exploitation activity focused heavily on credentials and Active Directory. Volexity observed the attackers extracting credentials stored on the VPN appliance, querying Active Directory, searching for Windows LAPS passwords and BitLocker recovery keys, performing password spraying, inspecting authentication logs, and collecting LDAP traffic.

The threat actor also used custom Python and Kerberos tooling to test credentials and access sensitive directory attributes. Files associated with reconnaissance and credential collection were temporarily staged under /tmp/ before exfiltration and cleanup.

Attribution remains uncertain. Volexity tracks the actor as UTA0576 and assesses with low confidence that its motivation may be criminal rather than espionage. The researchers also assessed with medium confidence that the actor may have used large language models to assist with exploit development or post-exploitation activity, based on operational characteristics of the intrusion.

No broadly available, validated CVE-2026-104935 PoC was identified in the primary sources reviewed at publication time. However, Volexity has published substantial technical detail about the attack chain, meaning organizations should assume that additional actors may attempt to reproduce the technique.

For CVE-2026-104935 detection, defenders should monitor for high volumes of requests to /dana-na/auth/url_default/welcome.cgi, especially when the X-DSCGI-PATH header references another CGI resource or a temporary file.

CVE-2026-104935 Mitigation

Ivanti has released fixes for the authentication bypass and RCE components covered by the CVE. Organizations running affected Connect Secure releases should update immediately rather than relying solely on integrity checks.

Ivanti’s October security guidance identifies fixed releases across supported branches, including 22.8R2.5, 25.1.1.2, 25.1.3.0, and 25.1.3.1, depending on the deployed code line. Ivanti recommends moving to the 25.x branch as soon as practical because the 22.x code line is approaching end of life.

The separate privilege-escalation vulnerability used in the observed three-zero-day chain was not yet fixed when Volexity published its analysis on October 13. Ivanti was preparing a patch for a future release. This makes installation of the CVE-2026-104935 fixes especially important because blocking the initial authentication bypass and RCE prevents attackers from reaching the stage required to exploit the local privilege escalation.

Organizations should also continue running Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool, as recommended by the vendor, but should not treat a clean result as definitive evidence that exploitation has not occurred. Ivanti itself recommends combining updates and integrity checks with network monitoring, log review, access controls, and ongoing appliance validation.

To Detect CVE-2026-104935 exploitation, defenders should inspect HTTP telemetry for mismatches between the requested URL and the value of the X-DSCGI-PATH header. Particularly suspicious values observed by Volexity include paths referencing wu.cgi or files under /home/runtime/tmp/.

Security teams should also inspect /tmp/ for unexplained scripts or reconnaissance artifacts and investigate unexpected activity originating from the VPN appliance toward Active Directory, LDAP services, DNS infrastructure, or internal authentication systems.

Known CVE-2026-104935 IOCs from the investigated incident include the attacker-controlled IP address 108.165.147[.]64, suspicious activity involving /data/.icscap/, and repeated requests targeting the exposed welcome CGI path. These indicators should be used alongside behavioral detection because attackers can easily rotate infrastructure or alter temporary filenames.

Organizations that identify signs of compromise should conduct network and memory forensics rather than relying exclusively on disk-based examination. Credentials stored or accessible through the appliance should be considered potentially exposed, including LDAP service credentials, and should be rotated following containment.

items.title: NIS2 Part One: Why Your NIS2 Supply Chain Strategy Is Already Falling Short
items.summary: Tens of thousands of European organizations are legally accountable for the security of companies they do not control but on whose services they rely. Under Article 21(2)(d) of the NIS2 Directive, any in-scope entity is required to manage supply chain security, including the security aspects of its relationships with its direct suppliers and service providers. Article 21(3) further specifies that an organization must take each supplier’s specific vulnerabilities into account.
