items.title: CVE-2026-96951: Actively Exploited Windows Shell Zero-Day Bypasses Mark of the Web
items.summary: Microsoft has patched CVE-2026-96951, a high-severity Windows Shell security feature bypass vulnerability that is already being exploited in real-world attacks. The flaw carries a CVSS score of 8.8 and allows an unauthenticated attacker to evade Mark of the Web (MOTW) protections by convincing a victim to interact with a specially crafted file. The zero-day was addressed as part of Microsoft’s October 2026 Patch Tuesday, an unusually large security release covering more than 1,400 vulnerabilities across Windows, Office, SharePoint Server, SQL Server, developer tools, and other Microsoft products. CVE-2026-96951 stands out because Microsoft has confirmed active exploitation in the wild. Mark of the Web is a fundamental Windows security mechanism that marks files originating from potentially untrusted locations such as the internet or email. Windows and applications can use this information to display security warnings, activate Protected View, or apply additional restrictions before potentially dangerous content executes. A vulnerability capable of bypassing this protection can therefore weaken several layers of defense commonly relied upon to mitigate phishing and malicious file delivery. Security teams can strengthen defenses against emerging exploitation with SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform, which enables organizations to operationalize threat intelligence and apply relevant detection content across their security stack. Prime Architect can further accelerate detection engineering by helping defenders research emerging threats, generate and refine detection logic, convert indicators into hunting queries, and adapt detections to organizational telemetry. Contact Sales CVE-2026-96951 analysis CVE-2026-96951 affects Windows Shell and results from improper neutralization of special elements used in a command, categorized as CWE-77 Command Injection. Microsoft describes the vulnerability as allowing an unauthorized attacker to bypass a security feature over a network. Microsoft assigned the flaw a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.8 with the vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H. This means exploitation can originate remotely, requires low attack complexity and no prior privileges, but depends on user interaction. Successful exploitation can have a high potential impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability. The security control at risk is Mark of the Web. When Windows receives a file from the internet or another untrusted source, MOTW metadata normally signals that the file originated outside the trusted environment. Windows security features and applications can then apply additional protections before opening or executing it. According to Microsoft, successful exploitation allows an attacker to evade these MOTW defenses. In an email or instant-messaging scenario, an attacker could send a specially crafted malicious file and persuade the target to open it. Alternatively, a threat actor could lure the victim to an attacker-controlled website and convince them to download & view malicious content. The attacker cannot force the victim to open the malicious content automatically. User interaction remains necessary, which makes phishing, social engineering, malicious attachments, and deceptive links likely delivery paths. The CVE record identifies a broad range of affected Windows environments, including Windows 10, multiple Windows 11 releases, and Windows Server editions from Server 2012 R2 through Server 2025. Microsoft’s record also lists Outlook.com as affected before the corresponding service-side fix. The vulnerability is especially relevant to enterprise environments because bypassing MOTW can undermine security layers intended to stop files delivered through phishing campaigns. Once a malicious file avoids expected warnings or restrictions, additional payload execution may become easier, depending on the content and subsequent attack chain. Microsoft confirmed that attackers were already exploiting the vulnerability before patches became publicly available, making it a zero-day. However, the company has not disclosed who is responsible for the attacks, which organizations were targeted, or the exact exploitation chain used in observed incidents. Microsoft credited Riku Bamba and Yuya Chudo of Fujitsu, Benoit Sevens using Claude with Anthropic, and security researcher yhw with reporting the vulnerability. The precise original discovery date has not been publicly disclosed. At the time of writing, the primary sources reviewed do not document a publicly available CVE-2026-96951 PoC. Nevertheless, confirmed exploitation significantly raises the urgency of patching even without public exploit code. For CVE-2026-96951 detection, defenders should monitor suspicious files originating from email, messaging platforms, browsers, and user download directories, particularly when subsequent activity indicates that normal MOTW protections may not have been applied. Potential behavioral signals can include unexpected child processes spawned by Windows Explorer or document-processing applications, script interpreters launched from downloaded content, abnormal execution from temporary or user-writable directories, and post-delivery activity inconsistent with the expected file type. CVE-2026-96951 Mitigation Microsoft addressed the vulnerability through its October 13, 2026 security updates. Organizations should prioritize deployment across supported Windows endpoints and servers, particularly systems exposed to email attachments, instant messaging, web downloads, and other common phishing delivery vectors. The CVE record lists patched build thresholds across affected platforms. Examples include Windows 11 23H2 build 22631.7652, Windows 11 24H2 build 26100.9711, Windows 11 25H2 build 26200.9711, and Windows Server 2025 build 26100.33650. Administrators should rely on Microsoft’s Security Update Guide and Windows Update mechanisms to determine the appropriate update for each supported operating system. Because active exploitation has already been confirmed, CISA added CVE-2026-96951 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 13, 2026, with a remediation deadline of October 16 for applicable U.S. federal civilian agencies. CISA characterizes exploitation as active and the potential technical impact as total. Organizations should not treat user awareness or MOTW itself as sufficient compensating controls for unpatched systems because the vulnerability specifically defeats that security boundary. Additional protections such as application control, attack surface reduction policies, email attachment filtering, endpoint protection, and restrictions on executable or script content from user-writable locations can provide defense in depth. To Detect CVE-2026-96951 exploitation, defenders should correlate suspicious file-delivery events with subsequent process activity and determine whether content obtained from an external source executed without the expected MOTW-related controls. Email gateway, browser, Windows process creation, PowerShell, script interpreter, and endpoint telemetry can provide useful context. Security teams should also retrospectively investigate potentially suspicious attachments or downloads observed before patch deployment. Since Microsoft has not publicly disclosed attack-specific CVE-2026-96951 IOCs such as file hashes, domains, or IP addresses tied to the observed exploitation, behavioral detection and attack-chain correlation are currently more reliable than static indicator matching. Organizations that identify suspicious activity should isolate affected endpoints, investigate payload execution and persistence, inspect credentials accessible from the compromised user context, and determine whether attackers established additional access after bypassing MOTW. SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform enables security teams to accelerate threat hunting and detection engineering for emerging vulnerabilities, while adapting relevant detection logic to their SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments. FAQ What is CVE-2026-96951 and how does it work? CVE-2026-96951 is an actively exploited command-injection vulnerability in Windows Shell that allows an unauthorized attacker to bypass Mark of the Web protections. An attacker can craft malicious content and use social engineering to convince a victim to open a file or visit attacker-controlled content. Successful exploitation causes Windows to fail to apply the security protections normally associated with files originating from untrusted locations. When was CVE-2026-96951 first discovered? Microsoft has not disclosed the exact initial discovery date. The vulnerability was publicly disclosed and patched on October 13, 2026. Microsoft credited Riku Bamba and Yuya Chudo of Fujitsu, Benoit Sevens using Claude with Anthropic, and researcher yhw for reporting the issue. What is the impact of CVE-2026-96951 on systems? Successful exploitation allows attackers to bypass Mark of the Web, weakening protections applied to files obtained from untrusted sources. This can help malicious content avoid expected warnings and restrictions and facilitate follow-on malware execution, credential theft, persistence, or broader system compromise. Microsoft rates the vulnerability at CVSS 8.8. Can CVE-2026-96951 still affect me in 2026? Yes. Windows systems that have not installed the relevant October 2026 security updates can remain vulnerable. The risk is particularly urgent because Microsoft has confirmed active exploitation and CISA has added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-96951? Install Microsoft’s October 2026 security updates on affected Windows systems without delay. Organizations should also strengthen email and web filtering, restrict execution of suspicious downloaded content, monitor unusual process chains following file delivery, and investigate potentially affected endpoints. Administrators should continue monitoring Microsoft’s advisory for updated details for CVE-2026-96951 as further information about real-world exploitation becomes available.

items.title: Multiple NGINX Flaws Let Remote Attackers Crash Servers and Execute Malicious Code
items.summary: F5 has disclosed three serious security flaws in NGINX Plus and NGINX Open Source that can let remote, unauthenticated attackers crash worker processes by sending crafted HTTP requests. In certain setups, the memory errors could also allow code execution, although F5 says that outcome requires Address Space Layout Randomization, known as ASLR, to be disabled or bypassed. All three issues affect the NGINX data plane, which handles user traffic, rather than its control plane. The flaws are tracked as CVE-2026-97205, CVE-2026-93479, and CVE-2026-15176. F5 published the three advisories on October 14, 2026, and rated every issue High at 8.1 under CVSS v3.1 and Critical at 9.2 under CVSS v4.0. The bugs do not make every NGINX server vulnerable by default because each one needs a specific software version and configuration. Multiple NGINX Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-97205 is a use-after-free flaw in ngx_http_core_module . It can be triggered when asynchronous file I/O, or AIO, is enabled and NGINX processes a Server Side Includes page containing an include virtual command. The worker may keep using memory after that memory has been released, leading to memory corruption or an unexpected worker shutdown. F5 credits security researcher Cyberlanc3r with reporting the issue. CVE-2026-93479 is a heap buffer overflow linked to the NGINX map directive and regular expression matching. The unsafe condition can appear when the root directive or an access-log format uses the map’s regex capture variables before the map output variable. A related path involves a non-cacheable variable used in a string expression. Crafted requests can then make a worker write beyond the allocated memory area and restart. F5 credits Matt Suiche of Tolmo and Mateusz Gierblinski for coordinated disclosure. CVE-2026-15176 is a separate heap buffer overflow in ngx_http_core_module . It affects a location block that combines alias with rewrite and a set or return directive that refers to $request_filename . The same risk can exist when $request_filename appears in an access log_format . items.summary_html:
F5 has disclosed three serious security flaws in NGINX Plus and NGINX Open Source that can let remote, unauthenticated attackers crash worker processes by sending crafted HTTP requests.

In certain setups, the memory errors could also allow code execution, although F5 says that outcome requires Address Space Layout Randomization, known as ASLR, to be disabled or bypassed. All three issues affect the NGINX data plane, which handles user traffic, rather than its control plane.

The flaws are tracked as CVE-2026-97205, CVE-2026-93479, and CVE-2026-15176. F5 published the three advisories on October 14, 2026, and rated every issue High at 8.1 under CVSS v3.1 and Critical at 9.2 under CVSS v4.0.

The bugs do not make every NGINX server vulnerable by default because each one needs a specific software version and configuration.

Multiple NGINX Vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-97205 is a use-after-free flaw in ngx_http_core_module. It can be triggered when asynchronous file I/O, or AIO, is enabled and NGINX processes a Server Side Includes page containing an include virtual command.

The worker may keep using memory after that memory has been released, leading to memory corruption or an unexpected worker shutdown. F5 credits security researcher Cyberlanc3r with reporting the issue.

CVE-2026-93479 is a heap buffer overflow linked to the NGINX map directive and regular expression matching. The unsafe condition can appear when the root directive or an access-log format uses the map’s regex capture variables before the map output variable.

A related path involves a non-cacheable variable used in a string expression. Crafted requests can then make a worker write beyond the allocated memory area and restart. F5 credits Matt Suiche of Tolmo and Mateusz Gierblinski for coordinated disclosure.

CVE-2026-15176 is a separate heap buffer overflow in ngx_http_core_module. It affects a location block that combines alias with rewrite and a set or return directive that refers to $request_filename.

The same risk can exist when $request_filename appears in an access log_format. F5 says a remote attacker can trigger the flaw without authentication, but the required server-side conditions remain outside the attacker’s control. The company found this issue internally.

The affected range is broad. CVE-2026-97205 and CVE-2026-15176 affect NGINX Open Source 1.31.0 through 1.31.6 and 1.0.0 through 1.30.5, while the older 0.x line is also listed for CVE-2026-15176. CVE-2026-93479 has a narrower open-source range of 1.31.2 through 1.31.6 and 1.30.0 through 1.30.5. NGINX Plus 37.0.0 through 37.0.4 is affected by all three bugs.

Related products, including NGINX Instance Manager, F5 WAF for NGINX, NGINX Gateway Fabric, and some NGINX Ingress Controller releases, are also affected.

Administrators should upgrade NGINX Open Source to 1.31.7 or 1.30.6. NGINX Plus users on the 37.x line should move to 37.0.5.1 or 37.1.0.1.

Fixed releases also include NGINX Instance Manager 2.24.0, F5 WAF for NGINX 5.16.0 or 5.14.2, NGINX Gateway Fabric 2.8.0, and NGINX Ingress Controller 5.7.0. Some older branches have no update, so F5 advises moving to a supported branch that contains a fix.

Where patching cannot happen at once, configuration changes can lower the risk. For CVE-2026-97205, F5 recommends disabling either AIO or SSI. Turning off AIO may reduce performance for large static files or media streaming under heavy load, while disabling SSI stops NGINX from processing SSI tags.

For CVE-2026-93479, administrators should replace unnamed regex captures with named captures and use them only inside the matching block. For CVE-2026-15176, F5 recommends avoiding alias inside a location block and avoiding $request_filename where possible.

Teams should first run nginx -T to review the full active configuration, including included files, then compare the installed build against each advisory. After any change, nginx -t can check the syntax before the configuration is reloaded. These checks matter because the presence of an affected version alone does not prove that the needed configuration is active.

The disclosure follows several other NGINX memory-safety fixes in 2026. Cybersecurity News previously reported three NGINX flaws involving heap overflow, memory disclosure, and use-after-free conditions and an earlier group of NGINX bugs that could cause code execution or denial of service.

F5’s advisories do not report active exploitation of these three newly disclosed flaws. Still, internet-facing NGINX systems should be reviewed quickly because a successful request can restart workers and disrupt service, while a working ASLR bypass could raise the impact to code execution.

Applying the fixed release remains the strongest response because the workarounds cover only the known unsafe configuration paths.

items.title: 24 Security Vulnerabilities Patched in curl Used Across 30 Billion Installations
items.summary: The curl project released curl 8.23.0 on October 14, 2026, announcing 24 security fixes affecting the widely used data transfer tool and its underlying library, libcurl. The vulnerabilities include credential leaks, authentication errors, command injection, and flaws that can disrupt applications. The release also removes SMB and SMBS protocol support, making compatibility checks important before deployment. According to security firm AISLE , it discovered 18 of the vulnerabilities announced with this release, representing 75 percent of the total. Its dedicated audit produced 24 CVEs across two releases, with six addressed in curl 8.22.0 and another eighteen associated with 8.23.0. Those figures describe AISLE’s audit findings, not the complete security count for either release. Daniel Stenberg Mastodon Post (Image Source: Aisle) curl Security Vulnerabilities One notable flaw, CVE-2026-86414, allows an HTTP proxy to trick libcurl into handing over credentials intended for the destination server. During a CONNECT tunnel request, the proxy can return a 401 response with a WWW-Authenticate header instead of the expected proxy authentication response. This can expose a Basic authentication password or a Negotiate/Kerberos ticket. The issue affects versions 7.10.8 through 8.22.0. Another vulnerability, CVE-2026-94266, can expose passwords through CURLINFO_EFFECTIVE_URL when curl obtains credentials from a .netrc file. The command-line tool can reveal the same information through its url_effective output variable. Applications that record these returned URLs could therefore place credentials in logs. Versions 7.62.0 through 8.22.0 are affected. These findings extend a recurring security concern around credential handling. Cybersecurity News previously covered a curl password leak involving redirects and .netrc files , where credentials could reach an unintended host under specific conditions. The official advisory for CVE-2026-87864 explains an IMAP command injection flaw involving message uploads and CURLOPT_CRLF. Curl advertised the original message size but sent additional bytes after converting line endings. A mail server could interpret those extra bytes as commands within the authenticated session. This concerns IMAP commands, not operating system shell commands. Importantly, this flaw was already fixed in curl 8.22.0, although its advisory was published on October 14. It affects versions 7.30.0 through 8.21.0 and carries a low severity rating. Avoiding CURLOPT_CRLF with IMAP is the documented workaround. Recently, cURL patched a 25-Year-Old Vulnerability with version 8.21.0. Other AISLE findings involve stale AWS signing headers, credentials crossing redirect boundaries, client certificate mix-ups, damaged cookie storage, and incorrect HSTS cache handling. Additional issues can cause an endless loop or exhaust the process stack. These failures often emerge when settings or connection state persist after the destination or identity changes. CVE-2026-86411 Reused FTP connection inherits a client certificate FTP connection reuse A transfer can reuse a connection authenticated with a client certificate from a previous configuration. CVE-2026-86412 Server-set cookie erases the cookie jar Cookie storage A server-provided cookie can cause stored cookies to be erased. CVE-2026-86413 Negotiate credentials sent to a redirected origin Redirects and Negotiate authentication Authentication information can reach a destination that should not receive it. CVE-2026-86414 Host credentials leaked to an HTTP proxy HTTP proxy CONNECT handling A proxy can obtain credentials intended for the destination server, including Basic authentication passwords or Negotiate/Kerberos tickets. CVE-2026-86415 Automatic client-certificate connection reuse mix-up Client certificates and connection reuse A connection can be reused under the wrong client-certificate identity. CVE-2026-87862 HSTS cache import drops a longer-lived child entry HSTS cache loading An existing child-domain entry with a longer lifetime can be lost during cache import. CVE-2026-87863 HSTS response erases persisted entries HSTS cache persistence Processing a server’s HSTS response can erase stored HTTPS enforcement entries. CVE-2026-87864 IMAP APPEND command injection during CRLF conversion IMAP uploads and CURLOPT_CRLF A mismatch between the declared message size and transmitted bytes can let extra bytes become IMAP commands in an authenticated session. This is not operating system shell injection. CVE-2026-92386 Server-set cookie aborts cookie-jar loading Cookie-file loading A server-provided cookie can interrupt the loading of stored cookies. CVE-2026-92388 FTP wildcard write callback mix-up FTP wildcard transfers Transfer data can reach the wrong application write callback. CVE-2026-92389 TFTP transfer direction confusion TFTP transfers Curl can confuse the intended transfer direction, causing incorrect protocol behavior. CVE-2026-92391 Recursive curl_mime_free calls exhaust the stack MIME cleanup Recursive cleanup can exhaust the process stack and crash the application. CVE-2026-94265 Authorization: Negotiate sent to a foreign origin HTTP Negotiate authentication An authentication header can be sent to a different origin that should not receive it. items.title: AI worms could spread across your smart devices, Anthropic warns
items.summary: Your streaming box might not look like much of a computer. But connect enough inexpensive devices together, and they can run an AI model. Researchers at Anthropic demonstrated this by running a Google Gemma model across 15 off-brand Android TV boxes. They warn that small models could soon spread across vulnerable internet-of-things (IoT) devices, including smart ovens and TV boxes, stating: “Our experiments suggest that small AI models may be months away from being capable enough to self-replicate on commercial internet-of-things (IoT) devices, like smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes.” In this scenario, AI isn’t simply helping an attacker write malicious code. It becomes part of the software carrying out the replication. Anthropic breaks that process into four stages: Find another device. Gain the ability to execute code on it. Set up the software needed to run an AI model. Continue spreading from the new host. The researchers tested whether AI agents could complete this sequence. They did not demonstrate a small model spreading and running independently on compromised household devices. The tests used Android emulators with unauthenticated debugging access, making it much easier for the agents to gain access than it would be on properly secured devices. Large file transfers and sustained communication between devices could make real-world replication easier to detect, while limited computing power could slow it. Crucially, the experiments did not demonstrate a model that was both capable enough to complete the replication process and small enough to run on the consumer hardware being targeted. Anthropic projects that smaller models could reach the necessary capability by the end of 2026 if improvement continues at its historical rate. Varun Chandrasekaran, an assistant professor at the University of Illinois, told AFP that the findings were consistent with related research but cautioned that Anthropic’s work had not been independently verified. He identified people using AI to improve attacks as the bigger current threat, rather than AI systems going rogue. Smart-device botnets are already a problem. Criminals hijacking connected devices is nothing new. Mirai and its descendants have recruited routers, security cameras, and digital video recorders into botnets used to launch distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, overwhelming services with traffic. BADBOX 2.0 illustrates another form of abuse: compromised consumer devices used for activities including residential proxy services, which route other people’s traffic through victims’ internet connections. Neither demonstrates autonomous AI replication, but both show that connected devices can become infrastructure for criminals. What you can do now The practical response is to reduce the opportunities for any attacker to misuse your connected devices: Keep operating systems, software, and firmware up to date to reduce exposure to known vulnerabilities. Buy from reputable vendors that provide ongoing firmware and security updates. A bargain device is less attractive if you cannot trust its software or obtain security fixes. Avoid unofficial app stores promising free streaming content. The FBI specifically flags these marketplaces in its BADBOX 2.0 guidance . Don’t disable protections to make an app work. Requests to turn off Google Play Protect are a warning sign, as are Android devices without Play Protect certification. If you notice something suspicious, disconnect the device from your network while you investigate. Put smart devices that are unable to run security software on a separate network isolated from your computers and phones, such as a guest network. Scammers know more about you than you think. items.title: How MSSPs Can Cut Tier 1 Bottlenecks Eating into Profit Margins
items.summary: As MSSPs take on more clients, alert volumes grow fast. Analyst capacity usually doesn’t. That gap shows up in triage and response first. Teams spend too much time checking IOCs, switching between tools, rebuilding context, and escalating cases that could have been closed earlier. Across thousands of investigations, those extra minutes turn into slower response, more pressure on Tier 2, and higher delivery costs. items.title: Warning: Phishing Attacks Are Using AI-Themed Ad Lures
items.summary: A phishing campaign is using AI-themed lures to target employees who operate advertising accounts, according to a new report from Island. The campaign is launched from a phishing platform that poses as a portfolio of AI advertising tools, using branding from Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Muse. The platform’s operator added a fake Muse Ads lure eight days after Meta launched its Muse AI agent.

items.title: Micropatches released for Windows Power Dependency Coordinator Elevation of Privilege (CVE-2026-69459)
items.summary: September 2026 Windows Updates brought a patch for CVE-2026-69459, a local privilege escalation vulnerability in Windows Power Dependency Coordinator, allowing a non-admin local user on the computer to elevate themselves to Local System. The vulnerability was found by two anonymous researchers who used it at the TyphoonPWN 2026 competition. Subsequently, SSD published a technical analysis of this issue, which allowed us to reproduce the issue and create patches for legacy Windows systems. The Vulnerability The vulnerability is a heap buffer overflow in the Component Resource Manager (CRM) state-monitor code of PsmServiceExtHost.dll. This module is loaded by Windows Power Dependency Coordinator running as Local System. A low-privileged local user can reach the vulnerable function through the documented power-settings API and overflow a fixed-size buffer, causing a memory corruption that can lead to arbitrary code execution. Microsoft's Patch Microsoft fixed this issue by adding a check to confirm that the length of a value provided by the caller exactly matches the expected length - and abandons the call if this fails.

September 2026 Windows Updates brought a patch for CVE-2026-69459, a local privilege escalation vulnerability in Windows Power Dependency Coordinator, allowing a non-admin local user on the computer to elevate themselves to Local System.
The vulnerability was found by two anonymous researchers who used it at the TyphoonPWN 2026 competition. Subsequently, SSD published a technical analysis of this issue, which allowed us to reproduce the issue and create patches for legacy Windows systems.

The Vulnerability 
The vulnerability is a heap buffer overflow in the Component Resource Manager (CRM) state-monitor code of PsmServiceExtHost.dll. This module is loaded by Windows Power Dependency Coordinator running as Local System. A low-privileged local user can reach the vulnerable function through the documented power-settings API and overflow a fixed-size buffer, causing a memory corruption that can lead to arbitrary code execution.

Microsoft's Patch
Microsoft fixed this issue by adding a check to confirm that the length of a value provided by the caller exactly matches the expected length - and abandons the call if this fails.

Be the Architect: Intentional AI Engagement for Cybersecurity Engineering
items.summary: TL;DR: How SpecterOps combined deliberate human engagement, model routing, and specialized tools to overhaul Ghostwriter’s user interface for $815.50 in model spend. Disclosure: SpecterOps participates in OpenAI’s Trusted Access for Cyber and Daybreak programs. Codex is the primary example in this article because it fits our engineering workflow and because of that relationship. The operating principles described here are vendor-neutral and can be applied to other model families and coding agents. AI access is not an AI strategy When organizations talk about using AI for engineering, the conversation often starts with the model: Which one is most capable? Which one is fastest? Which one is cheapest? Those questions matter, but they come after a more important one: How should people engage with the agent? Our answer is straightforward: be the architect. An agent can take on a substantial amount of labor. You can task an agent to explore a codebase, propose alternative solutions, implement a design, update hundreds of related components, and perform repeatable checks. But you should not transfer ownership of the problem to an agent. The human still sets the direction, establishes what success means, challenges assumptions, and accepts responsibility for the result. This is a leadership problem as much as it is a technical one. An AI agent is not a human team member: it does not share responsibility, understand organizational intent, or carry judgment from one situation into another unless that context is made available. Yet, some of the same principles that make delegation effective with people also matter here. Ambiguous direction produces ambiguous work. Missing constraints do not remain empty; the model fills them with a plausible interpretation. Incidental comments may receive more weight than we intended. Consider a deliberately silly prompt: “Beans. Beans. Beans. Write me a haiku.” The model will almost certainly write a haiku about beans. It has no reason to know the repeated word was an aside, a test, or irrelevant context. The same behavior becomes consequential when the subject is an application architecture, an accessibility requirement, a research hypothesis, or a security control. This is also why long-running chats can start to go off the rails; a comment or correction you made an hour ago for a different task may influence the next task in ways you did not intend. Prompt engineering, then, is not a search for magic phrasing. The human must begin with problem definition and proceed with deliberate and intentional expansion. Using an agent intentionally means deciding what context matters, what role the agent should play, what decisions remain open, and what evidence will be required before the work is accepted. Intentional engagement comes first At SpecterOps, we have been formalizing this with a framework called the AI Engagement Model , or AIEM, based on Mark Keith’s data science research at BYU. Its purpose is to make AI a force multiplier while keeping authorship, judgment, and understanding with the person responsible for the work. It begins with a simple premise: > AI performance is a function of the human, the model, and the workflow. AIEM follows a recurring loop: Frame, Challenge, Verify, Decide, Produce. We frame the problem and define success. We challenge assumptions and ask for alternatives. We verify claims and behavior. We decide which direction to take. Only then do we ask the agent to implement the work. The loop repeats as new information appears. Our role changes as we move through that loop. At the beginning of a project, we may act as the Problem Setter . We can ask the agent to become a Creative Expander when we need options or a Critical Challenger when we want to stress test an idea. Once the direction is clear, the agent can shift into an Implementation Assistant . Later, it can help verify the result. We choose the role that fits the state of the work. That choice also influences cost. Asking an expensive model to discover our goals, choose a direction, implement it, and judge its own success creates a long interaction shaped by assumptions we may never see. A mixed-model workflow can become just as expensive when every model is left to determine what the team wants. Clear framing reduces that uncertainty. Concrete success criteria allow much of the implementation to move to a less expensive model while reserving the more capable model for ambiguity, difficult diagnosis, and consequential review. Match the model to the work Our engineering guidance starts with the least expensive model that can handle the task. We escalate when the work shows us that we need more capability, then return to the economical tier when that need has passed. Starting too low creates rework. Starting every task with the most expensive model pays a premium for routine questions and clear changes. You must also consider reasoning effort, but don’t get caught up in these details. Reasoning effort is another routing choice that affects performance and cost. Higher effort can improve results when work requires more planning, analysis, or verification, although it also takes longer and consumes more tokens. Start with the model’s default effort and increase it when the task or the results justify the added expense. During the Ghostwriter project, Medium was a useful baseline and good for documentation, while High suited more involved engineering work. Extra High sometimes gave GPT-5.6 Luna enough reasoning time to complete tasks we might otherwise have routed to GPT-5.6 Terra. Treat reasoning effort as a tuning control alongside model selection, not as a substitute for clear direction. Effort levels like Max or Ultra should remain escalation choices. These unlock higher levels of reasoning or the ability to spawn subagents, and both can increase cost and how quickly you consume quotas. Names may change and levels may shift, so keep the approach simple: start with the model’s default and establish a baseline that produces reliable results for your usual work. Increase effort for difficult problems or when results suggest deeper analysis would help. Consider lowering it for straightforward documentation or simple changes, and reserve the highest settings for work that justifies them. Revisit the setting when the work or results change; you don’t need to tune it on every turn. For the Ghostwriter work described below, we used three GPT-5.6 models through OpenAI’s Codex agent with : State of the work Model choice Reasoning Effort Intended role A bounded question or clear change in a single file Luna Extra High Fast, economical execution A larger change with known direction and concrete success criteria Terra High Default engineering and implementation Ambiguous design, cross-cutting diagnosis, or consequential review Sol High Deeper exploration, challenge, and verification Note: While we were writing this article, OpenAI introduced the GPT-6 family without a Terra tier. GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6.1 Sol matches GPT-5.6 Terra’s input and cached-input rates while carrying a lower output rate, and in our early use it has handled work we previously divided between GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-5.6 Sol. OpenAI says the GPT-5.6 family will remain available during the rollout. The release made our exact pricing and cross-vendor comparisons age before we finished the article, reinforcing the need to track available models and route work deliberately as capabilities and economics change. Anthropic’s Haiku, Sonnet, Opus, and Fable models offer similar practical tiers, although the lineups no longer map cleanly one-to-one. The operating principles described here are vendor-neutral and can be applied to other model families and coding agents.

AI access is not an AI strategy

When organizations talk about using AI for engineering, the conversation often starts with the model: Which one is most capable? Which one is fastest? Which one is cheapest? Those questions matter, but they come after a more important one: How should people engage with the agent?

Our answer is straightforward: be the architect.

An agent can take on a substantial amount of labor. You can task an agent to explore a codebase, propose alternative solutions, implement a design, update hundreds of related components, and perform repeatable checks. But you should not transfer ownership of the problem to an agent. The human still sets the direction, establishes what success means, challenges assumptions, and accepts responsibility for the result.

This is a leadership problem as much as it is a technical one. An AI agent is not a human team member: it does not share responsibility, understand organizational intent, or carry judgment from one situation into another unless that context is made available. Yet, some of the same principles that make delegation effective with people also matter here. Ambiguous direction produces ambiguous work. Missing constraints do not remain empty; the model fills them with a plausible interpretation. Incidental comments may receive more weight than we intended.

Consider a deliberately silly prompt: “Beans. Beans. Beans. Write me a haiku.” The model will almost certainly write a haiku about beans. It has no reason to know the repeated word was an aside, a test, or irrelevant context. The same behavior becomes consequential when the subject is an application architecture, an accessibility requirement, a research hypothesis, or a security control. This is also why long-running chats can start to go off the rails; a comment or correction you made an hour ago for a different task may influence the next task in ways you did not intend.

Prompt engineering, then, is not a search for magic phrasing. The human must begin with problem definition and proceed with deliberate and intentional expansion. Using an agent intentionally means deciding what context matters, what role the agent should play, what decisions remain open, and what evidence will be required before the work is accepted.

Intentional engagement comes first

At SpecterOps, we have been formalizing this with a framework called the AI Engagement Model, or AIEM, based on Mark Keith’s data science research at BYU. Its purpose is to make AI a force multiplier while keeping authorship, judgment, and understanding with the person responsible for the work. It begins with a simple premise:

> AI performance is a function of the human, the model, and the workflow.

AIEM follows a recurring loop: Frame, Challenge, Verify, Decide, Produce. We frame the problem and define success. We challenge assumptions and ask for alternatives. We verify claims and behavior. We decide which direction to take. Only then do we ask the agent to implement the work. The loop repeats as new information appears.

Our role changes as we move through that loop. At the beginning of a project, we may act as the Problem Setter. We can ask the agent to become a Creative Expander when we need options or a Critical Challenger when we want to stress test an idea. Once the direction is clear, the agent can shift into an Implementation Assistant. Later, it can help verify the result. We choose the role that fits the state of the work.

That choice also influences cost. Asking an expensive model to discover our goals, choose a direction, implement it, and judge its own success creates a long interaction shaped by assumptions we may never see. A mixed-model workflow can become just as expensive when every model is left to determine what the team wants.

Clear framing reduces that uncertainty. Concrete success criteria allow much of the implementation to move to a less expensive model while reserving the more capable model for ambiguity, difficult diagnosis, and consequential review.

Our engineering guidance starts with the least expensive model that can handle the task. We escalate when the work shows us that we need more capability, then return to the economical tier when that need has passed. Starting too low creates rework. Starting every task with the most expensive model pays a premium for routine questions and clear changes.

We therefore cannot claim that deliberate engagement saved a specific amount or cut the bill by a particular percentage. Remaining the owner of the problem and the solution helped keep the model spend at $815.50 while producing an outcome we were willing to preview publicly.

The human labor involved was not free. During the core month, I spent roughly one to two hours per workday reviewing the agents’ work, testing critical workflows, and providing feedback—approximately 20 to 40 hours. Much of the agent work ran while I handled other responsibilities, which made it possible for one maintainer to direct the effort without devoting every workday to implementation.

Our estimate for a conventional implementation was two full-time engineers focused on the project for at least a month. Human engineers and agents would take different paths, so that estimate cannot produce a precise savings figure. It does establish the scale of the alternative we expected. Even acknowledging the human direction and verification involved, the combination of part-time oversight and $815.50 in model spend made a large, ambiguous UI overhaul economically practical for us, particularly for a free and open-source project like Ghostwriter.

These figures support a focused claim: intentional human engagement, deliberate model selection, and well-chosen tools allowed us to complete a substantial engineering task quickly and at a model cost we found remarkable. The result came from using the agents with purpose—planning the work, controlling the direction, and verifying the outcome—rather than simply allowing them to generate more work.

One rule for leaders

If an engineering leader asked for one rule their team should follow when using coding agents, ours would be this:

> Treat agents as delegated implementation capacity. You are still the architect.

That principle applies to commercial enterprises and government organizations alike. The operational controls will differ. A government team may need stricter authorization boundaries, data-handling rules, evidence retention, model-access controls, and approval gates. An enterprise may have more flexibility, but it still has obligations around sensitive data, production access, intellectual property, and release accountability. Neither environment can transfer judgment or responsibility to a model.

This guidance cuts against a common push toward greater agent autonomy and routine use of the most capable model. Strong models are most useful when humans make the problem and the boundaries legible. Clear leadership gives the agent room to execute while leaving implementation details to the agent.

We are beginning to see the same pattern beyond this project. People who have adopted the framework report completing the same work with no noticeable decline in quality while avoiding unnecessary model spend. We treat that as an early qualitative signal. A controlled quality study and company-wide savings benchmark remain for future work. Our prior baseline is weak because token cost was largely invisible to users. What we can say is that raising awareness of each model’s cost and providing model guidance has changed behavior without producing an obvious loss of capability.

Capability follows judgment

Model names, prices, and rankings will change. They changed while we wrote this article, and they may change again by the time you’ve read it. The need to frame a problem, challenge assumptions, verify evidence, make decisions, and own the result will not.

That is especially important in cybersecurity research and engineering. Sometimes the right choice will be an inexpensive model answering a bounded question. Sometimes it will be a frontier model investigating an ambiguous failure. Sometimes a specialized cyber model will be worth several times the price because the task genuinely requires it. Intentional engagement means matching the model to each of those states.

The Ghostwriter refresh succeeded because the human and agent roles changed with the work. We explored before we committed, made decisions before we scaled implementation, escalated when the evidence called for more capability, and verified before accepting the result.

The agent performed much of the labor. The human remained the architect and the problem owner.

The post Be the Architect: Intentional AI Engagement for Cybersecurity Engineering appeared first on SpecterOps.

items.title: Microsoft’s Recent Windows Updates Break Remote Desktop Services With Error “0xC000000D”
items.summary: Microsoft has confirmed a Windows 11 Remote Desktop issue that can prevent non-admin users from connecting to remote computers with Administrator protection enabled. The problem follows the September 22, 2026, non-security preview update, KB5124010 , or later updates. It mainly affects company-managed computers used as Remote Desktop hosts. Failed connections may return error 0xC000000D and display the message, “The token that was passed to the function is invalid.” Microsoft opened the issue on October 13 and updated its status to “Mitigated” that morning. A temporary workaround is available, but the company is still developing a permanent fix. Affected Windows 11 Systems Microsoft lists Windows 11 versions 24H2, 25H2, 26H1, and 26H2 as affected. Windows Server is not affected by this specific issue. The failure occurs when Administrator protection is enabled on the remote host, regardless of how administrators turned on the feature. This makes the host’s security settings an important part of troubleshooting. Support teams investigating matching failures should check the installed Windows updates, confirm the reported error, and review whether Administrator protection is active before making policy changes. These checks help identify computers that match Microsoft’s description of the problem. Administrator protection limits how Windows grants powerful system permissions. items.title: The Future of AI Cryptanalysis
items.summary: Matthew Green has been writing a rather pessimistic series of posts about the potential for AI systems to vastly outperform humans in cryptanalysis of both symmetric and public-key ciphers. I am more optimistic than he is. That is, I have stronger faith in the over-engineering cryptographers tend to do. I am trying to write this up in more detail.

items.title: Nearly Half of Organisations Report Unauthorised AI Agent Actions, Research Finds
items.summary: Nearly half (49.8%) of organisations have confirmed or suspected that an AI agent took an unintended, unexpected or unauthorised action in the past year, according to new research from Salt Security . The findings, published in the company’s State of Agentic AI and API Security 2H 2026 report, highlight growing concerns around the security of autonomous AI systems as enterprises increasingly integrate agents into everyday operations. Based on a survey of more than 380 security and technology professionals, alongside Salt Labs production telemetry from hundreds of customer environments, the research suggests that AI adoption is outpacing organisations’ ability to monitor, govern and contain agent activity. Among respondents who reported confirmed or suspected unintended agent actions, more than half experienced an unauthorised external API call or transaction, while over 40% reported an agent modifying or deleting data. The research also found that AI agents are now firmly embedded in enterprise environments, with 86.4% of respondents reporting at least one operating within their organisation and 59.5% running more than ten. Furthermore, 76.8% reported agents capable of chaining actions across other agents, tools and APIs, creating complex sequences that may not have been anticipated by individual teams. Despite this widespread adoption, visibility remains limited. Just 12.5% of organisations can consistently trace an agent’s complete journey, from its initial instruction through the tools and APIs it accesses to the final outcome. More than 60% would require hours or days of manual investigation to reconstruct an agent’s activity from the previous day. The ability to respond to unexpected behaviour is similarly concerning. Only 17.5% of respondents said their organisation could automatically stop an AI agent behaving unexpectedly in production. For the majority, intervention remains a manual process, potentially requiring an application to be taken offline. “The data shows a gap that is already producing real operational consequences,” said Roey Eliyahu, CEO of Salt Security. “Organisations are deploying agents and granting them access to enterprise data, APIs, and services before they can trace what those agents are doing or stop them automatically when something goes wrong.” Shadow AI Infrastructure and AI-Generated Code Raise Further Concerns The report also identified emerging risks associated with Model Context Protocol (MCP) infrastructure, which enables AI systems to interact with external tools and data sources. Nearly a third (32.9%) of respondents reported discovering an unauthorised, shadow or misconfigured MCP server in the past year, while 54.3% had either confirmed or suspected encountering one. Salt Labs’ own telemetry revealed that MCP-related infrastructure was detected in 21.6% of customer environments in August 2026, compared with 16.7% in January, representing a relative increase of approximately 30%. Meanwhile, AI-generated code is introducing additional application security challenges. Some 83.5% of respondents estimated that AI-generated or AI-assisted code contributed to at least some of their application security findings. However, just 6.8% reported resolving these issues directly within coding assistants at the point of generation, leaving vulnerabilities to be identified during subsequent code reviews, testing or after deployment. Recent Manus Vulnerability Highlights Agentic AI Risks The findings follow recent research from Salt Labs , which demonstrated how a single malicious email could be used to hijack the Manus agentic AI platform and potentially access a user’s connected email, cloud storage and code repository accounts. The attack did not require a stolen password or the victim to click a malicious link. Although the platform’s guardrails detected the malicious activity, they were unable to prevent the code from executing. The vulnerability was responsibly disclosed and has since been remediated. According to Salt Security, the incident demonstrates how traditional detection mechanisms may struggle to keep pace with autonomous systems capable of executing multiple actions before human intervention is possible. “The Manus research and this survey data are two views of the same problem,” said Yaniv Balmas, Head of Research at Salt Security. “In the field, we showed how an agent can be weaponised through a single malicious email, how the guardrail detected the attack at exactly the right moment, and still could not stop the code from running. The survey quantifies how widespread that architecture is.” The findings underline the need for organisations to strengthen visibility into agent activity, establish appropriate governance controls and develop automated containment capabilities as AI agents gain greater autonomy and access to critical enterprise systems. The full State of Agentic AI and API Security 2H 2026 report includes sector-specific findings, recommendations for CISOs and further analysis of Salt Labs production telemetry.

items.title: Cyberattack on Connected Fridges in France
items.summary: Another IoT cyberattack , this one in France: Hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units, forcing some to warm to 50C (120F) overnight, according to one supermarket chain affected. […] Normally, supermarket freezers go through a short period of defrosting overnight, in which temperatures rise slightly. But the hackers ordered the units to heat up and stay hot, although Danfoss did not confirm any reports about just how warm the fridges and freezers could become in that process. Danfoss said the affected cold units were older models whose security software could not be updated to ward off a risk they had identified. Any IoT device that can’t be updated is vulnerable. And, probably, any IoT device that can be updated is also vulnerable.

items.title: Hackers Use Fake WatchGuard VPN Download Site to Steal Login Credentials
items.summary: Hackers used a fake WatchGuard VPN download website to steal login details before offering visitors the real, digitally signed VPN installer. The attack collected a VPN server address, username, and password through a browser pop-up, leaving victims exposed without installing a malicious client. The campaign shows how a normal software search can lead to credential theft. Similar search engine poisoning attacks have pushed fake websites into trusted search results, making a high ranking a poor guide to whether a download page is safe. Researchers from Huntress identified the campaign while investigating an October 7 incident involving an administrator at a managed service provider. Their October 13 report described phishing, not a malware-laced installer: the theft happened inside the browser before the genuine software download. Hackers Use Fake WatchGuard VPN Download Site The administrator searched Bing for “watchguard vpn sll download,” then opened the fake website eight seconds later. Investigators traced the visit through Bing’s normal search-result redirect. That evidence supported search engine optimization poisoning, rather than a paid malicious advertisement, as the route into the trap. The landing page used WatchGuard branding, product information, and a questions section to appear useful. A download button led to a fake support page offering clients for different operating systems. End-to-end flow of the WatchGuard VPN credential phish (Source – Huntress) A footer called it an independent fan site, despite the download flow presenting itself as a support service. Selecting any download option opened a prompt requesting Server, Login, and Password. Those fields match the details needed for a normal VPN connection, making the request appear familiar. Earlier fake Ivanti download sites used similar vendor impersonation, although that campaign delivered altered installers rather than collecting everything through a browser form. The capture logic used roughly 150 lines of readable JavaScript. It placed the submitted values into JSON and sent them through an HTTP POST request to a separate collection server. Each submission included a label showing whether it was the first or second attempt. The script always rejected the first entry, cleared the fields, and displayed an “Incorrect data” message. This could prompt victims to correct a mistyped password or try another one, giving attackers another set of details. How the Credential Theft Worked Failed network requests only generated a browser-console warning, avoiding a visible error. After the second submission, the message turned green and a hidden link started downloading WatchGuard Mobile VPN with SSL version 12.11.5 from the vendor’s official content delivery network. Huntress verified that its digital signature remained valid and that the signed content had not changed. This differs from earlier VPN credential theft linked by Microsoft to Storm-2561, which used fake installers and malicious DLLs before directing victims toward genuine software. The lookalike domain for a routine VPN download search (Source – Huntress) Huntress did not establish that the same operators controlled both registrations of the reused phishing domain. In the investigated incident, browser history showed no download from WatchGuard’s delivery network. Huntress said this suggested the administrator had not completed both prompts, although a first submission remained possible. Managed Defender flagged the activity 21 seconds after the page loaded, allowing responders to provide remediation guidance before escalation. The lure domain was offline by October 13. Organizations should reset exposed passwords, treat submitted VPN server addresses as known to attackers, enforce multifactor authentication, and review unusual VPN logins. Staff should use bookmarked links to the official WatchGuard software portal rather than search results. A valid installer signature does not prove that the website supplying it handled credentials safely. items.title: Meta, Google, Microsoft and OpenAI Join Global Crackdown on West African Scam Networks
items.summary: Meta, Google, Microsoft and OpenAI joined an international crackdown on West African scam networks that removed more than 3.7 million Facebook and Instagram accounts, pages and groups. Announced on October 13, 2026, the operation led to 28 arrests and the rescue of 117 people forced to work inside scam centers. The United Kingdom’s National Crime Agency hosted the effort in London, bringing together technology companies and law enforcement partners from ten countries. The Joint Disruption Week began on October 6, with investigators sharing intelligence on operations in Nigeria, Ghana and other African countries, according to the Department of Justice announcement . Investigators from the Department of Justice and analysts at Meta identified scam networks and abusive online activity, not a named malware family. Neither organization’s published account disclosed malware samples, file hashes or an infection chain. The findings instead describe coordinated social engineering, fake identities and payment fraud spread across online platforms. Meta, Google, Microsoft and OpenAI Join Global Crackdown Meta said most removed accounts appeared to target people in the United States and United Kingdom using profiles that posed as American and British users. These removals extend the platform’s broader work on Meta’s latest anti-scam tools while taking away accounts that criminals used to reach potential victims. Microsoft suspended accounts suspected of links to the scams. Google and OpenAI also participated, although the announcements did not provide separate takedown totals for either company. OpenAI said it shared insights with partners and used AI to help identify scam networks across platforms. Authorities received leads on more than 30 suspected scam centers. In Sasaabi, near Accra, Ghanaian officers arrested 19 people and seized 303 electronic devices. They also identified 117 trafficking victims awaiting return to Nigeria and 89 fraud victims whose losses totaled about $8.3 million. Nigerian authorities arrested another nine people and seized 53 devices. The trafficking victims must be distinguished from suspects: Meta said people rescued in Ghana had been held against their will, lacked adequate food and suffered physical and psychological abuse. The latest figures add detail to earlier reporting on the Ghana scam center raid and underline why arrest totals cannot be treated as counts of everyone found inside a compound. People forced to send scam messages can themselves be victims of the criminal operation. How the Scam Networks Worked The networks used several fraud models rather than one technical attack. Investment scams began with fake romantic or professional relationships before victims were directed toward false investment offers, including cryptocurrency schemes. Other operations involved fake military identities, goods that never arrived and claims that criminals could recover previously stolen money. Law enforcement impersonation and digital arrest schemes used threats to pressure victims into paying. Job and task scams offered simple work but demanded fees or transfers from applicants. These methods rely on trust, fear and false authority rather than a disclosed software vulnerability. The technical response connected online accounts, web infrastructure, communication channels and financial activity. Silent Push said it mapped more than 35,000 malicious domains and nearly 700 communication channels tied to African scam centers, helping investigators link online operations to physical locations and operators. For readers assessing suspicious offers, earlier FBI warnings about fake work-from-home job scams explain why requests to pay cryptocurrency before receiving work deserve close scrutiny. The same payment pressure appeared among the fraud types identified during this operation. Industry partners identified more than $11 million in potentially freezable funds. That figure does not mean the full amount was frozen, seized or returned. Separately, Coinbase identified more than 65 active scam victims and stopped over $415,000 in potential losses before payments occurred. The operation shows why account removals alone are insufficient. Platforms can interrupt contact with victims, while financial tracing can expose payment routes and police can seize devices and arrest suspected organizers. Investigators now have additional leads, but the announcements do not establish that every linked scam center has been closed. Anyone targeted should preserve chats, payment records and transaction details to help investigators. Stop sending money, contact the payment provider and report the suspected online fraud. Avoid anyone promising to recover lost cryptocurrency in exchange for another upfront payment. The Joint Disruption Week began on October 6, with investigators sharing intelligence on operations in Nigeria, Ghana and other African countries, according to the Department of Justice announcement.

Investigators from the Department of Justice and analysts at Meta identified scam networks and abusive online activity, not a named malware family.

Neither organization’s published account disclosed malware samples, file hashes or an infection chain. The findings instead describe coordinated social engineering, fake identities and payment fraud spread across online platforms.

Meta, Google, Microsoft and OpenAI Join Global Crackdown

Meta said most removed accounts appeared to target people in the United States and United Kingdom using profiles that posed as American and British users.

These removals extend the platform’s broader work on Meta’s latest anti-scam tools while taking away accounts that criminals used to reach potential victims.

Microsoft suspended accounts suspected of links to the scams. Google and OpenAI also participated, although the announcements did not provide separate takedown totals for either company.

OpenAI said it shared insights with partners and used AI to help identify scam networks across platforms. Authorities received leads on more than 30 suspected scam centers. In Sasaabi, near Accra, Ghanaian officers arrested 19 people and seized 303 electronic devices.

They also identified 117 trafficking victims awaiting return to Nigeria and 89 fraud victims whose losses totaled about $8.3 million.

Nigerian authorities arrested another nine people and seized 53 devices. The trafficking victims must be distinguished from suspects: Meta said people rescued in Ghana had been held against their will, lacked adequate food and suffered physical and psychological abuse.

The latest figures add detail to earlier reporting on the Ghana scam center raid and underline why arrest totals cannot be treated as counts of everyone found inside a compound. People forced to send scam messages can themselves be victims of the criminal operation.

How the Scam Networks Worked

The networks used several fraud models rather than one technical attack. Investment scams began with fake romantic or professional relationships before victims were directed toward false investment offers, including cryptocurrency schemes.

Other operations involved fake military identities, goods that never arrived and claims that criminals could recover previously stolen money.

Law enforcement impersonation and digital arrest schemes used threats to pressure victims into paying. Job and task scams offered simple work but demanded fees or transfers from applicants. These methods rely on trust, fear and false authority rather than a disclosed software vulnerability.

The technical response connected online accounts, web infrastructure, communication channels and financial activity.

Silent Push said it mapped more than 35,000 malicious domains and nearly 700 communication channels tied to African scam centers, helping investigators link online operations to physical locations and operators.

For readers assessing suspicious offers, earlier FBI warnings about fake work-from-home job scams explain why requests to pay cryptocurrency before receiving work deserve close scrutiny. The same payment pressure appeared among the fraud types identified during this operation.

Industry partners identified more than $11 million in potentially freezable funds. That figure does not mean the full amount was frozen, seized or returned. Separately, Coinbase identified more than 65 active scam victims and stopped over $415,000 in potential losses before payments occurred.

The operation shows why account removals alone are insufficient. Platforms can interrupt contact with victims, while financial tracing can expose payment routes and police can seize devices and arrest suspected organizers.

Investigators now have additional leads, but the announcements do not establish that every linked scam center has been closed.

Anyone targeted should preserve chats, payment records and transaction details to help investigators. Stop sending money, contact the payment provider and report the suspected online fraud. Avoid anyone promising to recover lost cryptocurrency in exchange for another upfront payment.

  • CVE-2025-58360, an XML external entity (XXE) flaw in GeoServer's GetMap operation

CVE-2020-11899, an IPv6 out-of-bounds read in the Treck TCP/IP stack, drew far more exploitation attempts than any other CVE this week. The rest of the top five, in order: 

  1. A group of four Wind River VxWorks TCP buffer overflows: CVE-2019-12255, CVE-2019-12260, CVE-2019-12261, and CVE-2019-12263

  • CoinMiner: Linux cryptominers that hijack CPU and GPU resources

CISA's 14 ICS advisories covered 54 vulnerabilities, two-thirds of them rated high or medium. Toptech Systems and CISA itself disclosed the most flaws this week. 

Source: CISA ICS advisories analyzed by CRIL, Sept. 29–Oct. 5, 2026 · 54 vulnerabilities by vendor and severity

Combined with the XSS bug, it creates a realistic multistage attack path against devices that may be hard to inspect physically. Lantronix has published remediation details. 

CVE-2026-84411 — MikroTik RouterOS (Critical) 

CVE-2026-84411 is a critical integer underflow vulnerability in MikroTik RouterOS versions before 7.24. Updated versions are available from MikroTik's download page. 

CVE-2026-22755 — VIVOTEK Cameras (Critical) 

CVE-2026-22755 is a critical command injection flaw affecting 37 VIVOTEK camera models across its V, C, S, Dome, Bullet, and Panoramic series. VIVOTEK has posted an update package.

  • Critical ICS flaws in fuel distribution, cellular gateway, and camera products

  • Apply compensating controls, such as network isolation, for ICS products without available fixes

items.title: PoC Released for Linux Vhost Flaw Enabling Root Privilege Escalation and VM Escape
items.summary: A public proof of concept for Vghost, a high-severity Linux vhost flaw tracked as CVE-2026-74580, shows how the bug can let a local user gain root access or, in certain virtual machine setups, break out of a guest and affect the host. The issue has a CVSS v3.1 score of 8.8 and is fixed in updated Linux kernel releases. Vhost is a Linux kernel system that helps virtual machines handle network and other device traffic more quickly. It uses shared virtual queues, called virtqueues, to carry device data between a guest and the host. The flaw lies in how vhost caches IOTLB mappings used to find those queues in memory. The problem occurs when a virtual ring is reconfigured. Linux updates the ring’s address or size but doesn’t clear the cached mapping for the ring’s descriptor, available, or used data. A later cache hit can therefore skip the expected address check and translate the new address using an old mapping. The resulting pointer may reach kernel copy routines with an invalid target. Researchers on the Seclists mailing list traced the bug to two earlier kernel changes: one introduced the metadata cache, while the other deferred guest I/O address validation. PoC Released for Linux Vhost Flaw For local privilege escalation, an attacker first needs permission to open a vhost device such as /dev/vhost-net or /dev/vhost-vsock. The PoC primes the cache, changes a ring address without clearing the cached entry, then triggers the queue. The researchers say this can read and write kernel memory. The demonstrated chain uses a kernel memory read to work out the address randomization offset, then writes to the kernel’s modprobe_path setting. Triggering a kernel module request can then run an attacker-controlled helper with root privileges. The researchers report reproducing the chain on Ubuntu 26.04, RHEL 9.8, Amazon Linux 2023, Azure Linux 3.0, and Oracle Linux 10.2. Device permissions differed: the tested Ubuntu system limited access to the kvm group, while the other listed test systems exposed the device to ordinary users. That difference makes device permissions an important exposure check, but it does not replace patching. Membership in kvm or another group with access to vhost devices should be treated as privileged while a system remains unpatched. The second path starts inside a virtual machine. It requires a vhost device using a virtual IOMMU, iommu_platform, and the virtio queue-reset feature VIRTIO_F_RING_RESET. A guest can reset and re-enable a queue, leading the host to reconfigure its ring while the stale metadata remains cached. When the guest then triggers the queue, the stale mapping can send a used-ring write beyond guest memory and into the QEMU process heap. The researchers say the corruption can crash QEMU or affect its control flow. This is a configuration-dependent VM escape risk, not a claim that every virtual machine can be escaped through the flaw. The upstream fix clears the vring metadata cache when the ring address or size is changed, so the new configuration must pass IOTLB validation. The first fixed upstream stable releases listed for the affected series are 5.10.265, 5.15.216, 6.1.183, 6.6.152, 6.12.104, 6.18.45, 7.1.9, and 7.2. Administrators should install a fixed kernel or a vendor backport and reboot into it. Until then, restrict access to all vhost device nodes, including /dev/vhost-net, /dev/vhost-vsock, /dev/vhost-scsi, and /dev/vhost-vdpa-*. Do not pass these devices to untrusted containers. For unpatched virtualization hosts, avoid exposing vhost devices with iommu_platform behind a virtual IOMMU to untrusted guests. Permission changes do not revoke file descriptors that are already open, and they do not address the guest-triggered path. For related coverage, see Cyber Security News’ reports on Linux kernel privilege escalation flaws and KVM guest-to-host escape risks . The technical analysis and PoC are available from Tencent Zhuque Lab and GitHub. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. Integrate TI Feeds with data from 16K SOCs .
items.summary_html:
A public proof of concept for Vghost, a high-severity Linux vhost flaw tracked as CVE-2026-74580, shows how the bug can let a local user gain root access or, in certain virtual machine setups, break out of a guest and affect the host. The issue has a CVSS v3.1 score of 8.8 and is fixed in updated Linux kernel releases.

Vhost is a Linux kernel system that helps virtual machines handle network and other device traffic more quickly. It uses shared virtual queues, called virtqueues, to carry device data between a guest and the host. The flaw lies in how vhost caches IOTLB mappings used to find those queues in memory.

The problem occurs when a virtual ring is reconfigured. Linux updates the ring’s address or size but doesn’t clear the cached mapping for the ring’s descriptor, available, or used data.

A later cache hit can therefore skip the expected address check and translate the new address using an old mapping. The resulting pointer may reach kernel copy routines with an invalid target.

Researchers on the Seclists mailing list traced the bug to two earlier kernel changes: one introduced the metadata cache, while the other deferred guest I/O address validation.

PoC Released for Linux Vhost Flaw

For local privilege escalation, an attacker first needs permission to open a vhost device such as /dev/vhost-net or /dev/vhost-vsock. The PoC primes the cache, changes a ring address without clearing the cached entry, then triggers the queue. The researchers say this can read and write kernel memory.

The demonstrated chain uses a kernel memory read to work out the address randomization offset, then writes to the kernel’s modprobe_path setting. Triggering a kernel module request can then run an attacker-controlled helper with root privileges.

The researchers report reproducing the chain on Ubuntu 26.04, RHEL 9.8, Amazon Linux 2023, Azure Linux 3.0, and Oracle Linux 10.2. Device permissions differed: the tested Ubuntu system limited access to the kvm group, while the other listed test systems exposed the device to ordinary users.

That difference makes device permissions an important exposure check, but it does not replace patching. Membership in kvm or another group with access to vhost devices should be treated as privileged while a system remains unpatched.

The second path starts inside a virtual machine. It requires a vhost device using a virtual IOMMU, iommu_platform, and the virtio queue-reset feature VIRTIO_F_RING_RESET. A guest can reset and re-enable a queue, leading the host to reconfigure its ring while the stale metadata remains cached.

When the guest then triggers the queue, the stale mapping can send a used-ring write beyond guest memory and into the QEMU process heap. The researchers say the corruption can crash QEMU or affect its control flow. This is a configuration-dependent VM escape risk, not a claim that every virtual machine can be escaped through the flaw.

The upstream fix clears the vring metadata cache when the ring address or size is changed, so the new configuration must pass IOTLB validation.

The first fixed upstream stable releases listed for the affected series are 5.10.265, 5.15.216, 6.1.183, 6.6.152, 6.12.104, 6.18.45, 7.1.9, and 7.2. Administrators should install a fixed kernel or a vendor backport and reboot into it.

Until then, restrict access to all vhost device nodes, including /dev/vhost-net, /dev/vhost-vsock, /dev/vhost-scsi, and /dev/vhost-vdpa-*. Do not pass these devices to untrusted containers.

For unpatched virtualization hosts, avoid exposing vhost devices with iommu_platform behind a virtual IOMMU to untrusted guests. Permission changes do not revoke file descriptors that are already open, and they do not address the guest-triggered path.

For related coverage, see Cyber Security News’ reports on Linux kernel privilege escalation flaws and KVM guest-to-host escape risks. The technical analysis and PoC are available from Tencent Zhuque Lab and GitHub.
