items.title: Inside Hyperdrive: How we solved a rare Hyperdrive MySQL caching bug
items.summary: Hyperdrive support for MySQL is now generally available (GA). Hyperdrive , Cloudflare’s database connection pooler for Workers, initially only supported Postgres. Since we announced the beta for MySQL protocol support last year, we have been working on making our MySQL handling as reliable as our Postgres support. We’ve learned some things from building and running a MySQL connection pooler on Cloudflare’s network. It turns out that the difference between beta and GA is just 20 bug fixes in a trenchcoat. During the beta, our goal was to validate that real-world customer usage hit our production availability target of 99.99%. We knew there were gaps in our reliability since we track how often client connections from a Worker end in an error related to Hyperdrive. In addition, we had feedback from customers in the beta that led to the discovery of a rare and subtle bug in our production environment. To convey the complexity of this particular bug, we first need to explain how Hyperdrive works. What is Hyperdrive? Hyperdrive is a distributed database connection pooler that connects Cloudflare Workers to SQL databases. Hyperdrive holds warm SQL connections open on our global network and shares these connections across many Worker requests. In addition to connection pooling, Hyperdrive can also cache common queries in our global CDN cache, reducing latency and load on the origin database. Establishing a connection to a SQL database is expensive, taking a minimum of five network round trips. On a serverless compute platform like Workers, establishing a connection for each request would be impractical, both because of the amount of latency added to each request, but also because a large number of open connections can incur high per-connection resource costs. While MySQL fares better here than Postgres since MySQL doesn’t use an entire OS process per connection, a typical deployment can still run into resource issues with a large number of connections. For more details, see our blog post introducing Hyperdrive. A journey to stability Some of the issues we ran into were small and easy to fix once reported. One of the first problems reported in the beta was that emojis written to the database were not being correctly returned. This was a bug related to character set encoding. Hyperdrive negotiates the encoding for the connection in the startup handshake and we negotiate utf8 as the encoding. As it turns out, utf8 is a deprecated alias for utf8mb3 which is not all of UTF-8: it only supports 1-3 bytes per Unicode code point, while full UTF-8 has a max of 4 bytes per code point. To get all of UTF-8, we needed to change our handshake to use utf8mb4 , which fixed the emoji issue. Another encoding-related bug occurred when we added connection cleanup via COM_RESET_CONNECTION . This is a lightweight MySQL command to clear any session state in a given connection, which is exactly what Hyperdrive needs to ensure that no session-level state leaks between checkouts. But adding this connection cleanup step caused encoding issues once again! It turns out that COM_RESET_CONNECTION does not reset the connection state to the character set encoding we negotiated at connection startup; it instead resets the connection to the server default. This means that after negotiating utf8mb4 on a MySQL server instance that defaults to latin1 , once we run COM_RESET_CONNECTION, our connection now has an encoding of latin1 . The fix is to always run a command setting the encoding to utf8mb4 after a connection reset. A hard-to-find bug During the beta, our highest-volume MySQL customer reported a small but consistent rate of empty query responses for which a non-empty response was always expected. We started the investigation by combing through all of our telemetry and understanding the user’s logic. Then we also increased the trace rate for this Hyperdrive instance, hoping to see the execution flow of this bug. We searched for network issues that could explain the issue — but nothing seemed to account for this behavior. This error occurred about 0.001% of the time, which made it very hard to find relevant end-to-end execution traces. But we did have one clue: the bug only occurred on Hyperdrive instances with caching enabled. This made us suspect an issue with Hyperdrive’s MySQL caching. Hyperdrive caching To understand Hyperdrive's caching, we first need to talk about Hyperdrive's topology and how it interacts with the CDN cache. Every Hyperdrive instance has a split architecture with two nodes: a Client and an Endpoint. The Client node runs on the same machine as the user’s Worker, handles local caching (if enabled), and forwards queries to the Endpoint if needed. The Endpoint node holds the connection pool and is placed in the data center closest to the origin database. Each node uses the Cloudflare CDN cache local to the data center it is running in. Importantly, this means that if the two nodes are running in the same data center, they will share a cache. Sharing the cache between Client and Endpoint is generally good for performance. We use a hash of the contents of the query’s wire messages with some normalization and store the result bytes in the cache. If a Hyperdrive Client running in the same data center as its Endpoint receives a request, and that Endpoint has recently cached the results of the same query, the Client can serve the response directly from the shared data center cache. To work correctly, this scheme requires that the same bytes are cached for the same response, whether stored by the Client or the Endpoint. MySQL client/server protocol Since we couldn’t get a direct trace of the issue, we decided to spend time looking at the MySQL client / server protocol . Perhaps we had an assumption about Postgres’ protocol built into our MySQL handling that was causing these issues. The protocol describes how a MySQL client communicates with a MySQL server. This can be somewhat confusing in the case of database connection pooling since we have two components acting like clients and two acting like servers. The first client is the Worker using a MySQL client library, and it connects to the first component acting like a server, the Hyperdrive Client. The Hyperdrive Client connects to the Hyperdrive Endpoint which acts as a MySQL client connecting to the actual MySQL origin server. This protocol starts with the Connection Phase where the MySQL client and the MySQL server agree upon a common authentication method and capabilities. Once a connection is established, the client and server begin the Command Phase , where the client sends commands (e.g. SQL statements) to be executed with the server responding and waiting for the next command. Capabilities are exchanged during the Connection Phase to support protocol evolution while remaining backwards compatible. Each capability is a feature, like supporting compression during the Command Phase. The clients and servers must only use features which the other supports, otherwise a protocol desync can occur, leading to unexpected behavior. This capability negotiation can be tricky for Hyperdrive, since Hyperdrive acts as a client to the origin database, and acts as a server to the Worker. To ensure that Hyperdrive can parse the messages from the origin MySQL server, Hyperdrive has a fixed set of capability flags which are used to communicate to the origin database. Since it is possible for Hyperdrive’s set of capabilities to be different from the Worker client’s set of capabilities, Hyperdrive needs to translate all origin responses encoded by its capabilities to the capabilities that the Worker expects. While trying to debug this issue, we found that a popular MySQL client library for Node.js ( mysql2 ) does not currently support the CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF capability, which changes how result sets are terminated. Without this capability, the server sends an EOF packet between the column definitions and rows, then another EOF packet at the end of the result set. When CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF is negotiated, the metadata EOF packet is omitted and the final EOF packet is replaced with an OK packet. MySQL server 5.7.5 and later supports this capability, but the newer OK-packet behavior is only used when the client negotiates it. While Hyperdrive does support the CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF capability, it’s possible that the Worker’s MySQL driver does not. To handle this, Hyperdrive adjusts its behavior to support the capabilities that the Worker client driver expects. This means rewriting result sets to include EOFs and to translate all OK packets to EOFs when required. After days of looking through telemetry, documentation, and Hyperdrive code, everything clicked. We finally came across the last missing piece: a faulty assumption in our Hyperdrive Client caching code. We baked in an assumption when implementing the Client caching for Postgres: that we can cache exactly the bytes we wrote back to the Worker. While this was a reasonable assumption to make with Postgres’ wire protocol, it no longer holds due to the mismatch in MySQL capabilities. If a Client node is caching exactly what it writes back to the Worker, these bytes are in a different format than what an Endpoint node would be expecting. That’s because the Endpoint node is always working with Hyperdrive’s capabilities, while the Client node writes back bytes that are translated to match the Worker’s capabilities. Now if we put all these clues together, we can understand scenarios where Hyperdrive can return a MySQL response encoded with the wrong capabilities, leading to the unexpected empty results and hangs. The bug occurs when both the Client and Endpoint are in the same data center, sharing a cache, and when one reads a value cached by the other. Here’s a closer look at two such scenarios. Endpoint caches, Client reads The Endpoint is in the middle of servicing a request for query Q. It gets back a response R from the origin server and caches response result bytes R_hyperdrive (Response encoded with Hyperdrive capabilities) into the shared cache. Client receives another request for query Q, checks the shared cache and finds R_hyperdrive. Client responds to the Worker with R_hyperdrive without translating to the Worker’s capabilities. This diagram shows that flow: Client caches, Endpoint reads Client is finishing serving a request for query Q, and it writes the translated response bytes R_worker to cache. Endpoint is in the middle of servicing a request for Q, and checks the cache to find R_worker. Endpoint sends R_worker to a different Client, and this Client tries to translate R_worker to the Worker’s capabilities, and ends up sending an early EOF or hangs. You can see that here: Once we found this type of failure mode, the fix was simple. We now make sure that we always write back a canonical version of the query result bytes in the cache encoded using Hyperdrive’s capabilities, no matter which node stored it. After releasing this change, the empty row problem went away — and our success rate for Client connections reached 99.99%. Reliability is a feature You can use Hyperdrive support for MySQL today! Create a Hyperdrive to an existing MySQL-compatible database via the dashboard or wrangler, or connect to a new PlanetScale database . If you run into any issues or have questions, reach out on our Discord . npx wrangler hyperdrive create HYPERDRIVE_NAME --connection-string="mysql://user:password@db-host.example.com:3306/dbname"
items.summary_html:
Hyperdrive support for MySQL is now generally available (GA). Hyperdrive, Cloudflare’s database connection pooler for Workers, initially only supported Postgres. Since we announced the beta for MySQL protocol support last year, we have been working on making our MySQL handling as reliable as our Postgres support.

We’ve learned some things from building and running a MySQL connection pooler on Cloudflare’s network. It turns out that the difference between beta and GA is just 20 bug fixes in a trenchcoat.

During the beta, our goal was to validate that real-world customer usage hit our production availability target of 99.99%. We knew there were gaps in our reliability since we track how often client connections from a Worker end in an error related to Hyperdrive. In addition, we had feedback from customers in the beta that led to the discovery of a rare and subtle bug in our production environment. To convey the complexity of this particular bug, we first need to explain how Hyperdrive works.

What is Hyperdrive?

Hyperdrive is a distributed database connection pooler that connects Cloudflare Workers to SQL databases. Hyperdrive holds warm SQL connections open on our global network and shares these connections across many Worker requests. In addition to connection pooling, Hyperdrive can also cache common queries in our global CDN cache, reducing latency and load on the origin database.

Establishing a connection to a SQL database is expensive, taking a minimum of five network round trips. On a serverless compute platform like Workers, establishing a connection for each request would be impractical, both because of the amount of latency added to each request, but also because a large number of open connections can incur high per-connection resource costs. While MySQL fares better here than Postgres since MySQL doesn’t use an entire OS process per connection, a typical deployment can still run into resource issues with a large number of connections.

For more details, see our blog post introducing Hyperdrive.

A journey to stability

Some of the issues we ran into were small and easy to fix once reported. One of the first problems reported in the beta was that emojis written to the database were not being correctly returned. This was a bug related to character set encoding. Hyperdrive negotiates the encoding for the connection in the startup handshake and we negotiate utf8 as the encoding. As it turns out, utf8 is a deprecated alias for utf8mb3 which is not all of UTF-8: it only supports 1-3 bytes per Unicode code point, while full UTF-8 has a max of 4 bytes per code point. To get all of UTF-8, we needed to change our handshake to use utf8mb4 , which fixed the emoji issue.

Another encoding-related bug occurred when we added connection cleanup via COM_RESET_CONNECTION. This is a lightweight MySQL command to clear any session state in a given connection, which is exactly what Hyperdrive needs to ensure that no session-level state leaks between checkouts. But adding this connection cleanup step caused encoding issues once again! It turns out that COM_RESET_CONNECTION does not reset the connection state to the character set encoding we negotiated at connection startup; it instead resets the connection to the server default. This means that after negotiating utf8mb4 on a MySQL server instance that defaults to latin1, once we run COM_RESET_CONNECTION, our connection now has an encoding of latin1. The fix is to always run a command setting the encoding to utf8mb4 after a connection reset.

A hard-to-find bug

During the beta, our highest-volume MySQL customer reported a small but consistent rate of empty query responses for which a non-empty response was always expected. We started the investigation by combing through all of our telemetry and understanding the user’s logic. Then we also increased the trace rate for this Hyperdrive instance, hoping to see the execution flow of this bug. We searched for network issues that could explain the issue — but nothing seemed to account for this behavior. This error occurred about 0.001% of the time, which made it very hard to find relevant end-to-end execution traces.

But we did have one clue: the bug only occurred on Hyperdrive instances with caching enabled. This made us suspect an issue with Hyperdrive’s MySQL caching.

Hyperdrive caching

To understand Hyperdrive's caching, we first need to talk about Hyperdrive's topology and how it interacts with the CDN cache. Every Hyperdrive instance has a split architecture with two nodes: a Client and an Endpoint. The Client node runs on the same machine as the user’s Worker, handles local caching (if enabled), and forwards queries to the Endpoint if needed. The Endpoint node holds the connection pool and is placed in the data center closest to the origin database. Each node uses the Cloudflare CDN cache local to the data center it is running in. Importantly, this means that if the two nodes are running in the same data center, they will share a cache.

Sharing the cache between Client and Endpoint is generally good for performance. We use a hash of the contents of the query’s wire messages with some normalization and store the result bytes in the cache. If a Hyperdrive Client running in the same data center as its Endpoint receives a request, and that Endpoint has recently cached the results of the same query, the Client can serve the response directly from the shared data center cache. To work correctly, this scheme requires that the same bytes are cached for the same response, whether stored by the Client or the Endpoint.

MySQL client/server protocol

Since we couldn’t get a direct trace of the issue, we decided to spend time looking at the MySQL client / server protocol. Perhaps we had an assumption about Postgres’ protocol built into our MySQL handling that was causing these issues.

The protocol describes how a MySQL client communicates with a MySQL server. This can be somewhat confusing in the case of database connection pooling since we have two components acting like clients and two acting like servers. The first client is the Worker using a MySQL client library, and it connects to the first component acting like a server, the Hyperdrive Client. The Hyperdrive Client connects to the Hyperdrive Endpoint which acts as a MySQL client connecting to the actual MySQL origin server.

This protocol starts with the Connection Phase where the MySQL client and the MySQL server agree upon a common authentication method and capabilities. Once a connection is established, the client and server begin the Command Phase, where the client sends commands (e.g. SQL statements) to be executed with the server responding and waiting for the next command.

Capabilities are exchanged during the Connection Phase to support protocol evolution while remaining backwards compatible. Each capability is a feature, like supporting compression during the Command Phase. The clients and servers must only use features which the other supports, otherwise a protocol desync can occur, leading to unexpected behavior.

This capability negotiation can be tricky for Hyperdrive, since Hyperdrive acts as a client to the origin database, and acts as a server to the Worker. To ensure that Hyperdrive can parse the messages from the origin MySQL server, Hyperdrive has a fixed set of capability flags which are used to communicate to the origin database. Since it is possible for Hyperdrive’s set of capabilities to be different from the Worker client’s set of capabilities, Hyperdrive needs to translate all origin responses encoded by its capabilities to the capabilities that the Worker expects.

While trying to debug this issue, we found that a popular MySQL client library for Node.js (mysql2) does not currently support the CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF capability, which changes how result sets are terminated. Without this capability, the server sends an EOF packet between the column definitions and rows, then another EOF packet at the end of the result set. When CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF is negotiated, the metadata EOF packet is omitted and the final EOF packet is replaced with an OK packet. MySQL server 5.7.5 and later supports this capability, but the newer OK-packet behavior is only used when the client negotiates it.

While Hyperdrive does support the CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF capability, it’s possible that the Worker’s MySQL driver does not. To handle this, Hyperdrive adjusts its behavior to support the capabilities that the Worker client driver expects. This means rewriting result sets to include EOFs and to translate all OK packets to EOFs when required. 

After days of looking through telemetry, documentation, and Hyperdrive code, everything clicked. We finally came across the last missing piece: a faulty assumption in our Hyperdrive Client caching code. We baked in an assumption when implementing the Client caching for Postgres: that we can cache exactly the bytes we wrote back to the Worker. While this was a reasonable assumption to make with Postgres’ wire protocol, it no longer holds due to the mismatch in MySQL capabilities. If a Client node is caching exactly what it writes back to the Worker, these bytes are in a different format than what an Endpoint node would be expecting. That’s because the Endpoint node is always working with Hyperdrive’s capabilities, while the Client node writes back bytes that are translated to match the Worker’s capabilities.

Now if we put all these clues together, we can understand scenarios where Hyperdrive can return a MySQL response encoded with the wrong capabilities, leading to the unexpected empty results and hangs. The bug occurs when both the Client and Endpoint are in the same data center, sharing a cache, and when one reads a value cached by the other.

Here’s a closer look at two such scenarios.

Endpoint caches, Client reads
  1. The Endpoint is in the middle of servicing a request for query Q. It gets back a response R from the origin server and caches response result bytes R_hyperdrive (Response encoded with Hyperdrive capabilities) into the shared cache.
  2. Client receives another request for query Q, checks the shared cache and finds R_hyperdrive.
  3. Client responds to the Worker with R_hyperdrive without translating to the Worker’s capabilities.

This diagram shows that flow:

Client caches, Endpoint reads
  1. Client is finishing serving a request for query Q, and it writes the translated response bytes R_worker to cache.
  2. Endpoint is in the middle of servicing a request for Q, and checks the cache to find R_worker.
  3. Endpoint sends R_worker to a different Client, and this Client tries to translate R_worker to the Worker’s capabilities, and ends up sending an early EOF or hangs.

You can see that here:

Once we found this type of failure mode, the fix was simple. We now make sure that we always write back a canonical version of the query result bytes in the cache encoded using Hyperdrive’s capabilities, no matter which node stored it. After releasing this change, the empty row problem went away — and our success rate for Client connections reached 99.99%.

Reliability is a feature

You can use Hyperdrive support for MySQL today! Create a Hyperdrive to an existing MySQL-compatible database via the dashboard or wrangler, or connect to a new PlanetScale database. If you run into any issues or have questions, reach out on our Discord. 

npx wrangler hyperdrive create HYPERDRIVE_NAME --connection-string="mysql://user:password@db-host.example.com:3306/dbname"

items.title: The hidden network: Inside the phishing infrastructure ecosystem powering global cybercrime
items.summary: In this article Uncovering the shadow world of a phishing kit ecosystem Storm-3119: YAM Store, the power broker Storm-2990: The Iron Man System phishing kit Downstream activity from Storm-2990 phishing kits Mitigation and protection guidance Microsoft Defender detections Over the past year, Microsoft uncovered a Chinese-language cybercriminal ecosystem, an interconnected network of phishing kit operators, developers, and an illicit marketplace selling tools and infrastructure for large-scale phishing, enabling cybercriminal operations worldwide. Threat actors purchased and used these tools and infrastructure, including phishing kits and access to compromised or fraudulent Microsoft or Google cloud environments and related credentials, to target organizations across the healthcare, financial services, wholesale distribution, and information technology (IT) sectors in Japan, the United States, Australia, and India. In collaboration with law enforcement agencies and other partners worldwide, Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit (DCU) facilitated a disruption of the ecosystem’s primary developers and infrastructure . Microsoft’s research into one phishing kit unraveled a larger ecosystem, including the phishing kit developers, an infrastructure dealer, and the threat actors who buy from both. In this blog, we examine several phishing kits marketed and sold through YAM Store, an underground marketplace tracked by Microsoft as Storm-3119. We share our analysis of the technical aspects of this Chinese-language phishing kit ecosystem, the shared infrastructure, provisioning methods, and downstream activity by threat actors using these tools. Figure 1: Heat map of most impacted countries by combined Storm-3119 and Storm-2990-related activity. Uncovering the shadow world of a phishing kit ecosystem Microsoft, alongside industry partner Resecurity , identified three phishing kits sold through the YAM Store that make up this Chinese-language cybercriminal network: CoGUI (also known as NX or FA), Haozi (also known as Phoenix), and Iron Man System. Microsoft tracks the cluster of activity and the developers behind all three phishing kits as Storm-2990. Since January 2026, the threat actors behind these kits have been responsible for facilitating the sending of over one billion phishing emails and SMS messages to over 75 thousand organizations worldwide. Microsoft assesses with high confidence that these phishing kits were developed by Chinese-speaking threat actors, and, despite their distinct branding and separate Telegram-based sales channels, exhibit highly similar capabilities and functionality. The phishing kits provide phishing templates impersonating legitimate brands and organizations (including government, financial, and logistics) worldwide, and enable criminal actors to facilitate high-volume phishing and credential stealing operations. The similarity in their infrastructure and overlap in activity suggest either shared development origins, code reuse, or close collaboration among their developers. These phishing kits have been advertised through YAM Store, first CoGUI and Haozi, followed by Iron Man System starting in June 2026. YAM Store and affiliated phishing kit companies accepted payments through cryptocurrency, including USDT and Ethereum, adding another layer to conceal illicit activity. The scale and proliferation of this ecosystem demonstrate how readily available criminal infrastructure can lower the barrier to entry, enabling less skilled cybercriminals to target organizations at scale and contribute to fraud losses. By mapping the relationship between YAM Store and these phishing kits, we provide insight into the commercial infrastructure that supports modern phishing operations. Figure 2. YAM Store (Storm-3119) sells fraudulently acquired infrastructure to CoGUI, Haozi, and Iron Man System, all interconnected phishing kit operators, who then provide these services to other threat actors. Storm-3119: YAM Store, the power broker YAM Store is an initial access broker (IAB) that sells infrastructure using compromised or fraudulently obtained environments in providers like Microsoft and Google. The marketplace offers a variety of infrastructure based on age, subscription type, and environment types such as education (.edu) or non-profit (.org). Figure 3: YAM Store procurement and downstream activity chain The YAM Store marketplace provides cybercriminals with a platform to purchase fraudulently acquired Microsoft and Google domains associated with legitimate, expired, or previously used organization numbers, allowing actors to use seemingly legitimate infrastructure and obtain workspaces at relatively low cost. Storm-3119 uses automation to identify expired environment or organization names and leverages legitimate customer information associated with them to help circumvent existing detections. Figure 4. YAM Store interface and Telegram contact Anatomy of YAM Store operations: How Storm-3119 acquires, controls, and monetizes infrastructure During this investigation, Microsoft uncovered a five-stage attack pipeline often used in Storm-3119’s operations. YAM Store functions as an access broker, an intermediary that hijacks Microsoft 365 and Azure for Education tenants and resells the stolen accounts, licenses, and storage as a service to downstream operations, including the phishing kits tracked as Storm-2990. The pipeline below describes the supply side of that business: how the actor acquires, controls, and monetizes compromised environments. Stage 1 – Reconnaissance : Storm-3119 conducts automated reconnaissance of target environments. The actor uses Flask, a lightweight Python web framework, to covertly identify and profile cloud-enabled organizations. The tooling is designed to discover Microsoft 365 tenants, assess enrollment opportunities, gather licensing and Azure cloud information, and perform these activities anonymously through Tor infrastructure. Stage 2 – Environment takeover and app-only admin panels : Once a viable environment is identified, the threat actor centralizes associated information in an actor-controlled platform used to administer compromised Microsoft 365 environments. This platform is a separate set of administrative panels (implemented in PHP, Java/Spring, and Cloudflare Workers) that lets the operator maintain, monetize, and expand access using stolen application credentials. Over the past year, Microsoft uncovered a Chinese-language cybercriminal ecosystem, an interconnected network of phishing kit operators, developers, and an illicit marketplace selling tools and infrastructure for large-scale phishing, enabling cybercriminal operations worldwide.

Threat actors purchased and used these tools and infrastructure, including phishing kits and access to compromised or fraudulent Microsoft or Google cloud environments and related credentials, to target organizations across the healthcare, financial services, wholesale distribution, and information technology (IT) sectors in Japan, the United States, Australia, and India. In collaboration with law enforcement agencies and other partners worldwide, Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit (DCU) facilitated a disruption of the ecosystem’s primary developers and infrastructure.

Microsoft’s research into one phishing kit unraveled a larger ecosystem, including the phishing kit developers, an infrastructure dealer, and the threat actors who buy from both. In this blog, we examine several phishing kits marketed and sold through YAM Store, an underground marketplace tracked by Microsoft as Storm-3119. We share our analysis of the technical aspects of this Chinese-language phishing kit ecosystem, the shared infrastructure, provisioning methods, and downstream activity by threat actors using these tools.

Figure 1: Heat map of most impacted countries by combined Storm-3119 and Storm-2990-related activity. Uncovering the shadow world of a phishing kit ecosystem

items.title: Prioritize what's actually exploitable: Vulnerability reachability is now available in SonarQube Advanced Security
items.summary: If you run software composition analysis (SCA) at any scale, you know the problem isn't finding vulnerabilities—it's finding the ones that matter. A typical dependency tree pulls in hundreds, sometimes thousands of packages. Scan that tree against the CVE database and you'll get a backlog that no team can realistically work through: most of it in code paths your application never executes. Triage becomes a full-time job, “critical” loses its meaning, and the vulnerabilities that actually put you at risk get lost in the noise of the ones that don't. Today, we're announcing Vulnerability reachability , now available in SonarQube Advanced Security it answers the one question a CVSS score never could: does your code actually call the vulnerable function? The threat landscape is changing Frontier AI models can now find and weaponize vulnerabilities on their own, at a speed no patch cycle was built to match. The window between a vulnerability existing and it being actively exploited keeps shrinking, and what used to take attackers weeks now takes hours. Conducting a post-release audit or maintaining a backlog of thousands of unranked CVEs waiting for manual triage are no longer viable strategies against that timeline. That makes prioritization the whole game. When the exploit window is measured in hours, security teams can't afford to spend those hours investigating vulnerabilities their code never even touches. Knowing which risks are confirmed reachable, and fixing those first, is how teams keep pace with a threat landscape that no longer waits for a quarterly patch cycle. What is vulnerability reachability analysis and how does it work? For every vulnerability detected in a third-party dependency, SonarQube now performs a call graph analysis of your codebase to determine whether your code calls the specific functions associated with that vulnerability. The result is one of three reachability states, shown directly on the dependency risk card and available as a filter across your “Dependency Risks” view: Reachable: SonarQube found your code calling functions associated with the vulnerability. Treat these as your priority queue. Unreachable: SonarQube found no instances of your code directly calling the vulnerable functions. Worth noting: you may still be exposed through transitive calls from other dependencies, or other exploitation paths reachability analysis currently doesn't cover. This status lowers the threat, it doesn't clear the risk. Not analyzed: Reachability hasn't been calculated yet, whether because the vulnerability is in a currently unsupported language, the vulnerable package is a transitive dependency, or deep vulnerability analysis hasn't run yet. Reachable vulnerabilities should go to the front of the remediation line. If you run software composition analysis (SCA) at any scale, you know the problem isn't finding vulnerabilities—it's finding the ones that matter.

A typical dependency tree pulls in hundreds, sometimes thousands of packages. Scan that tree against the CVE database and you'll get a backlog that no team can realistically work through: most of it in code paths your application never executes. Triage becomes a full-time job, “critical” loses its meaning, and the vulnerabilities that actually put you at risk get lost in the noise of the ones that don't.

Today, we're announcing Vulnerability reachability, now available in SonarQube Advanced Security it answers the one question a CVSS score never could: does your code actually call the vulnerable function?

The threat landscape is changing

Frontier AI models can now find and weaponize vulnerabilities on their own, at a speed no patch cycle was built to match. The window between a vulnerability existing and it being actively exploited keeps shrinking, and what used to take attackers weeks now takes hours. Conducting a post-release audit or  maintaining a backlog of thousands of unranked CVEs waiting for manual triage are no longer viable strategies against that timeline.

items.title: Which LLM writes the best code? A 2026 comparison
items.summary: Search for the best LLM for coding and you will find confident rankings that disagree with one another and go stale within weeks. Since the start of September 2026, Anthropic , Google , OpenAI and SpaceXAI (formerly xAI) have each released at least one new model, according to their own documentation. A leaderboard snapshot cannot keep pace with that, and it cannot tell you how a model behaves in your repositories. This post gives you a decision framework instead of a winner: how to define “best,” what to measure, how to run a pilot, and why independent verification belongs in your stack whichever model you choose. The framework at a glance Define the tasks you want help with and what “accepted” means for each. Shortlist two or three models and pin exact versions. Pilot them on your own repositories and measure acceptance, not impressions. Validate in CI with the same checks and quality gate for every candidate. Set guardrails and re-run the pilot when a model or version changes. What does “best LLM for coding” actually mean? No single LLM writes the best code for every team. The best model is the one that performs best on your tasks, in your repositories, within your cost, latency and governance limits, and that performance has to be measured rather than assumed. Public leaderboards can shortlist candidates; they cannot make the final choice. Three things make a universal winner unlikely. First, the field is broad: hosted models from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and SpaceXAI sit alongside open-weight families from DeepSeek, Alibaba (Qwen) and Mistral, and each vendor documents different context windows, effort settings and retirement policies. Second, versions move quickly, so any comparison describes a moment, not a model. Third, “good code” is not one property. A change can pass its tests and still be insecure, hard to maintain or expensive to review. Developers already use more than one tool. In Stack Overflow’s 2026 Developer Survey , about 80% of respondents said they use two or more AI tools for work, and about two-thirds said they had switched AI tools during the year. Teams are not choosing a model once. They are managing several and changing them. What criteria should you use to compare AI coding models? A fair AI coding model comparison scores every candidate against the same seven criteria. Weight them by what your team can least afford to get wrong. Criterion Question to ask How to measure it in a pilot Code correctness Does the change do what was asked, including edge cases? Share of changes that pass your existing tests on the first attempt; review rounds before merge. Security Does the model introduce vulnerabilities or unsafe patterns by default? Run static analysis, secrets and dependency checks on every sample; count findings by severity. Maintainability Would a teammate want to own this code in six months? Complexity, duplication and code smells on changed code; reviewer rework time. Repository context Does it follow your conventions, APIs and architecture? Share of changes accepted without convention rework; invented or misused APIs. Latency Does response time fit the workflow, from inline suggestions to long agent runs? Time to first useful result at the effort setting you plan to use. Cost What does an accepted change cost? Spend and tokens per merged change, not per request. Governance Can you control versions, data flows and access? Retirement notice, data-handling terms, audit trail and an approved-model list. Check the license and model card for the exact model you plan to use. Terms differ between models from the same vendor. Cost and context interact. In Sonar’s own study of six repository pairs (27 tasks, about 540 runs with Claude Code and Sonnet 4.6), agents used 7.2% fewer input tokens and 8.5% fewer output tokens on average in the cleaner codebases, with a pass-rate difference under one percentage point. The authors argue: “What drives the cost isn’t how much the agent writes, it’s how much code the agent has to look at in order to write it.” The study is Sonar’s own rather than third-party, and savings varied widely from task to task. How do AI coding models compare on common development tasks? This post does not rank models. A ranking is only as good as its documented methodology, model versions, test set and refresh schedule, and a blog post cannot stand behind those for every task below. What you can compare reliably is what each task demands and how to test it. Task What good looks like What to test in your pilot Watch for Greenfield features Meets the spec, follows house conventions, ships with tests Time to a mergeable first draft; security and quality findings per feature Plausible code with hidden security flaws Refactoring Same behavior, lower complexity, contained diff Existing tests before and after; change in complexity and duplication; diff size Behavior drift where test coverage is thin; edits beyond the request Debugging Finds the root cause, makes a minimal fix, adds a regression test Fix rate on historical bugs you can reproduce; whether the fix addresses the cause Fixes that silence a symptom Test writing Tests that fail when behavior breaks Coverage of changed lines; failures on seeded defects Tests that pass trivially or restate the implementation Code review Finds real defects with few false alarms Detection rate on seeded defects; share of comments developers act on Shared blind spots when a model reviews its own output Check the license and model card for the exact model you plan to use. Terms differ between models from the same vendor. Studies that test many models point to gaps that span models rather than to one vendor. Veracode’s 2025 study analyzed 80 coding tasks across more than 100 models and found that in 45% of test cases the models introduced vulnerabilities classified within the OWASP Top 10. Its July 2026 update , which tested models without security-specific prompting, puts the average security pass rate at 56%, “virtually unchanged since last year’s report.” BaxBench , a 2025 benchmark of generated backends, found that exploits could be executed against around half of the correct programs each model generated, on average. In Sonar’s own Coding Personalities research (October 2025: six models of that period, more than 4,400 Java tasks each), every model produced vulnerabilities rated BLOCKER, and code smells made up roughly nine in ten of the issues for each model. Each study has limits. Veracode’s public summaries report syntax and security pass rates and describe no functional-correctness testing. Sonar’s research is first-party, covers Java only and tested 2025-era models. Read them as direction, not precision. The Sonar research also found that models differ in coding style, which it calls “coding personality,” one more reason to test on your own code. Pros and cons by model type Names change faster than trade-offs. Whichever list of the best AI models for code generation you start from, these three types cover most choices in 2026. Examples are listed alphabetically and are not a ranking. Type Examples Pros Cons Hosted frontier models Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, OpenAI GPT-6, SpaceXAI Grok Managed infrastructure; first-party coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity; context windows of roughly 500,000 to 1 million tokens; adjustable effort settings Code and prompts leave your environment unless a private deployment applies; cost and latency rise with effort; models retire on the vendor’s schedule Smaller, faster hosted tiers Claude Haiku, Gemini Flash-Lite, GPT-6 Luna Lower latency and cost per request; a fit for high-volume, narrow tasks Quality on long, multi-file changes varies; test where it drops for your work Open-weight models DeepSeek V4 Pro, Mistral Small 4, Qwen3.8-27B Run in your own environment; you control versions and data residency; some models use permissive licenses (MIT, Apache-2.0) You operate serving, scaling and security; licenses differ, even within one vendor’s lineup; you evaluate each new release yourself Check the license and model card for the exact model you plan to use. Terms differ between models from the same vendor. Why aren’t benchmark results enough to choose a coding model? A coding LLM leaderboard is a reasonable place to build a shortlist. It is a weak basis for a final decision, because the numbers depend on the test set, the harness, the scoring method and the date. Test sets age. In February 2026 OpenAI said it had stopped reporting SWE-bench Verified scores . An audit of a hard subset of 138 problems found that at least 59.4% had flawed test cases, and OpenAI found evidence of training-data contamination. A newer benchmark, SWE-bench Pro, has drawn similar scrutiny: in July 2026 OpenAI withdrew its recommendation of it , estimating that about 30% of its tasks were broken. Passing tests is not the same as being mergeable. METR had four maintainers from three open-source repositories review 296 AI-generated patches. Roughly half of the test-passing patches would not have been merged. Normalized to the roughly 68% merge rate of the human-written reference patches, maintainers’ merge rates ran about 24 percentage points below the automated score. METR tested agents from mid-2024 to late-2025 and cautions that this is a research note using one agent setup, not a claim about a fundamental limit on capability. Setup matters, though how much is debated. Anthropic reported a 6-percentage-point gap on Terminal-Bench 2.0 between the most- and least-resourced infrastructure setups, and advised that “leaderboard differences below 3 percentage points deserve skepticism until the eval configuration is documented and matched.” A September 2026 study published by Arena (HarnessTax) found that the average effect of the harness on success rate stayed within about 2% on SWE-bench Lite and about 5% on Terminal-Bench 2.0, while costs differed by up to 5x. Boards measure different things. Arena’s WebDev leaderboard ranks models from head-to-head votes (846,326 votes across 141 models as of 7 October 2026). SWE-bench-style boards score issue resolution against test suites. Terminal-Bench scores terminal tasks and is now on version 4.0 . Each measures something real. None measures your codebase, and the top of the table can differ by benchmark and date. Five questions to ask of any leaderboard Which model version and settings were tested: exact model ID, effort level and date? What is the test set, and is it still considered valid? What harness or agent ran the model, and is it the one you will use? How is success scored: automated tests, human preference or something else? How often is the board refreshed, and when was it last updated? A ranking that cannot answer these questions is a headline, not evidence. That is why this post does not publish one. How should teams choose an AI coding model? A five-step selection framework Here is how to choose an AI coding model as an experiment you can repeat, not a one-time purchase decision. 1. Define the tasks and the acceptance bar Pick the three to five tasks from the previous section that matter most to your team. Decide in advance what “accepted” means for each, for example merged without rework, or passing CI and one review. Writing the bar down first stops results from being reinterpreted later. 2. Shortlist two or three candidates and pin them Build the shortlist from public benchmarks and vendor documentation, and include a model of a different type if your constraints allow. Pin each candidate to an exact model ID or snapshot rather than a moving alias. Anthropic documents that it does not update an existing model ID and ships updated versions under new IDs, and OpenAI documents that snapshots let you lock in a specific model version, while an alias such as chat-latest points to a snapshot that is regularly updated. 3. Pilot on your own work and measure acceptance Use real tickets, with the same prompts, tools and repositories for every candidate. Record acceptance rate, review rounds, rework time, cost per accepted change and latency. A scorecard like this keeps the comparison honest. Metric Model A Model B Model C Accepted without rework (%) Review rounds per change (median) CI passed on first attempt (%) New issues per change, by severity Cost per accepted change Time to first usable result 4. Validate in CI, identically for every candidate Run the same build, tests, static analysis, secrets and dependency checks on every candidate’s output, and enforce the same quality gate . This replaces “which model felt better” with evidence, and it applies one standard to all candidates. 5. Set guardrails and re-run when things change Decide where AI-generated changes need human review, which paths are off limits, which models are approved, and what triggers a new pilot: a new model version, a retirement notice, a cost change or a rising rate of quality gate failures. How do you build an AI coding stack that separates generation from verification? Whichever model wins your pilot, treat it as one replaceable component. The model generates. A separate layer verifies. Keeping them apart lets you change models without changing your standards. There are two reasons. The first is the evidence above: studies across many models find security and quality gaps in generated code, and passing tests does not mean a change is mergeable. The second is that self-review is a weaker control than it sounds. In one 2025 study of 14 open-source non-reasoning models on non-coding tasks, models corrected errors in external input that they failed to correct in their own output ( Tsui ). The wider evidence is mixed and mostly outside coding, so independent review combined with deterministic checks is a safer default, not a proven fix. Sonar’s Agent Centric Development Cycle (AC/DC) organizes the work into three stages around the agent’s own generation. Layer Job What changes when you switch models Generate (model and agent) Writes and edits code Everything. This is the layer you are comparing. Guide Gives the agent your context and standards before it writes: instruction files and project context, for example through the SonarQube MCP Server Little. Prompts and instructions may need retuning. Verify Checks every change against one standard in the agent loop, the IDE and CI: static analysis, security checks, quality gates Nothing. The same standard applies to any model. Solve Fixes what verification finds, with the same checks confirming the fix Nothing. Sonar covers these layers with tools that work alongside the agents your teams already use. The SonarQube MCP Server connects supported agents and IDEs, including Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor, Gemini CLI and GitHub Copilot CLI, to SonarQube analysis, and is free and source-available. Sonar Vortex brings Guide, Verify and Solve into agents such as Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot CLI, Cursor and Antigravity; availability depends on your SonarQube edition and subscription. In CI, SonarQube checks each pull request against its project’s quality gate , applying the gate’s new-code conditions. Its built-in “Sonar way for agentic AI” gate is recommended for agent centric development, and with your DevOps platform integration configured, a failing gate can block the merge. The verification gap is real. In Sonar’s own State of Code survey (1,149 responses, fieldwork in October 2025), 96% of developers said they do not fully trust that AI-generated code is functionally correct, yet only 48% completely agree that they always check AI-assisted code before committing. Verify AI-generated code with Sonar The model you choose will change. The standard your code has to meet should not. Sonar verifies every change against one consistent standard, independently of the tool that generated it, before it reaches production. That holds whether you standardize on one model, run several, or switch next quarter. Next steps Start free. Try the free plan of SonarQube Cloud , SonarQube Community Build or SonarQube for IDE on a repository where AI-generated code already lands. Connect your agents. Add the SonarQube MCP Server or Sonar Vortex to the coding agents your teams already use. Apply one gate. Start from the built-in “Sonar way for agentic AI” quality gate, and read the quality gate guide . Go deeper.
