Passing tests is not the same as being mergeable. METR had four maintainers from three open-source repositories review 296 AI-generated patches. Roughly half of the test-passing patches would not have been merged. Normalized to the roughly 68% merge rate of the human-written reference patches, maintainers’ merge rates ran about 24 percentage points below the automated score. METR tested agents from mid-2024 to late-2025 and cautions that this is a research note using one agent setup, not a claim about a fundamental limit on capability.

Setup matters, though how much is debated. Anthropic reported a 6-percentage-point gap on Terminal-Bench 2.0 between the most- and least-resourced infrastructure setups, and advised that “leaderboard differences below 3 percentage points deserve skepticism until the eval configuration is documented and matched.” A September 2026 study published by Arena (HarnessTax) found that the average effect of the harness on success rate stayed within about 2% on SWE-bench Lite and about 5% on Terminal-Bench 2.0, while costs differed by up to 5x.

Boards measure different things. Arena’s WebDev leaderboard ranks models from head-to-head votes (846,326 votes across 141 models as of 7 October 2026). SWE-bench-style boards score issue resolution against test suites. Terminal-Bench scores terminal tasks and is now on version 4.0. Each measures something real. None measures your codebase, and the top of the table can differ by benchmark and date.

Five questions to ask of any leaderboard

  1. Which model version and settings were tested: exact model ID, effort level and date?
  2. What is the test set, and is it still considered valid?
  3. What harness or agent ran the model, and is it the one you will use?
  4. How is success scored: automated tests, human preference or something else?
  5. How often is the board refreshed, and when was it last updated?

A ranking that cannot answer these questions is a headline, not evidence. That is why this post does not publish one.

How should teams choose an AI coding model? A five-step selection framework

Here is how to choose an AI coding model as an experiment you can repeat, not a one-time purchase decision.

1. Define the tasks and the acceptance bar

Pick the three to five tasks from the previous section that matter most to your team. Decide in advance what “accepted” means for each, for example merged without rework, or passing CI and one review. Writing the bar down first stops results from being reinterpreted later.

2. Shortlist two or three candidates and pin them

Build the shortlist from public benchmarks and vendor documentation, and include a model of a different type if your constraints allow. Pin each candidate to an exact model ID or snapshot rather than a moving alias. Anthropic documents that it does not update an existing model ID and ships updated versions under new IDs, and OpenAI documents that snapshots let you lock in a specific model version, while an alias such as chat-latest points to a snapshot that is regularly updated.

3. Pilot on your own work and measure acceptance

Use real tickets, with the same prompts, tools and repositories for every candidate. Record acceptance rate, review rounds, rework time, cost per accepted change and latency. A scorecard like this keeps the comparison honest.

Metric

Model A

Model B

Model C

Accepted without rework (%)




Review rounds per change (median)




CI passed on first attempt (%)




New issues per change, by severity




Cost per accepted change




Time to first usable result




4. Validate in CI, identically for every candidate

Run the same build, tests, static analysis, secrets and dependency checks on every candidate’s output, and enforce the same quality gate. This replaces “which model felt better” with evidence, and it applies one standard to all candidates.

5. Set guardrails and re-run when things change

Decide where AI-generated changes need human review, which paths are off limits, which models are approved, and what triggers a new pilot: a new model version, a retirement notice, a cost change or a rising rate of quality gate failures.

How do you build an AI coding stack that separates generation from verification?

Whichever model wins your pilot, treat it as one replaceable component. The model generates. A separate layer verifies. Keeping them apart lets you change models without changing your standards.

There are two reasons. The first is the evidence above: studies across many models find security and quality gaps in generated code, and passing tests does not mean a change is mergeable. The second is that self-review is a weaker control than it sounds. In one 2025 study of 14 open-source non-reasoning models on non-coding tasks, models corrected errors in external input that they failed to correct in their own output (Tsui). The wider evidence is mixed and mostly outside coding, so independent review combined with deterministic checks is a safer default, not a proven fix.

Sonar’s Agent Centric Development Cycle (AC/DC) organizes the work into three stages around the agent’s own generation.

Layer

Job

What changes when you switch models

Generate (model and agent)

Writes and edits code

Everything. This is the layer you are comparing.

Guide

Gives the agent your context and standards before it writes: instruction files and project context, for example through the SonarQube MCP Server

Little. Prompts and instructions may need retuning.

Verify

Checks every change against one standard in the agent loop, the IDE and CI: static analysis, security checks, quality gates

Nothing. The same standard applies to any model.

Solve

Fixes what verification finds, with the same checks confirming the fix

Nothing.

Sonar covers these layers with tools that work alongside the agents your teams already use. The SonarQube MCP Server connects supported agents and IDEs, including Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor, Gemini CLI and GitHub Copilot CLI, to SonarQube analysis, and is free and source-available. Sonar Vortex brings Guide, Verify and Solve into agents such as Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot CLI, Cursor and Antigravity; availability depends on your SonarQube edition and subscription. In CI, SonarQube checks each pull request against its project’s quality gate, applying the gate’s new-code conditions. Its built-in “Sonar way for agentic AI” gate is recommended for agent centric development, and with your DevOps platform integration configured, a failing gate can block the merge.

The verification gap is real. In Sonar’s own State of Code survey (1,149 responses, fieldwork in October 2025), 96% of developers said they do not fully trust that AI-generated code is functionally correct, yet only 48% completely agree that they always check AI-assisted code before committing.

Verify AI-generated code with Sonar

The model you choose will change. The standard your code has to meet should not. Sonar verifies every change against one consistent standard, independently of the tool that generated it, before it reaches production. That holds whether you standardize on one model, run several, or switch next quarter.

Next steps
  • Start free. Try the free plan of SonarQube Cloud, SonarQube Community Build or SonarQube for IDE on a repository where AI-generated code already lands.
  • Connect your agents. Add the SonarQube MCP Server or Sonar Vortex to the coding agents your teams already use.
  • Apply one gate. Start from the built-in “Sonar way for agentic AI” quality gate, and read the quality gate guide.
  • Go deeper. Read Code verification in software development, The coding personalities of leading LLMs and the State of Code survey report

items.title: Sonar's new JS/TS engine: Tracing meaning, not syntax, to hunt down real vulnerabilities
items.summary: What theory-grounded static analysis is supposed to buy you Static analysis covers a range of techniques. Linters sit at one end: they parse the code into a syntax tree and match against shapes in that tree: eval() called with anything other than a string literal, a dynamic value assigned straight into .innerHTML , a shell command assembled by concatenating in a variable, a string literal that looks like a hardcoded API key. That approach is cheap to build and cheap to run, and it catches real bugs, but it only catches the shapes someone thought to encode. It does not know what the code does, only what it looks like. Further along that spectrum, some tools take a genuine step up and reason over a call graph : which function calls which, and along which edges a value might travel between them. In a language where functions are ordinary values, passed around as callbacks and stored on objects, building an accurate call graph runs into the same chicken-and-egg problem as the analysis it is meant to support: resolving a call site often means knowing what a variable can point to, and answering that usually assumes a call graph already exists. Tools that try to get a call graph cheaply end up approximating it heavily, missing real edges or inventing ones that cannot happen. And even a reasonably complete graph does not, by itself, track which specific call produced which specific return: propagate a value along it without that context, and it can appear to leave through a return that belongs to an entirely different call to the same function. Data-flow analysis by abstract interpretation is a rigorous mathematical framework for approximating what a program actually does, with formal definitions of what it means for an analysis to be sound or precise. Source , sink , and sanitizer are taint analysis's own vocabulary, built on top of that foundation to ask one specific question: can a value at one program point reach another. An engine built on that theory does not match syntax at all. It computes whether a value at a given source can actually reach a given sink, through whatever the code actually does. Calls are resolved as the analysis goes, not in a separate pass beforehand: a call site's target falls out of what the abstract state already knows about the value being called, sidestepping the chicken-and-egg problem instead of suffering from it, and convergence is guaranteed through joins over the abstract lattice , at some cost to precision. That distinction stops being academic the moment the code stops looking like a textbook example. A syntactic rule for "tainted value reaches res.send() " written against a five-line example breaks the instant the value gets destructured, repackaged into an object, or routed through a second file, because none of that changes what the tree looks like at any one matched node, it just moves the value somewhere the rule was not written to look. A semantic analysis does not have that problem, because it was never matching a shape in the first place; it is still asking the same question, can this value reach this sink , regardless of how many hops sit in between. The hard part is real JavaScript and TypeScript Most backend JavaScript and TypeScript is not written to be easy to analyze. It is written to be maintainable: logic split across modules, request handling decomposed into routing layers and middleware chains, repeated UI or response-building logic factored into shared helper functions that take a single configuration object instead of a long parameter list. Frameworks like Express encourage exactly this shape, and it is good engineering practice. It is also what turns a single tainted value into a moving target: by the time a query parameter reaches wherever it is actually used, it may have passed through several function calls, been repackaged into an object alongside a handful of unrelated fields, crossed a module boundary through an ordinary import, and been reassembled into a new string through template-literal interpolation . An analysis that only tracks direct assignment within a single function has no chance here. It either misses the finding or, just as often, keeps the finding but cannot reconstruct a path that a human reviewer can actually verify, which is close to useless in practice. Handling this class of code requires modeling destructuring , including destructured, typed function parameters, object-literal shorthand properties as pass-through, positional argument-to-parameter binding across calls, resolution across ES module imports, return-value propagation through several stacked functions, fine-grained tracking inside long template literals with multiple interpolation points, and framework-specific knowledge of what actually constitutes a sink. The vulnerability below shipped inside a single commit that bundled about ten unrelated tool integrations at once: 62 files, roughly 16,800 lines changed , of which the vulnerable path accounts for a few hundred. That is an ordinary way for this kind of bug to enter a codebase, as one small, unremarkable-looking piece of a much larger, mostly unrelated change. Whoever looks at that diff, a human under deadline pressure or an agent asked to check it for problems, has to give one destructured field passed between two files the same attention as the other sixty files asking for it at the same time. Agents are increasingly good at writing this kind of code and at skimming it for what looks reasonable, and they can also lose the thread in a large diff or state with confidence that something is fine when it isn't. Skimming for what looks reasonable and proving where a value can and cannot end up are different tasks, and it is easy to mistake one for the other. The FlowiseAI callback below is a concrete example of exactly this terrain, and a demonstration of what the underlying analysis is capable of when all of the above holds together end to end. Technical details Component routes/oauth2/index.ts & routes/oauth2/templates.ts Endpoint GET /api/v1/oauth2-credential/callback Auth required None Class Reflected HTML injection (partially mitigated by an existing sanitization middleware) Introduced in A single feature commit bundling unrelated integrations (62 files, ~16,800 lines) Commit 30c4180d9737f937ec9c943c6241e4039a90e3d4 Status Fixed independently by the FlowiseAI team Flowise credentials can go through an OAuth2 authorization-code flow. When the provider redirects back, it hits the endpoint above, implemented in index.ts . The handler reads the query string and, on any failure path, renders an HTML error page describing what went wrong. All snippets are from the commit where the issue was present. BrowserGET .../callbackindex.tsroute handlertemplates.tsHTML rendererBrowserstate= generateErrorPage()res.send(html) The request's state parameter travels from the route handler into the template renderer and back out as the response body. The source router.get('/callback', async (req: Request, res: Response) => { try { const { code, state, error, error_description } = req.query The handler itself is an anonymous callback handed to Express's routing API, not a function called directly anywhere in this file. It only runs when Express invokes it with a real req and res for a matching request, so recognizing req.query as a source here means knowing what router.get(path, handler) does with handler . state , error , and error_description come straight from the query string with no validation. Building the message if (!credential) { const errorHtml = generateErrorPage( 'Credential not found', `Credential not found for the provided state: ${state}`, 'Please try the authorization process again.' ) res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/html') return res.status(404).send(errorHtml) } state is folded into a new string through template-literal interpolation, then passed as the second positional argument of generateErrorPage . The engine has to know which parameter binds to which argument here, since the first and third arguments aren't tainted. Crossing the file boundary export const generateErrorPage = (error: string, message: string, details?: string): string => { return generateOAuth2ResponsePage({ title: 'OAuth2 Authorization Error', statusIcon: '✗', statusText: 'Authorization Failed', statusColor: '#f44336', message, details, postMessageType: 'OAUTH2_ERROR', postMessageData: { success: false, message, error }, autoCloseDelay: 3000 }) } The tainted argument lands in the message parameter, then is repackaged using object-literal shorthand ( message, ) as one field of a nine-field options object , most of which are hardcoded literals unrelated to the request. Destructured again, into the sink template export const generateOAuth2ResponsePage = (options: OAuth2PageOptions): string => { const { title, statusIcon, statusText, statusColor, message, details, ... } = options ${message} generateOAuth2ResponsePage destructures the object directly in its parameter list, then interpolates message into a ~70-line template literal alongside several untainted interpolations. The returned string bubbles back up through two call frames to index.ts , gets assigned to errorHtml , and is handed to res.send() . Issue explorer · tssecurity:S5131 The real 16-location flow our engine reported, condensed to its 10 meaningful hops. Click a step to see exactly where it lands. 1. Source: req.query.state index.ts:159 2. Template literal `...${state}` index.ts:190 3. Argument #2 of generateErrorPage(...) index.ts:188 4. Parameter `message` templates.ts:112 5. Shorthand property in options object templates.ts:118 6. Argument of generateOAuth2ResponsePage(...) templates.ts:113 7. Destructured from typed parameter templates.ts:21 8. Template literal ` ${message} ` templates.ts:69 ↑ return value, 2 call frames up 9. Sink: res.send(errorHtml) index.ts:195 packages/server/src/routes/oauth2/index.ts // OAuth2 callback endpoint router.get('/callback', async (req: Request, res: Response) => { try { const { code, state, error, error_description } = req.query if (error) { const errorHtml = generateErrorPage( error as string, (error_description as string) || 'An error occurred', error_description ? `Description: ${error_description}` : undefined ) res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/html') return res.status(400).send(errorHtml) } if (!code || !state) { const errorHtml = generateErrorPage('Missing required parameters', 'Missing code or state', 'Please try again later.') res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/html') return res.status(400).send(errorHtml) } const appServer = getRunningExpressApp() const credentialRepository = appServer.AppDataSource.getRepository(Credential) // Find credential by state (assuming state contains the credential ID) const credential = await credentialRepository.findOneBy({ id: state as string }) if (!credential) { const errorHtml = generateErrorPage( 'Credential not found', `Credential not found for the provided state: ${state}`, 'Please try the authorization process again.' ) res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/html') return res.status(404).send(errorHtml) } packages/server/src/routes/oauth2/templates.ts export interface OAuth2PageOptions { title: string statusIcon: string statusText: string statusColor: string message: string details?: string postMessageType: 'OAUTH2_SUCCESS' | 'OAUTH2_ERROR' postMessageData: any autoCloseDelay: number } export const generateOAuth2ResponsePage = (options: OAuth2PageOptions): string => { const { title, statusIcon, statusText, statusColor, message, details, postMessageType, postMessageData, autoCloseDelay } = options return ` ${title} ${statusIcon} ${statusText} ${message} ${details ? ` ${details} ` : ''} ` } export const generateErrorPage = (error: string, message: string, details?: string): string => { return generateOAuth2ResponsePage({ title: 'OAuth2 Authorization Error', statusIcon: '✗', statusText: 'Authorization Failed', statusColor: '#f44336', message, details, postMessageType: 'OAUTH2_ERROR', postMessageData: { success: false, message, error }, autoCloseDelay: 3000 }) } Source: req.query.state : state is destructured straight from the query string. A user can put anything here. None of the individual steps above are exotic. This is idiomatic TypeScript, the kind any team, or any coding agent, writes every day. That is precisely why it makes a good demonstration: it is the theory doing the same work it does in the literature, applied to code nobody wrote with a scanner in mind. To carry this taint from source to sink, an engine needs, at minimum: Destructuring as a taint-carrying construct, in both const { x } = obj statements and destructured, typed function parameters. Object-literal shorthand properties as pass-through, distinguishing the one tainted field from eight untainted siblings in the same object. Positional argument-to-parameter binding across a call, not just "this function was called with a tainted argument somewhere." Resolution across a plain ES import , treating two files as one call graph rather than two independent units. Return-value propagation through multiple stacked function calls. Fine-grained tracking inside a long template literal , separating the one tainted interpolation from several untainted ones next to it. Framework-aware entry-point knowledge : router.get(path, handler) is what invokes handler with a real req and res at request time, which is what makes req.query a source in the first place, inside a callback nobody calls directly. Framework-aware sink knowledge : res.send() on an Express Response renders as HTML, and that holds a few lines after an unrelated res.setHeader() call, inside a conditional branch, inside an async route handler, inside a try block. A tool built on regexes or single-function pattern matching does not get past the second step. A tool with only shallow interprocedural support loses the value at the object-literal repackaging, or at the destructured-parameter unpacking. Miss any one of these and the engine either drops the finding or keeps it without being able to justify the path, which, for a reviewer deciding whether to trust the report, amounts to the same failure. Real-world impact and fix Flowise runs a global sanitization middleware on every query parameter, backed by sanitize-html , specifically to guard against XSS. Its default configuration strips

items.title: AI coding ROI is a throughput problem, and verification is how you solve it
items.summary: Planning season is around the corner, and for many engineering leaders this year's budget conversation includes a line item that barely existed two years ago: AI coding tools and the tokens they consume. The adoption story is easy to tell, since most software developers now work with coding agents every week and code volume has grown accordingly. The harder question, and the one finance teams are increasingly asking, is what all of that code has actually delivered to the business. Before we get into what to do about it, let's look at where the value of AI-generated code sits and where it tends to leak away. What does business value look like in AI-assisted development? AI coding agents are now part of everyday professional development. JetBrains' 2026 Developer Ecosystem Survey found that 90% of professional developers use AI coding agents at work at least weekly, and 68% use them daily. In BairesDev's Q3 2026 Dev Barometer , 42% of the software developers surveyed said AI writes at least half their code, up from 12% a year earlier. These figures measure adoption and activity, and they tell you very little about return. Software development produces value only when working change reaches production and does what the business needs it to do. Until that happens, code carries cost in tokens, compute, review hours, and engineering attention without giving the business anything it can use. That is where the picture gets uncomfortable, because activity and value are now moving apart. Telemetry from 22,000 developers in Faros's Q2 2026 AI Engineering Report shows teams with high AI adoption completing 66% more epics, while deployments per week fell by nearly 12% and incidents per pull request tripled. CloudBees' State of Code Abundance 2026 found that 67% of enterprise technology leaders report a significant increase in code volume, yet only 31% of AI spend can be attributed to specific business outcomes, and 81% have seen production issues from AI-generated code increase. Code is moving faster while the value it delivers lags behind. Agentic development ROI therefore comes down to the ratio between verified changes that ship and stay shipped and the full cost of producing them. Raising the first and lowering the second is what makes AI pay for itself, whereas measuring generation volume alone tends to produce gains that never show up in the P&L. Where does the value of AI-generated code leak away? Value rarely disappears in one dramatic moment. It erodes through four distinct forces, each with its own cost profile, which is why it helps to look at them one at a time. Production cycles stretched by retries. Agents rarely ship on the first attempt. When a generation fails a build or a review, the agent tries again, often regenerating far more than the defect required, and every loop consumes tokens and calendar time. As AI coding tools move from flat-rate licenses to usage-based billing, those loops become a cost finance can see, and code quality has a direct effect on the size of the bill: Sonar research found that agents working in cleaner codebases used 7.2% fewer input tokens and 8.5% fewer output tokens on the same tasks, with no meaningful change in completion rate. Rework. AI-generated code has an awkward habit of looking right. 61% of developers say AI often produces code that looks correct but isn't reliable, and 38% say reviewing it takes more effort than reviewing a colleague's work. Defects that pass a quick review surface later, after integration or release, and the work has to be done twice, so the time saved in generation gets spent again in correction. Developers still lose roughly a quarter of their week to toil, regardless of how heavily they use AI. Remediation. Issues that slip past review settle into the codebase as debt. Carnegie Mellon researchers studying 807 open-source repositories that adopted Cursor found a three-to-five-times increase in lines of code added in the first month that proved temporary, alongside a persistent 30% increase in static analysis warnings and a 41% increase in code complexity. The study covers open-source projects and a single tool, so it doesn't describe every enterprise team or coding agent, but it shows the risk clearly. Debt of this kind is costly in two ways: it slows down the engineers who maintain the code, and it raises the cost of every future agent run that has to work through it. Incidents. Problems that get past the earlier stages eventually reach customers. DORA's 2024 research associated every 25% increase in AI adoption with an estimated 7.2% decrease in delivery stability, and its 2025 report found AI still associated with rising instability. Incidents are where engineering cost turns into business cost, through lost revenue, breached SLAs, regulatory exposure, and executive attention pulled away from growth. How do AI coding costs compound? AI coding costs compound because the four forces, while distinct, reinforce each other when nobody intervenes. Unverified code that leaves the agent loop can become rework at review, and rework that misses something can turn into remediation debt. That debt makes the codebase harder for both people and agents to change, which lengthens the next cycle and raises the next token bill, and the defects that escape all of it become incidents. The result is a cost that grows with every cycle that runs without verification, and a problem that would have taken minutes to fix inside the agent loop can end up as a postmortem. Why is throughput the number that matters? Generation speed is the easiest number to collect, which is probably why it ends up on so many dashboards, but it is also the number least connected to value. Throughput is the rate at which verified, working change reaches production, and it holds up when speed and stability improve together. DORA's data illustrates the risk when the two diverge: in 2024, a 25% increase in AI adoption was associated with an estimated 1.5% decrease in delivery throughput, alongside the drop in stability. By 2025 the throughput association had turned positive, while the association with instability persisted. DORA describes AI as an amplifier that magnifies the strengths of strong delivery systems and the weaknesses of weak ones. Anyone who has queued at a supermarket with a single open checkout already knows the principle behind this: the line moves only as fast as its slowest point. Agents moved that slowest point from writing code to verifying it. Every change that loops back for another attempt consumes the capacity of that stage a second time, so reducing those loops is one of the most direct ways to raise throughput where it is constrained. This is the business case for verification. Done well, it protects AI speed by giving it a chance to survive into delivery, and a verification program that works shows up as rising throughput and a falling cost per accepted change. The number of findings it produces says much less about whether it is working. How can teams reduce rework in agentic development? There is no single switch that fixes this, but five practices make a measurable difference when they are applied together. 1. Guide agents before they write. Many retries start with an agent that lacks context about your architecture and standards. Supplying that context up front raises first-pass quality and removes the codebase discovery work that inflates token costs. 2. Verify inside the agent loop. Check code as it is generated, so problems surface while the agent is still working on the change. An agent that sees a security flaw or logic error while writing can correct it before the change reaches a reviewer, whereas the same flaw found at review costs a full cycle, and found in production it costs an incident. 3. Hold every change to one independent standard before merge. Teams reduce rework most reliably when they apply a single, deterministic quality and security standard to human and AI code alike, run by a system separate from the one that generated the code, because a model grading its own output cannot provide independent verification. DORA's research also points to small batch sizes and strong testing as fundamentals that shape whether AI improves delivery, so it pays to keep changes small enough to review properly. 4. Fix what verification finds, automatically. Findings that wait in a backlog become debt, so resolve them at the pull request when a quality gate fails and work down the existing backlog continuously, re-verifying every fix before a developer sees it. 5. Report metrics that tie AI spend to shipped value. Replace activity metrics with software delivery metrics a CFO can audit, such as cost per accepted change, first-pass acceptance rate, time from first draft to merge, rework rate, change failure rate, and the trend in the remediation backlog. CI loop effectiveness, meaning the share of problems caught before merge, is the leading indicator behind all of them. But does verification actually pay off? It's a fair question, especially when verification sounds like one more step between an agent and a merged pull request. Organizations that verify systematically report better results. In the 2026 State of Code Developer Survey , SonarQube users were 44% less likely to report production outages caused by AI-generated code. They were also more likely than non-users to say AI had a positive impact on rework and patch costs (47% versus 40%) and defect rates (44% versus 37%), with a similar gap on vulnerability rates (39% versus 31%). Costs move with quality as well. As we saw earlier, Sonar research found that agents working in healthier codebases used 7.2% fewer input tokens and 8.5% fewer output tokens on the same tasks, which makes code quality an AI cost lever in its own right. Context has a separate effect on top of that: when Sonar Vortex gives agents precise, governed context instead of leaving them to search the codebase file by file, Sonar research shows up to 36% lower token consumption on refactoring tasks . How does Sonar help turn AI speed into shipped software? Sonar provides independent AI code verification across the full agentic development cycle, from the agent's first draft to the main branch, with each capability aimed at a specific force: Sonar Vortex gives agents your project's standards and codebase context before they write, then verifies their output while they work, which reduces retries and the token costs that come with them. SonarQube applies deterministic analysis across more than 40 languages with a 3.2% false-positive rate, and its quality gates enforce one standard on every pull request, whether a person or an agent wrote the code, which reduces rework and the incidents that follow from it. Gitar reviews every pull request and diagnoses CI failures, then iterates on fixes until the build passes, shortening the time from first draft to merge. SonarQube Remediation Agent generates fixes when a quality gate fails and works down the existing backlog in the background, re-verifying every fix before it opens a pull request, so the backlog shrinks over time instead of compounding. Together, these capabilities give the time AI saves in generation a much better chance of reaching production as working software, delivered faster and at a lower cost per change. Where to start AI-generated code becomes business value only when it ships and holds up in production. Retries, rework, remediation, and incidents are where that value leaks, and they compound when left unchecked, so the earlier you catch them, the more of your AI investment you keep. If you're preparing next year's AI budget, start by measuring what share of your AI-generated changes ship and stay shipped, and what each of those changes cost to get there. That baseline will tell you more about your AI coding ROI than any count of lines generated, and it gives you something concrete to show finance once verification starts moving the number. Start reducing AI coding waste with Sonar .

That is where the picture gets uncomfortable, because activity and value are now moving apart. Telemetry from 22,000 developers in Faros's Q2 2026 AI Engineering Report shows teams with high AI adoption completing 66% more epics, while deployments per week fell by nearly 12% and incidents per pull request tripled. CloudBees' State of Code Abundance 2026 found that 67% of enterprise technology leaders report a significant increase in code volume, yet only 31% of AI spend can be attributed to specific business outcomes, and 81% have seen production issues from AI-generated code increase. Code is moving faster while the value it delivers lags behind.

Agentic development ROI therefore comes down to the ratio between verified changes that ship and stay shipped and the full cost of producing them. Raising the first and lowering the second is what makes AI pay for itself, whereas measuring generation volume alone tends to produce gains that never show up in the P&L.

Where does the value of AI-generated code leak away?

Value rarely disappears in one dramatic moment. It erodes through four distinct forces, each with its own cost profile, which is why it helps to look at them one at a time.

Production cycles stretched by retries. Agents rarely ship on the first attempt. When a generation fails a build or a review, the agent tries again, often regenerating far more than the defect required, and every loop consumes tokens and calendar time. As AI coding tools move from flat-rate licenses to usage-based billing, those loops become a cost finance can see, and code quality has a direct effect on the size of the bill: Sonar research found that agents working in cleaner codebases used 7.2% fewer input tokens and 8.5% fewer output tokens on the same tasks, with no meaningful change in completion rate.

Rework. AI-generated code has an awkward habit of looking right. 61% of developers say AI often produces code that looks correct but isn't reliable, and 38% say reviewing it takes more effort than reviewing a colleague's work. Defects that pass a quick review surface later, after integration or release, and the work has to be done twice, so the time saved in generation gets spent again in correction. Developers still lose roughly a quarter of their week to toil, regardless of how heavily they use AI.

Remediation. Issues that slip past review settle into the codebase as debt. Carnegie Mellon researchers studying 807 open-source repositories that adopted Cursor found a three-to-five-times increase in lines of code added in the first month that proved temporary, alongside a persistent 30% increase in static analysis warnings and a 41% increase in code complexity. The study covers open-source projects and a single tool, so it doesn't describe every enterprise team or coding agent, but it shows the risk clearly. Debt of this kind is costly in two ways: it slows down the engineers who maintain the code, and it raises the cost of every future agent run that has to work through it.

Incidents. Problems that get past the earlier stages eventually reach customers. DORA's 2024 research associated every 25% increase in AI adoption with an estimated 7.2% decrease in delivery stability, and its 2025 report found AI still associated with rising instability. Incidents are where engineering cost turns into business cost, through lost revenue, breached SLAs, regulatory exposure, and executive attention pulled away from growth.

How do AI coding costs compound?

AI coding costs compound because the four forces, while distinct, reinforce each other when nobody intervenes. Unverified code that leaves the agent loop can become rework at review, and rework that misses something can turn into remediation debt. That debt makes the codebase harder for both people and agents to change, which lengthens the next cycle and raises the next token bill, and the defects that escape all of it become incidents. The result is a cost that grows with every cycle that runs without verification, and a problem that would have taken minutes to fix inside the agent loop can end up as a postmortem.

Why is throughput the number that matters?

Generation speed is the easiest number to collect, which is probably why it ends up on so many dashboards, but it is also the number least connected to value.

Throughput is the rate at which verified, working change reaches production, and it holds up when speed and stability improve together. DORA's data illustrates the risk when the two diverge: in 2024, a 25% increase in AI adoption was associated with an estimated 1.5% decrease in delivery throughput, alongside the drop in stability. By 2025 the throughput association had turned positive, while the association with instability persisted. DORA describes AI as an amplifier that magnifies the strengths of strong delivery systems and the weaknesses of weak ones.

Anyone who has queued at a supermarket with a single open checkout already knows the principle behind this: the line moves only as fast as its slowest point. Agents moved that slowest point from writing code to verifying it. Every change that loops back for another attempt consumes the capacity of that stage a second time, so reducing those loops is one of the most direct ways to raise throughput where it is constrained.

This is the business case for verification. Done well, it protects AI speed by giving it a chance to survive into delivery, and a verification program that works shows up as rising throughput and a falling cost per accepted change. The number of findings it produces says much less about whether it is working.

How can teams reduce rework in agentic development?

There is no single switch that fixes this, but five practices make a measurable difference when they are applied together.

1. Guide agents before they write. Many retries start with an agent that lacks context about your architecture and standards. Supplying that context up front raises first-pass quality and removes the codebase discovery work that inflates token costs.

2. Verify inside the agent loop. Check code as it is generated, so problems surface while the agent is still working on the change. An agent that sees a security flaw or logic error while writing can correct it before the change reaches a reviewer, whereas the same flaw found at review costs a full cycle, and found in production it costs an incident.

3. Hold every change to one independent standard before merge. Teams reduce rework most reliably when they apply a single, deterministic quality and security standard to human and AI code alike, run by a system separate from the one that generated the code, because a model grading its own output cannot provide independent verification. DORA's research also points to small batch sizes and strong testing as fundamentals that shape whether AI improves delivery, so it pays to keep changes small enough to review properly.

4. Fix what verification finds, automatically. Findings that wait in a backlog become debt, so resolve them at the pull request when a quality gate fails and work down the existing backlog continuously, re-verifying every fix before a developer sees it.

5. Report metrics that tie AI spend to shipped value. Replace activity metrics with software delivery metrics a CFO can audit, such as cost per accepted change, first-pass acceptance rate, time from first draft to merge, rework rate, change failure rate, and the trend in the remediation backlog. CI loop effectiveness, meaning the share of problems caught before merge, is the leading indicator behind all of them.

But does verification actually pay off?

It's a fair question, especially when verification sounds like one more step between an agent and a merged pull request. Organizations that verify systematically report better results. In the 2026 State of Code Developer Survey, SonarQube users were 44% less likely to report production outages caused by AI-generated code. They were also more likely than non-users to say AI had a positive impact on rework and patch costs (47% versus 40%) and defect rates (44% versus 37%), with a similar gap on vulnerability rates (39% versus 31%).

Costs move with quality as well. As we saw earlier, Sonar research found that agents working in healthier codebases used 7.2% fewer input tokens and 8.5% fewer output tokens on the same tasks, which makes code quality an AI cost lever in its own right. Context has a separate effect on top of that: when Sonar Vortex gives agents precise, governed context instead of leaving them to search the codebase file by file, Sonar research shows up to 36% lower token consumption on refactoring tasks.

How does Sonar help turn AI speed into shipped software?

Sonar provides independent AI code verification across the full agentic development cycle, from the agent's first draft to the main branch, with each capability aimed at a specific force:

  • Sonar Vortex gives agents your project's standards and codebase context before they write, then verifies their output while they work, which reduces retries and the token costs that come with them.
  • SonarQube applies deterministic analysis across more than 40 languages with a 3.2% false-positive rate, and its quality gates enforce one standard on every pull request, whether a person or an agent wrote the code, which reduces rework and the incidents that follow from it.
  • Gitar reviews every pull request and diagnoses CI failures, then iterates on fixes until the build passes, shortening the time from first draft to merge.
  • SonarQube Remediation Agent generates fixes when a quality gate fails and works down the existing backlog in the background, re-verifying every fix before it opens a pull request, so the backlog shrinks over time instead of compounding.

Together, these capabilities give the time AI saves in generation a much better chance of reaching production as working software, delivered faster and at a lower cost per change.

Where to start

AI-generated code becomes business value only when it ships and holds up in production. Retries, rework, remediation, and incidents are where that value leaks, and they compound when left unchecked, so the earlier you catch them, the more of your AI investment you keep.

If you're preparing next year's AI budget, start by measuring what share of your AI-generated changes ship and stay shipped, and what each of those changes cost to get there. That baseline will tell you more about your AI coding ROI than any count of lines generated, and it gives you something concrete to show finance once verification starts moving the number.

items.title: FBI Disrupts North Korean Famous Chollima Laptop Farms Used to Infiltrate U.S. Companies
items.summary: The FBI disrupted several U.S. laptop farms used by North Korean threat group FAMOUS CHOLLIMA in late September 2026, cutting off infrastructure that helped fake remote workers enter American companies. CrowdStrike disclosed the joint operation on October 13, describing it as the start of a wider effort against the group’s domestic support network. The farms housed company laptops that overseas operatives controlled remotely while posing as U.S. employees. This setup helped them hide their locations, collect salaries for North Korea’s regime, and keep access to employer systems. CrowdStrike said dozens of affected organizations operated across aerospace, energy, finance, healthcare, cybersecurity, defense engineering, government technology, and consumer technology. CrowdStrike researchers identified false identities, technical indicators, and U.S. computers supporting the scheme between April 2025 and June 2026. Their report on the disruption describes remote access tools and hardware abuse, not a newly identified malware family. The team combined device activity with targeted investigations to uncover local facilitators and share findings with the FBI. FBI Disrupts North Korean Famous Chollima Laptop Farms Used The operation depended on a simple gap: a worker hired under a stolen identity could not easily receive a company laptop abroad without raising questions. As earlier reporting on North Korean identity fraud explains, local helpers provide the addresses and equipment needed to make overseas workers appear domestic. CrowdStrike observed operatives filing false police reports claiming laptops had been stolen, then requesting replacements at farm addresses. Others claimed sudden moves to redirect deliveries or rotated through residential addresses to hide the final destination. Some obtained jobs through IT staffing firms, allowing client devices to reach farms without those firms knowing. Once a laptop arrived, a facilitator added hardware and software for remote control. The physical device stayed in the United States while its operator worked elsewhere. This local presence helped the group pass location checks, handle employer equipment, and support identity and financial checks needed to receive wages. The farms also supplied a trusted local presence for financial checks. CrowdStrike described facilitators as providing a physical address, a legal identity, and a route through bank due diligence requirements. That makes the support network more than a place to store laptops: it connects hiring, access, and payment. Taking a farm offline forces operators to rebuild that chain, even when the wider group can move elsewhere. Device Spoofing Complicates Detection Since May 2026, CrowdStrike has observed FAMOUS CHOLLIMA spoofing device hashes, including making a video capture card appear to be a webcam. Researchers also saw the same disguised device across separate victim organizations, suggesting operators reused device identifiers while trying to avoid detection. Farm networks shared identifiers across several fake worker identities at the same time, offering another clue to coordinated activity. The findings complement earlier coverage of remote interview fraud tactics , where stand-ins and remote desktop tools helped hide who was actually completing interviews and technical work. The distinction matters for defenders: a legitimate tool can support an illegal operation without being malware. CrowdStrike names Astrill VPN, AnyDesk, OBS Studio, and PiKVM as technologies to review in context. Their presence alone does not prove compromise, but unexplained use alongside identity or shipping inconsistencies deserves investigation. CrowdStrike recommends standard background checks and reviews for reused phone numbers, email addresses, bank accounts, resume wording, and website content across profiles. Other warning signs include differences between identity documents and video appearances, suspicious job references, new public profiles, and login activity inconsistent with a worker’s claimed location. The latest disruption follows earlier nationwide laptop farm searches reported in June 2025, but the operations should not be treated as the same case. CrowdStrike did not disclose an exact farm count, arrest total, or seized device count for the September 2026 action. CrowdStrike warned that the disruption will likely have a limited local effect rather than stop the wider operation. FAMOUS CHOLLIMA remains active and is expected to adapt, making continued checks on worker identity, device delivery, and remote access important beyond the initial hiring process. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Type Source-reported indicator Context Hashes No values published Device spoofing described only Tools Astrill VPN, AnyDesk, OBS Studio, PiKVM Review unexpected use Hardware Capture card disguised as webcam Device identity mismatch Infrastructure Shared identifiers across fake personas Possible coordinated farms Identity Reused contact, banking, or resume details Compare applicant records Location Shipping address and login discrepancies Check claimed residence Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally defanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM . Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. Automated discovery and adaptive deception help keep decoys and breadcrumbs realistic as infrastructure and attack surfaces change. Strong security integrations allow deception alerts to support investigation, correlation, containment, and broader incident response workflows. Buyers should evaluate the quality of attacker intelligence, including visibility into reconnaissance, lateral movement, tools, targets, and TTPs. For security teams comparing deception technology vendors, the differences matter. Its deception capabilities include honeypots, Honey Users, Honey Files, and Honey Credentials, which create fake systems, identities, data, and credentials that legitimate users should have no reason to access. Honeypots can detect network reconnaissance and connection attempts, while Honey Users provide Active Directory deception. Honey Credentials inject fake credentials into Windows endpoint memory to expose credential harvesting and pass-the-hash activity. Rapid7 also supports AWS honeypots for monitoring lateral movement and reconnaissance within VPC environments. Commvault Threatwise Commvault Threatwise approaches deception from a cyber resilience perspective, using cyber deception technology to identify threats before attackers can compromise critical systems or data. It deploys authentic threat sensors that mimic real IT, OT, network, and backup assets, creating false resources designed to attract and divert attackers away from production environments. Threatwise focuses heavily on early-warning detection . Interactions with deceptive assets can expose reconnaissance, lateral movement, unwanted privileged access, ransomware, and other advanced attacks that bypass conventional security controls. The platform provides real-time visibility into this activity, helping security teams investigate and respond before attackers progress to encryption, data exfiltration, or other damaging actions. Deployment and scalability are also central to the platform. Threatwise is cloud-delivered and designed to deploy and scale deception quickly across on-premises, cloud, and backup environments. AI-guided recommendations can assist with intelligent decoy placement, while integrations with other security solutions allow deception signals to contribute to broader response workflows. Key capabilities: Early-warning ransomware and cyberattack detection Authentic threat sensors that mimic IT, OT, network, and backup assets Attacker diversion using deceptive resources Reconnaissance and lateral movement detection Detection of unwanted privileged access Real-time threat visibility and precision alerts AI-guided recommendations for decoy placement What Should Organizations Look for in a Deception Technology Solution in 2027? A comparison of top deception technology solutions should look beyond individual feature lists and assess how effectively each platform supports an organization’s infrastructure, attack surface, security workflows, and threat detection priorities. When evaluating the best deception technology software, organizations should remember that the strongest deception platform is not necessarily the one that deploys the largest number of decoys. Organizations should evaluate how effectively deception represents their real infrastructure and whether it can continue doing so as that infrastructure changes. Each deception technology vendor should also be evaluated based on how well its platform integrates with the organization’s existing detection, investigation, and response workflows. Coverage across the attack surface is critical. Modern cyber deception solutions should extend beyond traditional networks to identities, endpoints, cloud workloads, containers, IoT, and, where relevant, OT environments. Automation and adaptability are equally important. Static deception assets can become less effective as environments evolve. Platforms that discover infrastructure and dynamically adapt deception can reduce management overhead while maintaining authenticity. Identity deception should also receive greater attention. Attackers increasingly use legitimate credentials to move through environments, making deceptive accounts, credentials, and identity artifacts valuable detection points. Organizations should also examine integration with detection and response workflows. A deception alert becomes considerably more useful when analysts can correlate it with endpoint activity, network traffic, identity events, threat intelligence, and other telemetry. When comparing top deception-based breach solutions, organizations should consider whether deception-generated signals can contribute directly to investigation, containment, and broader incident response processes. Finally, evaluate the quality of attacker intelligence produced by the platform. Knowing that someone interacted with a decoy is useful; understanding their reconnaissance behavior, attempted lateral movement, tools, targets, and TTPs gives defenders significantly more information for investigation and future defense. The leading deception technology solutions in 2027 offer capabilities such as decoys, breadcrumbs, credential deception, lateral movement detection, automated response, and integration with broader security platforms. items.title: Update Windows: Record Patch Tuesday fixes flaw already under attack
items.summary: Microsoft’s October Patch Tuesday release addresses a record-breaking 1,413 vulnerabilities , including an actively exploited Windows Shell zero-day and two other publicly disclosed flaws. Just when you thought a previous record would stand for a while, Microsoft comes out again with the largest monthly Patch Tuesday release. Microsoft has said its growing use of AI to find and fix security vulnerabilities means users should expect more fixes in its monthly updates. How to apply patches and check if you’re protected These updates fix security problems and help keep your Windows PC protected. Here’s how to make sure you’re up to date: Click the Start button, then open Settings . Select Windows Update (usually at the bottom of the menu on the left). Click Check for updates . Windows will search for the latest security updates. If you’ve enabled Get the latest updates as soon as they’re available under More options , you may be prompted to restart immediately to complete the update. Otherwise, continue to the next step. If updates are available, they’ll start downloading automatically. When they’re ready, click Install or Restart now if prompted. Your computer may need a restart to finish the update. After restarting, go back to Windows Update and check again. If it says You’re up to date , you’re all set. Technical details As usual, we’ve selected a few vulnerabilities to highlight for readers interested in the technical details. We’ll start with the actively exploited vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-96951 ( CVSS score 8.8 out of 10), a Windows Shell security feature bypass vulnerability. The security feature it can bypass is the Mark of the Web (MOTW) defense, which can warn users about potentially unsafe downloaded files. Successful exploitation requires user interaction. For example, in an email or instant message attack, the attacker could send the targeted user a specially crafted file designed to exploit the vulnerability, but the user would have to click a link or open an attachment. Another one to keep an eye on is CVE-2026-108398 (CVSS score 8.8 out of 10), where an untrusted search path in .NET Framework allows an authorized attacker to bypass a security feature locally. The bypassed feature is Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC), which could lead to the ability to run unauthorized applications on target systems. This vulnerability was publicly disclosed before the patch. Another publicly disclosed vulnerability is CVE-2026-92707 (CVSS score 5.3 out of 10). The flaw can let an unauthenticated remote attacker exhaust memory in affected applications that process specially crafted MessagePack data. MessagePack-CSharp is a software component that helps applications pack and unpack data in a compact format, making it efficient to store or exchange information. Exposure depends on how a service uses the library to pack and unpack the information. From reporting threats to removing them. Cybersecurity risks should never spread beyond a headline. Keep threats off your devices by downloading Malwarebytes today .

items.title: Fake Calendly “Meta Careers” pages steal Facebook and Google logins
items.summary: We found a wave of websites posing as Calendly booking pages for job interviews at Meta. Visitors pick a slot for a 30-minute phone call with a recruiter, fill in their details, and pass what looks like a CAPTCHA. Then the page asks them to log in to Facebook. The interview is fake. The pages are designed to steal the visitor’s Facebook login details, including the two-factor authentication (2FA) codes meant to protect the account. Visitors are then asked to sign in to their Google account too, supposedly “for security.” These pages are not affiliated with Meta, Calendly, or Google. If you’ve already entered a password or approved a sign-in prompt, secure the affected accounts straight away. See “How to stay safe” below. Why Calendly makes a convincing disguise Calendly is a widely used scheduling tool, and recruiters use it to book interviews. Clicking a booking link, picking a time, and typing in your name and email is something people do without a second thought. There’s no account to create and nothing to download. That routine makes it a good disguise. By the time the page asks for something unusual, the visitor has already picked a slot and shared their details. Going along with one more step can feel easier than starting to doubt the whole thing. For someone who has sent out application after application without hearing back, an invitation to interview at Meta may be exactly the kind of message they hope for. Excitement, and the fear of missing a rare chance, can push people to move quickly instead of checking who actually sent the link. Job seekers are also used to sharing personal details with strangers. Handing your name, email, and phone number to a recruiter you’ve never met is a normal part of applying, so a form asking for them may not raise any alarms. A job interview that starts with a calendar The fake page copies Calendly’s booking screen, titled “Calendly | Meta Careers.” It shows a monthly calendar, a time zone picker, and a 30-minute “Phone call.” The available times are loaded from the attackers’ server, so the calendar looks like a real recruiter’s schedule. After the visitor picks a time, the page walks them through a series of steps: Your details. A form asks for your name, email address, and phone number, plus anything that “will help prepare for our meeting.” A fake CAPTCHA. A grid of images asks you to “Select all images with…”. It makes the page feel legitimate, and it may also stop automated security scanners from seeing what comes next. A Facebook login. A window within the page copies Facebook’s login page. It even draws its own fake address bar showing a Facebook web address, so it looks like a genuine browser pop-up. The copy comes complete with realistic error messages such as “The login information you entered is incorrect.” The page also asks visitors to sign up for a “Career Profile.” Your Facebook security code. If the account has 2FA, the page asks for the code from your authentication app, text message, WhatsApp, or email. A Google sign-in. The page claims “Facebook requires you to sign in to the Gmail address” on your account. To make the request seem harmless, the page adds that “Facebook will not share any of your data with your Google Account.” Fake Google screens, again under a fake address bar, ask for your password and then whatever Google asks for: a tap on a phone prompt, a code from Google Authenticator, a text message code, or your recovery email address. Everything you type into these screens, including the Google password, is sent to the attackers’ collection server. A fake confirmation. Finally, the page says a calendar invitation has been sent and that you’ll hear back within 90 minutes. By the time you start wondering, the attackers may already be inside your accounts. How the scam can get past two-factor authentication Many phishing pages simply collect a password and stop. This one keeps going. While the visitor is on the page, it keeps checking in with the attackers’ server and waits to be told which screen to show next. That allows the attackers to try the stolen password on the real Facebook site right away. If Facebook asks for a code, the fake page asks the visitor for the same code, and the attackers can use it before it expires. If the code doesn’t work, the page simply says “Incorrect code. Please try again.” The Google screens support the same approach. If Google sends a sign-in prompt to the visitor’s phone, the fake page can tell them to “tap Yes,” potentially approving the attackers’ login. The visitor sees the fake page while the attackers attempt to sign in to the real service out of sight. Codes and phone prompts still make accounts much harder to take over, so keep them turned on. But a code entered into a fake page, or a prompt approved for someone else’s login, can let attackers in. Passkeys and compatible hardware security keys are tied to the genuine website, so a fake page like this cannot relay them in the same way. That protection won’t help if you instead choose a password-and-code fallback and give those details to the attackers. Signs of a reusable phishing kit The code carries a version number ( 0.8.0 ), detailed error logging, and a “campaign key” sent with every message to the attackers’ server. These features suggest a reusable kit with support for identifying different campaigns. The collection address uses Amazon API Gateway in AWS’s Singapore region, ap-southeast-1 . A comment left in the code is written in Vietnamese. It translates to: “Change the key here when deploying to production.” Neither the hosting region nor the language of a code comment establishes who is behind the pages or where they operate. Facebook accounts, especially those linked to business pages or ad accounts, are valuable to criminals. Taking over the Google account as well could expose email and other data, and let attackers reset passwords for accounts linked to that address. The domains are another warning sign. All 11 follow the same pattern: join plus a recruiting-sounding word, such as joinhire , joinquest , or jointheteam , on the .cfd , .info , and .works top-level domains. None mention Calendly or Meta. These generic names could also be reused for other companies’ job lures. How to stay safe Check the address, not the design. Direct Calendly booking links use calendly.com , although legitimate forms can also be embedded on other websites. Treat an unfamiliar recruiting domain as a reason to verify the invitation independently. Don’t give a booking page your Facebook password. Scheduling a call doesn’t require handing your social media password to a recruiter. If a booking flow suddenly asks you to sign in elsewhere, verify both the request and the actual login domain. Look at your browser’s real address bar. These fake login windows draw their own address bars showing Facebook or Google web addresses. For a separate pop-up, check the address displayed by the browser itself. A login window that cannot be dragged outside the webpage may be part of the page rather than a separate browser window. Verify the recruiter and role. Go directly to the company’s official careers site. A genuine job listing doesn’t prove the person contacting you represents the company, so verify unexpected invitations through an independent contact. Don’t share codes or approve unexpected prompts. Only enter a code on the genuine service for a login you initiated. Never approve a phone prompt just because a recruiter or booking page tells you to. Use passkeys or a security key where you can. They resist this kind of phishing. Be wary if a page pushes you to use a password and code instead. Already entered a password or approved a prompt? From a trusted device, go directly to the affected service and change your password. Sign out other sessions and check your security methods, recovery email, and phone number. If both accounts were affected, secure your Google account promptly because email access can help attackers reset other passwords. Check Gmail for unfamiliar forwarding rules and filters, and review any Facebook business pages or ad accounts you manage. Change the password anywhere else you reused it. Locked out of your account? Use Meta’s account recovery support or Google’s compromised-account gui d ance . If you only shared contact details, watch for follow-up scams that use them to sound convincing. How Malwarebytes helps Malwarebytes Browser Guard can block phishing and scam sites before you interact with them. That matters in campaigns like this one, where the page closely copies a service people use every day. items.summary_html:
We found a wave of websites posing as Calendly booking pages for job interviews at Meta. Visitors pick a slot for a 30-minute phone call with a recruiter, fill in their details, and pass what looks like a CAPTCHA.

Then the page asks them to log in to Facebook.

The interview is fake. The pages are designed to steal the visitor’s Facebook login details, including the two-factor authentication (2FA) codes meant to protect the account. Visitors are then asked to sign in to their Google account too, supposedly “for security.”

These pages are not affiliated with Meta, Calendly, or Google. If you’ve already entered a password or approved a sign-in prompt, secure the affected accounts straight away. See “How to stay safe” below.

Why Calendly makes a convincing disguise

Calendly is a widely used scheduling tool, and recruiters use it to book interviews. Clicking a booking link, picking a time, and typing in your name and email is something people do without a second thought. There’s no account to create and nothing to download.

That routine makes it a good disguise. By the time the page asks for something unusual, the visitor has already picked a slot and shared their details. Going along with one more step can feel easier than starting to doubt the whole thing.

For someone who has sent out application after application without hearing back, an invitation to interview at Meta may be exactly the kind of message they hope for. Excitement, and the fear of missing a rare chance, can push people to move quickly instead of checking who actually sent the link.

Job seekers are also used to sharing personal details with strangers. Handing your name, email, and phone number to a recruiter you’ve never met is a normal part of applying, so a form asking for them may not raise any alarms.

A job interview that starts with a calendar

The fake page copies Calendly’s booking screen, titled “Calendly | Meta Careers.” It shows a monthly calendar, a time zone picker, and a 30-minute “Phone call.” The available times are loaded from the attackers’ server, so the calendar looks like a real recruiter’s schedule.

After the visitor picks a time, the page walks them through a series of steps:

  1. Your details. A form asks for your name, email address, and phone number, plus anything that “will help prepare for our meeting.”
  2. A fake CAPTCHA. A grid of images asks you to “Select all images with…”. It makes the page feel legitimate, and it may also stop automated security scanners from seeing what comes next.
  3. A Facebook login. A window within the page copies Facebook’s login page. It even draws its own fake address bar showing a Facebook web address, so it looks like a genuine browser pop-up. The copy comes complete with realistic error messages such as “The login information you entered is incorrect.” The page also asks visitors to sign up for a “Career Profile.”
  4. Your Facebook security code. If the account has 2FA, the page asks for the code from your authentication app, text message, WhatsApp, or email.
  5. A Google sign-in. The page claims “Facebook requires you to sign in to the Gmail address” on your account. To make the request seem harmless, the page adds that “Facebook will not share any of your data with your Google Account.” Fake Google screens, again under a fake address bar, ask for your password and then whatever Google asks for: a tap on a phone prompt, a code from Google Authenticator, a text message code, or your recovery email address. Everything you type into these screens, including the Google password, is sent to the attackers’ collection server.
  6. A fake confirmation. Finally, the page says a calendar invitation has been sent and that you’ll hear back within 90 minutes. By the time you start wondering, the attackers may already be inside your accounts.
How the scam can get past two-factor authentication

Many phishing pages simply collect a password and stop. This one keeps going.

While the visitor is on the page, it keeps checking in with the attackers’ server and waits to be told which screen to show next. That allows the attackers to try the stolen password on the real Facebook site right away. If Facebook asks for a code, the fake page asks the visitor for the same code, and the attackers can use it before it expires. If the code doesn’t work, the page simply says “Incorrect code. Please try again.”

The Google screens support the same approach. If Google sends a sign-in prompt to the visitor’s phone, the fake page can tell them to “tap Yes,” potentially approving the attackers’ login.

The visitor sees the fake page while the attackers attempt to sign in to the real service out of sight.

Codes and phone prompts still make accounts much harder to take over, so keep them turned on. But a code entered into a fake page, or a prompt approved for someone else’s login, can let attackers in. Passkeys and compatible hardware security keys are tied to the genuine website, so a fake page like this cannot relay them in the same way. That protection won’t help if you instead choose a password-and-code fallback and give those details to the attackers.

Signs of a reusable phishing kit

The code carries a version number (0.8.0), detailed error logging, and a “campaign key” sent with every message to the attackers’ server. These features suggest a reusable kit with support for identifying different campaigns.

The collection address uses Amazon API Gateway in AWS’s Singapore region, ap-southeast-1. A comment left in the code is written in Vietnamese. It translates to:

“Change the key here when deploying to production.”

Neither the hosting region nor the language of a code comment establishes who is behind the pages or where they operate.

Facebook accounts, especially those linked to business pages or ad accounts, are valuable to criminals. Taking over the Google account as well could expose email and other data, and let attackers reset passwords for accounts linked to that address.

The domains are another warning sign. All 11 follow the same pattern: join plus a recruiting-sounding word, such as joinhire, joinquest, or jointheteam, on the .cfd, .info, and .works top-level domains. None mention Calendly or Meta. These generic names could also be reused for other companies’ job lures.

How to stay safe
  • Check the address, not the design. Direct Calendly booking links use calendly.com, although legitimate forms can also be embedded on other websites. Treat an unfamiliar recruiting domain as a reason to verify the invitation independently.
  • Don’t give a booking page your Facebook password. Scheduling a call doesn’t require handing your social media password to a recruiter. If a booking flow suddenly asks you to sign in elsewhere, verify both the request and the actual login domain.
  • Look at your browser’s real address bar. These fake login windows draw their own address bars showing Facebook or Google web addresses. For a separate pop-up, check the address displayed by the browser itself. A login window that cannot be dragged outside the webpage may be part of the page rather than a separate browser window.
  • Verify the recruiter and role. Go directly to the company’s official careers site. A genuine job listing doesn’t prove the person contacting you represents the company, so verify unexpected invitations through an independent contact.
  • Don’t share codes or approve unexpected prompts. Only enter a code on the genuine service for a login you initiated. Never approve a phone prompt just because a recruiter or booking page tells you to.
  • Use passkeys or a security key where you can.They resist this kind of phishing. Be wary if a page pushes you to use a password and code instead.
  • Already entered a password or approved a prompt? From a trusted device, go directly to the affected service and change your password. Sign out other sessions and check your security methods, recovery email, and phone number. If both accounts were affected, secure your Google account promptly because email access can help attackers reset other passwords. Check Gmail for unfamiliar forwarding rules and filters, and review any Facebook business pages or ad accounts you manage. Change the password anywhere else you reused it.
  • Locked out of your account? Use Meta’s account recovery support or Google’s compromised-account guidance. If you only shared contact details, watch for follow-up scams that use them to sound convincing.
How Malwarebytes helps

Malwarebytes Browser Guard can block phishing and scam sites before you interact with them. That matters in campaigns like this one, where the page closely copies a service people use every day.

If you receive an interview link and aren’t sure about it, Malwarebytes Scam Guard can help assess the link before you click.

Indicators of compromise

Phishing domains

  • joinconnect[.]cfd
  • joinconnect[.]works
  • joinhire[.]cfd
  • joinhire[.]info
  • joinquest[.]cfd
  • joinquest[.]info
  • joinquest[.]works
  • jointhetalent[.]cfd
  • jointhetalent[.]info
  • jointhetalent[.]works
  • jointheteam[.]cfd

Collection endpoint

  • rkrt01c0mc[.]execute-api[.]ap-southeast-1[.]amazonaws[.]com
