items.title: Package managers have an integrity problem
items.summary: I tested 25 of the most popular package managers to check whether they detect a compromised package repository injecting malicious code into legitimate packages. This code integrity problem could be solved using cryptographic hashes or signatures, but many package managers are still vulnerable to this threat. Of the 25 package managers reviewed 1 , fewer than half used lockfiles that checked for tampering by default, and only two verified the integrity of every package they downloaded. Supply-chain attacks caused by developer compromise are a common story, but imagine what happens if ongoing mitigation attempts, including work by Trail of Bits 2 , are successful. If developers of popular packages are no longer the easiest targets, attackers will shift their focus to the next weakest link in the system: the package repositories that serve the code. The cryptographic answers to this problem are more subtle than they appear, and many implementations fall short due to deliberate design choices, resource prioritization, or the complexity of developer-friendly solutions. One natural answer is to include a cryptographic hash of a package’s contents in a lockfile and compare hashes after downloading the package. This automatic verification was the default behavior in about half of the package managers I tested, but others required extra configuration to include or verify these hashes, used hashes in a cryptographically insecure way, or lacked hashes entirely. This is summarized in the following table. Verifies integrity Go, vcpkg Verifies if lockfile is present Bun, Bundler, Cargo, npm, pnpm, Poetry, SwiftPM, uv, Yarn Verifies with lockfile + extra steps Conda, Gradle, Pip, NuGet, Pub Does not verify with lockfile or N/A CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, cpanminus, Gem, Maven, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, R Table 1: Lockfile-based security of a package manager fetching dependencies from a malicious repository, categorized by how much work it takes a developer to achieve integrity. Experimentally verified for a particular configuration. Caveats detailed below. Another natural approach is to use signatures, avoiding the need to securely distribute a hash for every package. However, in my tests, only Go verified signatures by default; others required extra configuration, lacked verification code, or did not support signatures. Verifies signatures Go Verifies with configuration Bundler, Gem, Gradle, Maven, npm, NuGet Missing or incomplete verification Bun, cpanminus, Pip, pnpm, Poetry, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, uv, Yarn No signatures available for verification Cargo, CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, Conda, Pub, R, SwiftPM, vcpkg Table 2: Signature-based security of various package managers. Also experimentally verified and subject to similar caveats. As both tables show, I found a surprising variation in the cryptographic designs and the level of protection they provide. Despite the challenges, I also found several communities on the frontier of this integrity problem that are bringing improved designs to reality. This post explores those variations, showing where certain designs fall short, why code integrity is harder to solve than it appears, and what cryptographic designs might be adopted in the future. Simulating malicious package repositories Studying the cryptographic behavior of 25 package managers is quite the challenge. I wanted to minimize manual analysis, but also be 100% confident when I claim an attack from a malicious package repository is possible. To solve this problem, I built a testing harness based on Docker containers and mitmproxy that dynamically evaluates the security of package managers against a malicious server. Figure 1: Experimental design of the test harness used to simulate malicious package repositories The Ubuntu-based Docker images include a package manager, sample code, and optionally a lockfile. There are conflicting opinions about whether to include lockfiles in source code repositories, so I tested both configurations. The harness instructs the package manager to fetch dependencies from the repository, and the resulting network request routes through a WireGuard network to a custom mitmproxy addon. Because the mitmproxy TLS CA is installed in the Docker image, the addon can fully manipulate the plaintext from the package repository, simulating a compromised server. I assumed any web-facing server could be compromised (e.g., Composer fetches metadata from Packagist and packages from GitHub), but backend resources, like any private signing keys, remain secure. The simulated repository embeds malicious code into the downloaded packages, and if the sample code executes the malware, the attack is successful. I tried to keep the experimental setup reflective of real-world usage, but there are limitations. I installed the latest package manager versions, followed quickstart guides for setting up sample projects inside the container, and picked popular packages from public repositories to infect. I ran package manager commands with default flags to see if extra steps, like modifying the project manifest or running extra commands, were needed to enforce cryptographic integrity. However, I am limited to testing a single package with a single package manager version on a single platform, and the test conditions (e.g., PowerShell and CocoaPods on Ubuntu) may not represent the most common usage patterns. The setup isn’t meant to show that every developer is vulnerable to a malicious package repository, just that a developer following reasonable conventions is. With the package managers installed and network intercept functional, one (mostly) promising observation is clear. HTTPS is (almost) everywhere Our harness architecture captures all network traffic, so it’s easy to test that package managers are using TLS and validating the certificates. In almost every package manager, they are. The exception is cpanminus, the frequently recommended package manager for Perl. cpanminus uses unencrypted HTTP by default to connect to the Perl package repository, allowing any active network attacker to inject malicious code into downloaded packages. This vulnerability has been known for years, but the cpanminus developer has not switched to HTTPS, since doing so would be a breaking change to default behavior. 3 Hash functions don’t always provide integrity By using the mitmproxy addon to modify the package repository responses, I could investigate how different package managers use cryptographic hashes. Hashes are a natural way to ensure that a downloaded file has not been tampered with, but the main question is how the package manager learns the correct hash in the first place. Microsoft’s vcpkg package manager for C and C++ libraries offers an interesting example. The package manager source code includes content hashes for thousands of dependencies. When a developer updates their library and wants to register the new content in vcpkg, they recompute the hash of their package and open a pull request against the vcpkg source code with the new hash and link to the package. When a package is downloaded by vcpkg, the hash is checked. So as long as the package manager is trusted, this approach is fully secure against a malicious package repository. 4 Hashes in lockfiles It is significantly more common that the package manager learns the correct hash via a lockfile. A lockfile is frequently created by a package manager, resides alongside a project’s source code, and references specific versions of dependencies needed by the project. If a developer checks a lockfile with cryptographic hashes into the source code repository, and the user’s package manager validates downloaded packages against the hashes, then the user’s dependencies perfectly match the developer’s. This is how it works for the Bun package manager for JavaScript projects. Installing a package with bun add updates the bun.lock lockfile; committing the lockfile to Git and calling bun install on another copy of the repo verifies the hash in the lockfile against the new copy of the dependency. Similar behavior is found in npm, pnpm, and Yarn (also JavaScript package managers); uv and Poetry (Python package managers); Bundler (for Ruby); Cargo (for Rust); and SwiftPM (for Swift). Other package managers support lockfiles, but with more steps than the standard add/restore process. Python’s Pip has experimental support for the pylock.toml format, and Conda has the optional library Conda lock . NuGet, the .NET package manager, generates a lockfile after adding the RestorePackagesWithLockFile property to the project. Many package managers (Maven, R, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, and cpanminus) do not have dedicated lockfiles, and some have lockfiles (Gradle’s gradle.lockfile 5 and Gem’s Gemfile.lock ) without hashes in them. Hashes present, but not for integrity Surprisingly, I found a few examples where the lockfiles had a hash, but could still be compromised by a malicious server. This is not necessarily reflective of a vulnerability, since the underlying behavior is clearly documented, but it shows how there are multiple valid opinions about how lockfiles should be structured and consumed. Nevertheless, a user who is accustomed to the behavior of one package manager may be surprised by that of another. The first example is the Pub package manager for Dart and Flutter. The following excerpt of a pubspec.lock file includes a SHA-256 hash for the uuid package. uuid : dependency : "direct main" description : name : uuid sha256 : "9b129329f58692f6e6578329498a8fe9fbe98f090beb764ffbb8ee2eadd01dcd" url : "https://pub.dev" source : hosted version : "4.6.0" If a user calls flutter pub get to fetch dependencies, Pub downloads the package from the pub.dev server and computes the hash of the returned binary. If there is a mismatch, Pub detects the error, but installs the package anyway. The existing content-hash from pubspec.lock doesn't match contents for: * uuid-4.6.0 from "https://pub.dev" This indicates one of: * The content has changed on the server since you created the pubspec.lock. * The pubspec.lock has been corrupted. The content-hashes in pubspec.lock has been updated. This is documented behavior , and requires the non-default --enforce-lockfile option to block installation 6 . Overwriting the lockfile after a hash mismatch was also the default behavior in pnpm until version 11.4 from May 2026, when it was changed to close “supply-chain holes.” Like Pub, pnpm also supported a non-default --frozen-lockfile flag, indicating that the previous behavior which updated the lockfile was expected. Next, here is an excerpt of a conan.lock file, used by the Conan package manager for C and C++. "requires" : [ "zlib/1.3.1#cac0f6daea041b0ccf42934163defb20%1765284699.337" ] , This includes the package name ( zlib ), the version number ( 1.3.1 ), a recipe revision cac0f6daea041b0ccf42934163defb20 , and a timestamp. The 128-bit revision is an MD5 hash that includes source code. However, this hash is not intended to provide cryptographic security, but rather serves as a unique identifier. When Conan installs dependencies using this lockfile, it uses the recipe revision hash to download a particular file from the ConanCenter repository, but it does not recompute the recipe hash. Even if it did, there’s a separate package revision hash for platform-specific binaries that is not in the lockfile, and MD5 collisions could allow an attacker to create two distinct recipes with different behavior but the same hash. The CocoaPods dependency manager for Swift and Objective-C has a similar pattern. Here is part of a Podfile.lock file for a project that uses the popular Files dependency. SPEC CHECKSUMS : Files : d88e31b84d65e754935053b1c584ea8e2320698a This 160-bit checksum is the SHA-1 hash of the Files Podspec , which contains the following link to the source code. CocoaPods uses this link to fetch the Git repository. "source" : { "git" : "https://github.com/johnsundell/files.git" , "tag" : "4.0.2" } , So even though the lockfile can prevent tampering with the GitHub URL in the Podspec (setting aside expensive SHA-1 collision attacks), a compromised GitHub server could just serve a malicious version of the repository with the same tag. Finally, the Composer dependency manager for PHP includes commit hashes in the composer.lock file, as in the following excerpt. "dist" : { "type" : "zip" , "url" : "https://api.github.com/repos/guzzle/psr7/zipball/b094ded77ee97a6027ad6cf0e8c7b9f88381814c" , "reference" : "b094ded77ee97a6027ad6cf0e8c7b9f88381814c" , "shasum" : "" } , However, even though the b094ded... commit hash uniquely identifies the code, the ZIP archive in the URL does not include the Git tree as a way to verify the hash. Once again, GitHub could serve a malicious ZIP archive without detection by Composer. Lockfiles have many roles besides supply-chain integrity The previous experimental results show that lockfile hashes often can be used to enforce package integrity, but this is not their sole or even original purpose. Alternatively, they can lock dependencies to a particular functionality, enable an easy way for application developers to share a consistent environment, or facilitate reproducible builds. Analyzing package manager lockfiles through the lens of supply-chain security is a recent interpretation that can be at odds with their original design. The recent change to pnpm’s --frozen-lockfile is one example. Another example of this tension is the question of whether the lockfile should be committed to version control. Most modern guidance recommends committing the lockfile for applications, since the final build environment is fully controlled. The question is more complicated for libraries, since package managers often ignore libraries’ lockfiles to avoid locking to conflicting transitive dependencies. Committing the lockfile makes it easier to develop the library by sharing a consistent build environment with other developers, but excluding the lockfile makes it easier to catch conflicts with different dependency versions before they are found by users. Many package managers recommend committing the lockfile for libraries (e.g., npm , pnpm , Poetry , uv , and Yarn ), some recommend excluding it (e.g., Bundler ), and some leave it up to the developer (e.g., Cargo ). Many of these questions are explored in a recent study by Gamage et al. The authors explore lockfile design decisions for seven package managers, analyze published projects, and perform semi-structured interviews with 15 developers. They find that the practice of committing a lockfile varies by which package manager is used, and categorize five benefits to using lockfiles, as perceived by the interview subjects: build determinism, integrity, transparency into indirect dependencies, debugging, and security scanning. Some of the developers also preferred to not use lockfiles, citing a preference for end users to resolve to the latest version of a dependency, which may have more bug fixes and vulnerability patches. The diversity of package manager designs and views surrounding the purpose of lockfiles makes it difficult to prescribe a single recommendation. With regard to supply-chain integrity, it is common, but not universal, to view lockfiles as a source of integrity that should be committed with the source code. For package managers with lockfiles that do not provide cryptographic integrity, it is worth considering whether their users share that expectation. Even when lockfile hashes can provide cryptographic integrity, locking to specific package hashes means that users do not immediately receive subsequent updates or security fixes, since the newer package has a different hash. This leads to frequent lockfile bumping to distribute the latest hashes. Wanting immediate updates is a separate concern from wanting package integrity, but the current, common approach of using hashes in lockfiles is at odds with that goal. In conclusion, lockfile hashes are often, but not always, effective at providing cryptographic integrity, but do not work in every situation. Signatures are common; verification is not Signatures are a natural way to address these shortcomings, but implementations frequently fall short. In theory, developers could sign every release with their own private key, and the package manager could check the signature of the package it downloads from the package repository. In fact, signatures are relatively common in different package ecosystems, but proper signature validation is surprisingly lacking. The reality of using signatures to provide code integrity is more nuanced than it seems, and package managers have different approaches to the problem. Many package managers have no signatures available. Arguably, vcpkg does not need them, because all package hashes are distributed with the manager, but this leaves Cargo, CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, Conda, Pub, R, and SwiftPM 7 . The Conan developers are aware and previously decided not to fix it, citing several implementation challenges and suggesting organizations where integrity is critical could run their own repository server. Cargo developers are actively considering different signing designs, but this effort is still in progress. Composer developers have been implementing many new protections against supply-chain attacks, with future plans for artifact integrity. Repository signing One straightforward approach, known as repository signing, is when the package repository signs every package once it’s uploaded, and the repository’s public key is distributed with the package manager. This doesn’t solve the problem of a totally compromised package repository, since a malicious package repository could legitimately sign a malicious package, but it would protect against untrusted mirrors or a partial compromise of a package repository’s serving infrastructure. Repository signatures are used by the npm Registry , the NuGet Registry , and the PAUSE server for Perl module distribution. In the npm Registry, signatures are distributed within package metadata with repository-specific public keys . NuGet Registry repository signatures are found in .signature.p7s files within the distributed ZIP package, again with repository-specific public keys . The PAUSE server takes a different approach, using its GPG key to batch sign the cryptographic hashes of several packages at a time. Developer signing Developer signing involves the developer maintaining the private key and signing the package before uploading it to the repository for distribution. This prevents the package repository from tampering with the contents, but it also provides a way for the package repository to authenticate the uploader. There are two common approaches for a developer asserting their public key. In the first approach, the public key is distributed out-of-band. The Maven Central repository (used by Maven and Gradle) and the RubyGems repository (used by the gem and Bundler package managers) both support this type of developer signing. Maven Central uses PGP signatures, and developer keys are distributed by public keyservers . RubyGems uses self-signed certificates, and their distribution is left to the developers (e.g., rspec ). The major difference is that developer signing is mandatory for Maven Central, and optional for RubyGems. Developer signing is rare for RubyGems, due to the lack of an established chain of trust, and a previous attempt to introduce a certificate authority failed . The second approach involves a chain of trust. The NuGet Registry and PowerShell Gallery both support developer signatures. Neither makes signatures mandatory, but the PowerShell Gallery recommends it and the NuGet Registry has strict requirements if developer signing is used. In both, the developer’s key must chain to a trusted CA , and acquiring a valid code-signing certificate can cost hundreds of dollars per year. The benefit of this approach is that trusted root certificates can be preinstalled on the platform, allowing package managers to verify public keys. One downside of developer signing is that developers are responsible for key management, and they can lose the ability to update their code if they lose access to their key. Identity-based signing An increasingly common middle ground is “identity-based” or “keyless” signing from Sigstore . Rather than require developers to manage long-term private keys, a developer can use Sigstore’s Fulcio CA to issue a fresh signing certificate on demand, for free. To prevent impersonation, the developer proves their identity with an OIDC token: a cryptographically signed statement from a third party like Google, Microsoft, or GitHub that attests to the email address, username, or potentially other claims about the developer’s identity. The verifier can check that the username is correct and the certificate chain links back to Sigstore Fulcio’s root certificate, proving that someone with access to that account created the signature. Keyless signing is particularly useful because it can be integrated into a developer’s existing workflow-based deployment pipeline. This is frequently called provenance attestation or trusted publishing 8 . GitHub and GitLab provide OIDC tokens to Actions and CI/CD workflows that attest to the build workflow, the repository, and the commit hash. A workflow can use this token to obtain a signing certificate from Sigstore, sign the built package, and upload the signed package to the package repository. Since the signing certificate includes the commit hash and workflow details, this cryptographically links the built binary artifact to its source code. Provenance attestation via Sigstore is supported by Python’s PyPI , the npm Registry , RubyGems repository , and Maven Central . While Sigstore attestations are not mandatory, there is already better adoption than RubyGems’ optional support for developer-managed signing keys. Verification code is skipped, unconfigured, or nonexistent Unfortunately, just because these signatures exist does not mean they are being verified by package managers. In the npm package manager, the repository signatures are not checked when running npm install . Checking the signatures requires running npm audit signatures , which uses Sigstore to validate the registry public keys and then validates the signatures of the installed packages. pnpm recently added the pnpm audit signatures command , but that implementation fetches the registry public keys from the potentially malicious registry rather than verifying with Sigstore, so an adversary could simply add their own key and signature. Bun and Yarn currently lack an equivalent audit signatures command. In the NuGet package manager, the default signatureValidationMode is accept , which installs invalidly signed packages. The user must set this to require and configure the list of trusted signers, such as with dotnet nuget trust source . These configurations (which include the repository public keys) can be securely distributed within a nuget.config configuration file, functioning as a lockfile that locks the trusted signers. Ruby’s Gem and Bundler, and Java’s Maven and Gradle, which all use repositories with developer signatures, do not verify signatures by default. They require the user to manually add developer public keys ( gem cert --add ) or list the allowed public keys that should be trusted. In Maven, one can use the third-party pgpverify-maven-plugin with pgp-keys-map.list to specify the trusted PGP fingerprints. Gradle offers dependency verification , which works similarly. Finally, several package managers seemingly lack any sort of verification code at all. Pip , uv , and Poetry do not currently have a way to verify identity-based attestations described in PEP740. cpanminus does not have a way to verify the integrity of the repository-signed CHECKSUMS file. It once did, but in response to a verification bypass vulnerability , this verification code was removed . Even though PowerShell is supported on non-Windows platforms, Authenticode signature verification is not 9 . At one point, the PowerShell repository noted that this issue “should be fixed in a future release.” Go package management and transparency logs Go’s built-in package manager is the only one I tested that verifies signatures by default, and it also introduces one final concept for cryptographic package integrity. When go get or go mod download fetches a package 10 , it hashes the package contents and compares the hash, package name, and version against the checksum database . The contents of the database are registry-signed (analogous to PGP signatures in Perl’s PAUSE server), and the default checksum database public key is hardcoded in Go’s source code. As long as the checksum database’s private key is used honestly, this design ensures that the package name and version are enough to uniquely identify the binary contents of a package. As a result, the go.mod lockfile achieves package integrity without needing to store cryptographic hashes. 11 Go’s checksum database is an example of a transparency log, or an immutable, global, tamper-resistant log of metadata. The same capability is provided by Sigstore’s Rekor and certificate transparency logs. In package managers, it cryptographically ensures that the package manager only ever installs the same binaries recorded by the transparency log. If everyone agrees on the transparency log, then everyone agrees on the package contents. This makes it more difficult for an adversary to selectively and undetectably target a victim with a malicious package. Transparency logs can still fail if there are other vulnerabilities , the log’s private key is compromised, or no one checks the transparency log for malicious behavior. Of all the package managers I tested, Go performed the best at maintaining cryptographic integrity in the face of a compromised package repository or proxy. However, the registry-signature-like design means that much of the system’s trust is concentrated in a single private key. A proposed cryptographic design for package managers One potential approach that combines the ideas in this post is to include signature information in the lockfile. Rather than commit to the hash of a particular package, the lockfile could commit to a developer’s identity or public key. This reuses much of the infrastructure in place for lockfile hashes, but it separates the question of immediate updates from the question of package integrity. With this design, the lockfile could specify a single dependency version (for build reproducibility) or a lower bound (for immediate updates), and the included identity ensures that a malicious repository or proxy cannot easily tamper with whatever package version the manager resolves to. In addition, a transparency log can protect against selective targeting, building on Sigstore’s identity-based signing and transparency log service. Sigstore avoids long-lived keys by default, but it also supports self-managed keys, KMS providers, and hardware tokens. This gives an easily adopted and secure default while still giving flexibility to developers who desire more control over their keys. This idea is not new and not my own. Attestation identities are part of the pylock.toml Python lockfile specification , the trusted-keys in Gradle’s verification metadata , and the pgp-keys-map.list file in the pgpverify-maven-plugin for Maven. This is the direction that many package managers are already moving towards, as evidenced by the increasing adoption of Sigstore into publishing workflows, attention on supply-chain security, and bugfixes that specifically cite potential tampering by a malicious adversary. There is increasing recognition that this is a problem, and increasing appetite to fix it. It won’t be easy. There are many subtle nuances that have to be considered and addressed, signing verification code needs to be developed and audited, and developers need to adopt the resulting design. In many of the package managers I reviewed as part of this project, I found communities of people who have been thinking about and pushing for cryptographic integrity and package signing for years. They know best what those package managers need, and they deserve the resources to make this a reality. One of the greatest cryptographic success stories in the past decade has been the nearly universal adoption of HTTPS, driven in part by industry and community recognition of the security risks of unencrypted traffic, and the nonprofit Let’s Encrypt providing free and easy-to-use TLS certificates as a public good. Package signing is in a similar state now to where HTTPS was a decade ago: persistent adversaries are a huge concern, and cryptographic security is nearly nonexistent. Universal package signing is not here yet, but it is on the horizon. With the right attention and investment, we can make it a reality. items.summary_html:
I tested 25 of the most popular package managers to check whether they detect a compromised package repository injecting malicious code into legitimate packages. This code integrity problem could be solved using cryptographic hashes or signatures, but many package managers are still vulnerable to this threat. Of the 25 package managers reviewed1, fewer than half used lockfiles that checked for tampering by default, and only two verified the integrity of every package they downloaded.

Supply-chain attacks caused by developer compromise are a common story, but imagine what happens if ongoing mitigation attempts, including work by Trail of Bits2, are successful. If developers of popular packages are no longer the easiest targets, attackers will shift their focus to the next weakest link in the system: the package repositories that serve the code. The cryptographic answers to this problem are more subtle than they appear, and many implementations fall short due to deliberate design choices, resource prioritization, or the complexity of developer-friendly solutions.

One natural answer is to include a cryptographic hash of a package’s contents in a lockfile and compare hashes after downloading the package. This automatic verification was the default behavior in about half of the package managers I tested, but others required extra configuration to include or verify these hashes, used hashes in a cryptographically insecure way, or lacked hashes entirely. This is summarized in the following table.

Verifies integrity Go, vcpkg Verifies if lockfile is present Bun, Bundler, Cargo, npm, pnpm, Poetry, SwiftPM, uv, Yarn Verifies with lockfile + extra steps Conda, Gradle, Pip, NuGet, Pub Does not verify with lockfile or N/A CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, cpanminus, Gem, Maven, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, R

Table 1: Lockfile-based security of a package manager fetching dependencies from a malicious repository, categorized by how much work it takes a developer to achieve integrity. Experimentally verified for a particular configuration. Caveats detailed below.

Another natural approach is to use signatures, avoiding the need to securely distribute a hash for every package. However, in my tests, only Go verified signatures by default; others required extra configuration, lacked verification code, or did not support signatures.

Verifies signatures Go Verifies with configuration Bundler, Gem, Gradle, Maven, npm, NuGet Missing or incomplete verification Bun, cpanminus, Pip, pnpm, Poetry, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, uv, Yarn No signatures available for verification Cargo, CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, Conda, Pub, R, SwiftPM, vcpkg

Table 2: Signature-based security of various package managers. Also experimentally verified and subject to similar caveats.

As both tables show, I found a surprising variation in the cryptographic designs and the level of protection they provide. Despite the challenges, I also found several communities on the frontier of this integrity problem that are bringing improved designs to reality. This post explores those variations, showing where certain designs fall short, why code integrity is harder to solve than it appears, and what cryptographic designs might be adopted in the future.

Simulating malicious package repositories

Studying the cryptographic behavior of 25 package managers is quite the challenge. I wanted to minimize manual analysis, but also be 100% confident when I claim an attack from a malicious package repository is possible. To solve this problem, I built a testing harness based on Docker containers and mitmproxy that dynamically evaluates the security of package managers against a malicious server.

Figure 1: Experimental design of the test harness used to simulate malicious package repositories

The Ubuntu-based Docker images include a package manager, sample code, and optionally a lockfile. There are conflicting opinions about whether to include lockfiles in source code repositories, so I tested both configurations. The harness instructs the package manager to fetch dependencies from the repository, and the resulting network request routes through a WireGuard network to a custom mitmproxy addon.

Because the mitmproxy TLS CA is installed in the Docker image, the addon can fully manipulate the plaintext from the package repository, simulating a compromised server. I assumed any web-facing server could be compromised (e.g., Composer fetches metadata from Packagist and packages from GitHub), but backend resources, like any private signing keys, remain secure. The simulated repository embeds malicious code into the downloaded packages, and if the sample code executes the malware, the attack is successful.

I tried to keep the experimental setup reflective of real-world usage, but there are limitations. I installed the latest package manager versions, followed quickstart guides for setting up sample projects inside the container, and picked popular packages from public repositories to infect. I ran package manager commands with default flags to see if extra steps, like modifying the project manifest or running extra commands, were needed to enforce cryptographic integrity. However, I am limited to testing a single package with a single package manager version on a single platform, and the test conditions (e.g., PowerShell and CocoaPods on Ubuntu) may not represent the most common usage patterns. The setup isn’t meant to show that every developer is vulnerable to a malicious package repository, just that a developer following reasonable conventions is.

With the package managers installed and network intercept functional, one (mostly) promising observation is clear.

HTTPS is (almost) everywhere

Our harness architecture captures all network traffic, so it’s easy to test that package managers are using TLS and validating the certificates. In almost every package manager, they are.

The exception is cpanminus, the frequently recommended package manager for Perl. cpanminus uses unencrypted HTTP by default to connect to the Perl package repository, allowing any active network attacker to inject malicious code into downloaded packages. This vulnerability has been known for years, but the cpanminus developer has not switched to HTTPS, since doing so would be a breaking change to default behavior.3

Hash functions don’t always provide integrity

By using the mitmproxy addon to modify the package repository responses, I could investigate how different package managers use cryptographic hashes. Hashes are a natural way to ensure that a downloaded file has not been tampered with, but the main question is how the package manager learns the correct hash in the first place.

Microsoft’s vcpkg package manager for C and C++ libraries offers an interesting example. The package manager source code includes content hashes for thousands of dependencies. When a developer updates their library and wants to register the new content in vcpkg, they recompute the hash of their package and open a pull request against the vcpkg source code with the new hash and link to the package. When a package is downloaded by vcpkg, the hash is checked. So as long as the package manager is trusted, this approach is fully secure against a malicious package repository.4

Hashes in lockfiles

It is significantly more common that the package manager learns the correct hash via a lockfile. A lockfile is frequently created by a package manager, resides alongside a project’s source code, and references specific versions of dependencies needed by the project. If a developer checks a lockfile with cryptographic hashes into the source code repository, and the user’s package manager validates downloaded packages against the hashes, then the user’s dependencies perfectly match the developer’s.

This is how it works for the Bun package manager for JavaScript projects. Installing a package with bun add updates the bun.lock lockfile; committing the lockfile to Git and calling bun install on another copy of the repo verifies the hash in the lockfile against the new copy of the dependency. Similar behavior is found in npm, pnpm, and Yarn (also JavaScript package managers); uv and Poetry (Python package managers); Bundler (for Ruby); Cargo (for Rust); and SwiftPM (for Swift).

Other package managers support lockfiles, but with more steps than the standard add/restore process. Python’s Pip has experimental support for the pylock.toml format, and Conda has the optional library Conda lock. NuGet, the .NET package manager, generates a lockfile after adding the RestorePackagesWithLockFile property to the project.

Many package managers (Maven, R, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, and cpanminus) do not have dedicated lockfiles, and some have lockfiles (Gradle’s gradle.lockfile5 and Gem’s Gemfile.lock) without hashes in them.

Hashes present, but not for integrity

Surprisingly, I found a few examples where the lockfiles had a hash, but could still be compromised by a malicious server. This is not necessarily reflective of a vulnerability, since the underlying behavior is clearly documented, but it shows how there are multiple valid opinions about how lockfiles should be structured and consumed. Nevertheless, a user who is accustomed to the behavior of one package manager may be surprised by that of another.

The first example is the Pub package manager for Dart and Flutter. The following excerpt of a pubspec.lock file includes a SHA-256 hash for the uuid package.

uuid:
 dependency: "direct main"
 description:
 name: uuid
 sha256: "9b129329f58692f6e6578329498a8fe9fbe98f090beb764ffbb8ee2eadd01dcd"
 url: "https://pub.dev"
 source: hosted
 version: "4.6.0"

If a user calls flutter pub get to fetch dependencies, Pub downloads the package from the pub.dev server and computes the hash of the returned binary. If there is a mismatch, Pub detects the error, but installs the package anyway.

The existing content-hash from pubspec.lock doesn't match contents for:
 * uuid-4.6.0 from "https://pub.dev"

This indicates one of:
 * The content has changed on the server since you created the pubspec.lock.
 * The pubspec.lock has been corrupted.

The content-hashes in pubspec.lock has been updated.

This is documented behavior, and requires the non-default --enforce-lockfile option to block installation6.

Overwriting the lockfile after a hash mismatch was also the default behavior in pnpm until version 11.4 from May 2026, when it was changed to close “supply-chain holes.” Like Pub, pnpm also supported a non-default --frozen-lockfile flag, indicating that the previous behavior which updated the lockfile was expected.

Next, here is an excerpt of a conan.lock file, used by the Conan package manager for C and C++.

"requires": [
 "zlib/1.3.1#cac0f6daea041b0ccf42934163defb20%1765284699.337"
],

This includes the package name (zlib), the version number (1.3.1), a recipe revision cac0f6daea041b0ccf42934163defb20, and a timestamp. The 128-bit revision is an MD5 hash that includes source code. However, this hash is not intended to provide cryptographic security, but rather serves as a unique identifier. When Conan installs dependencies using this lockfile, it uses the recipe revision hash to download a particular file from the ConanCenter repository, but it does not recompute the recipe hash. Even if it did, there’s a separate package revision hash for platform-specific binaries that is not in the lockfile, and MD5 collisions could allow an attacker to create two distinct recipes with different behavior but the same hash.

The CocoaPods dependency manager for Swift and Objective-C has a similar pattern. Here is part of a Podfile.lock file for a project that uses the popular Files dependency.

SPEC CHECKSUMS:
 Files: d88e31b84d65e754935053b1c584ea8e2320698a

This 160-bit checksum is the SHA-1 hash of the Files Podspec, which contains the following link to the source code. CocoaPods uses this link to fetch the Git repository.

"source": {
 "git": "https://github.com/johnsundell/files.git",
 "tag": "4.0.2"
},

So even though the lockfile can prevent tampering with the GitHub URL in the Podspec (setting aside expensive SHA-1 collision attacks), a compromised GitHub server could just serve a malicious version of the repository with the same tag.

Finally, the Composer dependency manager for PHP includes commit hashes in the composer.lock file, as in the following excerpt.

"dist": {
 "type": "zip",
 "url": "https://api.github.com/repos/guzzle/psr7/zipball/b094ded77ee97a6027ad6cf0e8c7b9f88381814c",
 "reference": "b094ded77ee97a6027ad6cf0e8c7b9f88381814c",
 "shasum": ""
},

However, even though the b094ded... commit hash uniquely identifies the code, the ZIP archive in the URL does not include the Git tree as a way to verify the hash. Once again, GitHub could serve a malicious ZIP archive without detection by Composer.

Lockfiles have many roles besides supply-chain integrity

The previous experimental results show that lockfile hashes often can be used to enforce package integrity, but this is not their sole or even original purpose. Alternatively, they can lock dependencies to a particular functionality, enable an easy way for application developers to share a consistent environment, or facilitate reproducible builds. Analyzing package manager lockfiles through the lens of supply-chain security is a recent interpretation that can be at odds with their original design. The recent change to pnpm’s --frozen-lockfile is one example.

Another example of this tension is the question of whether the lockfile should be committed to version control. Most modern guidance recommends committing the lockfile for applications, since the final build environment is fully controlled. The question is more complicated for libraries, since package managers often ignore libraries’ lockfiles to avoid locking to conflicting transitive dependencies. Committing the lockfile makes it easier to develop the library by sharing a consistent build environment with other developers, but excluding the lockfile makes it easier to catch conflicts with different dependency versions before they are found by users. Many package managers recommend committing the lockfile for libraries (e.g., npm, pnpm, Poetry, uv, and Yarn), some recommend excluding it (e.g., Bundler), and some leave it up to the developer (e.g., Cargo).

Many of these questions are explored in a recent study by Gamage et al. The authors explore lockfile design decisions for seven package managers, analyze published projects, and perform semi-structured interviews with 15 developers. They find that the practice of committing a lockfile varies by which package manager is used, and categorize five benefits to using lockfiles, as perceived by the interview subjects: build determinism, integrity, transparency into indirect dependencies, debugging, and security scanning. Some of the developers also preferred to not use lockfiles, citing a preference for end users to resolve to the latest version of a dependency, which may have more bug fixes and vulnerability patches.

The diversity of package manager designs and views surrounding the purpose of lockfiles makes it difficult to prescribe a single recommendation. With regard to supply-chain integrity, it is common, but not universal, to view lockfiles as a source of integrity that should be committed with the source code. For package managers with lockfiles that do not provide cryptographic integrity, it is worth considering whether their users share that expectation. Even when lockfile hashes can provide cryptographic integrity, locking to specific package hashes means that users do not immediately receive subsequent updates or security fixes, since the newer package has a different hash. This leads to frequent lockfile bumping to distribute the latest hashes. Wanting immediate updates is a separate concern from wanting package integrity, but the current, common approach of using hashes in lockfiles is at odds with that goal. In conclusion, lockfile hashes are often, but not always, effective at providing cryptographic integrity, but do not work in every situation.

Signatures are common; verification is not

Signatures are a natural way to address these shortcomings, but implementations frequently fall short. In theory, developers could sign every release with their own private key, and the package manager could check the signature of the package it downloads from the package repository. In fact, signatures are relatively common in different package ecosystems, but proper signature validation is surprisingly lacking. The reality of using signatures to provide code integrity is more nuanced than it seems, and package managers have different approaches to the problem.

Many package managers have no signatures available. Arguably, vcpkg does not need them, because all package hashes are distributed with the manager, but this leaves Cargo, CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, Conda, Pub, R, and SwiftPM7. The Conan developers are aware and previously decided not to fix it, citing several implementation challenges and suggesting organizations where integrity is critical could run their own repository server. Cargo developers are actively considering different signing designs, but this effort is still in progress. Composer developers have been implementing many new protections against supply-chain attacks, with future plans for artifact integrity.

Repository signing

One straightforward approach, known as repository signing, is when the package repository signs every package once it’s uploaded, and the repository’s public key is distributed with the package manager. This doesn’t solve the problem of a totally compromised package repository, since a malicious package repository could legitimately sign a malicious package, but it would protect against untrusted mirrors or a partial compromise of a package repository’s serving infrastructure.

Repository signatures are used by the npm Registry, the NuGet Registry, and the PAUSE server for Perl module distribution. In the npm Registry, signatures are distributed within package metadata with repository-specific public keys. NuGet Registry repository signatures are found in .signature.p7s files within the distributed ZIP package, again with repository-specific public keys. The PAUSE server takes a different approach, using its GPG key to batch sign the cryptographic hashes of several packages at a time.

Developer signing

Developer signing involves the developer maintaining the private key and signing the package before uploading it to the repository for distribution. This prevents the package repository from tampering with the contents, but it also provides a way for the package repository to authenticate the uploader.

There are two common approaches for a developer asserting their public key. In the first approach, the public key is distributed out-of-band. The Maven Central repository (used by Maven and Gradle) and the RubyGems repository (used by the gem and Bundler package managers) both support this type of developer signing. Maven Central uses PGP signatures, and developer keys are distributed by public keyservers. RubyGems uses self-signed certificates, and their distribution is left to the developers (e.g., rspec). The major difference is that developer signing is mandatory for Maven Central, and optional for RubyGems. Developer signing is rare for RubyGems, due to the lack of an established chain of trust, and a previous attempt to introduce a certificate authority failed.

The second approach involves a chain of trust. The NuGet Registry and PowerShell Gallery both support developer signatures. Neither makes signatures mandatory, but the PowerShell Gallery recommends it and the NuGet Registry has strict requirements if developer signing is used. In both, the developer’s key must chain to a trusted CA, and acquiring a valid code-signing certificate can cost hundreds of dollars per year. The benefit of this approach is that trusted root certificates can be preinstalled on the platform, allowing package managers to verify public keys.

One downside of developer signing is that developers are responsible for key management, and they can lose the ability to update their code if they lose access to their key.

Identity-based signing

An increasingly common middle ground is “identity-based” or “keyless” signing from Sigstore. Rather than require developers to manage long-term private keys, a developer can use Sigstore’s Fulcio CA to issue a fresh signing certificate on demand, for free. To prevent impersonation, the developer proves their identity with an OIDC token: a cryptographically signed statement from a third party like Google, Microsoft, or GitHub that attests to the email address, username, or potentially other claims about the developer’s identity. The verifier can check that the username is correct and the certificate chain links back to Sigstore Fulcio’s root certificate, proving that someone with access to that account created the signature.

Keyless signing is particularly useful because it can be integrated into a developer’s existing workflow-based deployment pipeline. This is frequently called provenance attestation or trusted publishing8. GitHub and GitLab provide OIDC tokens to Actions and CI/CD workflows that attest to the build workflow, the repository, and the commit hash. A workflow can use this token to obtain a signing certificate from Sigstore, sign the built package, and upload the signed package to the package repository. Since the signing certificate includes the commit hash and workflow details, this cryptographically links the built binary artifact to its source code.

Provenance attestation via Sigstore is supported by Python’s PyPI, the npm Registry, RubyGems repository, and Maven Central. While Sigstore attestations are not mandatory, there is already better adoption than RubyGems’ optional support for developer-managed signing keys.

Verification code is skipped, unconfigured, or nonexistent

Unfortunately, just because these signatures exist does not mean they are being verified by package managers.

In the npm package manager, the repository signatures are not checked when running npm install. Checking the signatures requires running npm audit signatures, which uses Sigstore to validate the registry public keys and then validates the signatures of the installed packages. pnpm recently added the pnpm audit signatures command, but that implementation fetches the registry public keys from the potentially malicious registry rather than verifying with Sigstore, so an adversary could simply add their own key and signature. Bun and Yarn currently lack an equivalent audit signatures command.

In the NuGet package manager, the default signatureValidationMode is accept, which installs invalidly signed packages. The user must set this to require and configure the list of trusted signers, such as with dotnet nuget trust source. These configurations (which include the repository public keys) can be securely distributed within a nuget.config configuration file, functioning as a lockfile that locks the trusted signers.

Ruby’s Gem and Bundler, and Java’s Maven and Gradle, which all use repositories with developer signatures, do not verify signatures by default. They require the user to manually add developer public keys (gem cert --add) or list the allowed public keys that should be trusted. In Maven, one can use the third-party pgpverify-maven-plugin with pgp-keys-map.list to specify the trusted PGP fingerprints. Gradle offers dependency verification, which works similarly.

Finally, several package managers seemingly lack any sort of verification code at all. Pip, uv, and Poetry do not currently have a way to verify identity-based attestations described in PEP740. cpanminus does not have a way to verify the integrity of the repository-signed CHECKSUMS file. It once did, but in response to a verification bypass vulnerability, this verification code was removed. Even though PowerShell is supported on non-Windows platforms, Authenticode signature verification is not9. At one point, the PowerShell repository noted that this issue “should be fixed in a future release.”

Go package management and transparency logs

Go’s built-in package manager is the only one I tested that verifies signatures by default, and it also introduces one final concept for cryptographic package integrity. When go get or go mod download fetches a package10, it hashes the package contents and compares the hash, package name, and version against the checksum database. The contents of the database are registry-signed (analogous to PGP signatures in Perl’s PAUSE server), and the default checksum database public key is hardcoded in Go’s source code. As long as the checksum database’s private key is used honestly, this design ensures that the package name and version are enough to uniquely identify the binary contents of a package. As a result, the go.mod lockfile achieves package integrity without needing to store cryptographic hashes.11

Go’s checksum database is an example of a transparency log, or an immutable, global, tamper-resistant log of metadata. The same capability is provided by Sigstore’s Rekor and certificate transparency logs. In package managers, it cryptographically ensures that the package manager only ever installs the same binaries recorded by the transparency log. If everyone agrees on the transparency log, then everyone agrees on the package contents. This makes it more difficult for an adversary to selectively and undetectably target a victim with a malicious package. Transparency logs can still fail if there are other vulnerabilities, the log’s private key is compromised, or no one checks the transparency log for malicious behavior.

Of all the package managers I tested, Go performed the best at maintaining cryptographic integrity in the face of a compromised package repository or proxy. However, the registry-signature-like design means that much of the system’s trust is concentrated in a single private key.

A proposed cryptographic design for package managers

One potential approach that combines the ideas in this post is to include signature information in the lockfile. Rather than commit to the hash of a particular package, the lockfile could commit to a developer’s identity or public key. This reuses much of the infrastructure in place for lockfile hashes, but it separates the question of immediate updates from the question of package integrity.

With this design, the lockfile could specify a single dependency version (for build reproducibility) or a lower bound (for immediate updates), and the included identity ensures that a malicious repository or proxy cannot easily tamper with whatever package version the manager resolves to. In addition, a transparency log can protect against selective targeting, building on Sigstore’s identity-based signing and transparency log service. Sigstore avoids long-lived keys by default, but it also supports self-managed keys, KMS providers, and hardware tokens. This gives an easily adopted and secure default while still giving flexibility to developers who desire more control over their keys.

This idea is not new and not my own. Attestation identities are part of the pylock.toml Python lockfile specification, the trusted-keys in Gradle’s verification metadata, and the pgp-keys-map.list file in the pgpverify-maven-plugin for Maven. There is increasing recognition that this is a problem, and increasing appetite to fix it.

It won’t be easy. There are many subtle nuances that have to be considered and addressed, signing verification code needs to be developed and audited, and developers need to adopt the resulting design. In many of the package managers I reviewed as part of this project, I found communities of people who have been thinking about and pushing for cryptographic integrity and package signing for years. They know best what those package managers need, and they deserve the resources to make this a reality.

One of the greatest cryptographic success stories in the past decade has been the nearly universal adoption of HTTPS, driven in part by industry and community recognition of the security risks of unencrypted traffic, and the nonprofit Let’s Encrypt providing free and easy-to-use TLS certificates as a public good. items.title: Fake WatchGuard VPN site steals credentials, then serves the genuine signed client
items.summary: Huntress researchers have uncovered an SEO-poisoning campaign that harvests SSL VPN credentials through a lookalike WatchGuard download page, then hands victims the real, validly signed installer from WatchGuard’s own CDN, leaving endpoint tools with nothing to detect. The activity, detailed by the Huntress SOC on 13 October, centres on watchguard-vpn[.]net, a lookalike domain posing as a download page for WatchGuard’s Mobile VPN with SSL client. Unlike earlier waves of the campaign, which relied on trojanised installers, this iteration strips the malware out entirely. A typo and a search result The incident Huntress investigated began on 7 October, when an administrator at a managed service provider searched Bing for “watchguard vpn sll download”. Eight seconds later they had clicked through to the fake site via a standard Bing result redirect, which Huntress says points to SEO poisoning rather than malvertising. Two bites at the password Clicking any download option on the site opens a pop-up asking for the VPN server address, username and password, the same three values the legitimate client requests. The logic sits in roughly 150 lines of unobfuscated JavaScript (popup.js), which posts the entries as JSON to a separate collection domain, watchguard-ssl[.]online. The first submission is always rejected with an “incorrect data” message, prompting victims to retype carefully or try a different password. That gives the operators a second, likely more accurate, set of credentials, along with the server address they need to log in. The payload is the real thing After the second submission, the script triggers a download of WatchGuard’s genuine Mobile VPN with SSL installer (version 12.11.5) direct from cdn.watchguard.com. Huntress verified the file’s Authenticode signature from WatchGuard Technologies and confirmed the binary had not been altered. With no trojanised MSI or sideloaded DLL in the chain, there is nothing for EDR to flag, and the victim gets exactly the install they expected. Detection was thin across the board: as of 8 October only seven VirusTotal vendors flagged the lure domain and two flagged the collector. Old domain, new backend WatchGuard’s Secplicity team first reported watchguard-vpn[.]net in January as part of a wider credential-harvesting campaign spoofing WatchGuard, F5, Fortinet, SonicWall and Sophos clients, though at that point the domain had no working backend. Microsoft later attributed related activity to Storm-2561, a financially motivated actor active since May 2025. WHOIS data shows the domain was registered again on 22 August, with the collector domain following on 14 September. Huntress says it cannot establish whether the same operators controlled both registrations. In the case investigated, Huntress flagged the activity 21 seconds after the site loaded, and browser history suggests the user did not complete both rounds. The domain was offline as of 13 October, and Huntress has shared infrastructure details with WatchGuard. Recommendations Reset passwords for any account entered on the site and treat the associated VPN endpoint as known to the attacker. Enforce MFA on SSL VPN access. Monitor for VPN logins from hosting providers, unfamiliar ASNs or new countries. Block watchguard-vpn[.]net, watchguard-ssl[.]online, 80.249.132[.]140 and 158.94.209[.]19. Publish and bookmark official download links such as software.watchguard.com. Full research: https://www.huntress.com/blog/fake-watchguard-vpn-credential-phishing

items.title: VirusTotal Integrates Threat Intelligence With ChatGPT for Malware Analysis
items.summary: VirusTotal can now bring threat intelligence into ChatGPT through VirusTotal AI (VTAI), allowing users to investigate suspicious files, URLs, domains, and IP addresses within a conversation. The connection helps analysts retrieve existing reports and explain detection results while keeping the source, analysis date, and coverage visible. The integration uses Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard that connects AI tools with external services. VirusTotal’s ChatGPT connection guide describes setup through Developer mode and an OAuth connection. Users sign in with Google through VTAI without supplying a VirusTotal API key. Availability depends on account and workspace settings. VirusTotal ChatGPT Integration For an explicitly authorized ChatGPT attachment, the connector can fetch and hash the original file content. It checks whether VirusTotal already knows that hash before uploading anything. Known files return existing reports, while only confirmed unknown files are submitted. Creating the connection alone does not prove attachment support works. This approach separates report retrieval from file contribution. Retrieving an existing report consumes query quota, including repeated lookups and analysis status checks. At Cybersecuritynews, we have successfully integrated VirusTotal with ChatGPT to enhance our analysis capabilities. Recently, we conducted an in-depth check on a PDF file, and here are the results. VirusTotal GPT Analysis (Source: Cybersecuritynews.com) Uploading a confirmed unknown file does not spend that quota, although separate contribution limits apply. Receipt recovery is free, helping users resume interrupted work without resubmitting the same sample. For network investigations, users can request URL submissions or domain and IP reanalysis when authorized. Keeping each request identifier helps track the registered analysis after an interruption. These checks extend workflows covered in Cyber Security News’ VirusTotal threat research guide , bringing report review into a conversational interface. The connection also builds on VirusTotal’s earlier use of AI, including Code Insight for malware analysis . However, threat report access should not be mistaken for a final security verdict. Missing reports mean the result is unknown. Pending analysis and zero detections do not establish that a file or website is safe. Privacy remains a concern. Standard submissions share content with VirusTotal and may expose it to security community members and partners. Analysts should obtain permission before submitting personal documents, internal code, credentials, or sensitive data. Complete submitted URLs can disclose information carried in query strings and fragments, making review before submission essential. According to the VTAI overview , access is free within quotas. Permissions and allowances apply across account connections, not per chat. For security teams, the benefit is easier access to evidence, not a replacement for investigation. VirusTotal can now bring threat intelligence into ChatGPT through VirusTotal AI (VTAI), allowing users to investigate suspicious files, URLs, domains, and IP addresses within a conversation.

The connection helps analysts retrieve existing reports and explain detection results while keeping the source, analysis date, and coverage visible.

The integration uses Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard that connects AI tools with external services. VirusTotal’s ChatGPT connection guide describes setup through Developer mode and an OAuth connection. Users sign in with Google through VTAI without supplying a VirusTotal API key. Availability depends on account and workspace settings.

VirusTotal ChatGPT Integration

For an explicitly authorized ChatGPT attachment, the connector can fetch and hash the original file content. It checks whether VirusTotal already knows that hash before uploading anything.

Known files return existing reports, while only confirmed unknown files are submitted. Creating the connection alone does not prove attachment support works.

This approach separates report retrieval from file contribution. Retrieving an existing report consumes query quota, including repeated lookups and analysis status checks.

At Cybersecuritynews, we have successfully integrated VirusTotal with ChatGPT to enhance our analysis capabilities. Recently, we conducted an in-depth check on a PDF file, and here are the results.

VirusTotal GPT Analysis (Source: Cybersecuritynews.com)

Uploading a confirmed unknown file does not spend that quota, although separate contribution limits apply. Receipt recovery is free, helping users resume interrupted work without resubmitting the same sample.

For network investigations, users can request URL submissions or domain and IP reanalysis when authorized. Keeping each request identifier helps track the registered analysis after an interruption.

These checks extend workflows covered in Cyber Security News’ VirusTotal threat research guide, bringing report review into a conversational interface.

The connection also builds on VirusTotal’s earlier use of AI, including Code Insight for malware analysis. However, threat report access should not be mistaken for a final security verdict.

Missing reports mean the result is unknown. Pending analysis and zero detections do not establish that a file or website is safe.

Privacy remains a concern. Standard submissions share content with VirusTotal and may expose it to security community members and partners. Analysts should obtain permission before submitting personal documents, internal code, credentials, or sensitive data.

Complete submitted URLs can disclose information carried in query strings and fragments, making review before submission essential. According to the VTAI overview, access is free within quotas. Permissions and allowances apply across account connections, not per chat.

For security teams, the benefit is easier access to evidence, not a replacement for investigation. Analysts still need to assess report age, coverage, and context before deciding whether to block, isolate, or escalate.

An EDR alert reveals an attack. But can it tell the full story? Discover how to reconstruct the attack timeline.

items.title: Police receive fake murder tip from Anthropic’s Claude AI
items.summary: Police tip hotlines already have their fair share of crank callers. Apparently they now have to contend with crank AI agents as well. AI agents have already been caught hacking software companies , breaching an Australian government portal , and trying to hack a Canadian government website . Now Anthropic’s Claude has added a made-up murder tip to the list. Claude’s Haiku 4.5 model filed a false tip in an unsolved Philadelphia homicide via the police department’s online public tip form, Anthropic disclosed . The tip was flagged as spam and didn’t reach investigators. AI’s latest “what does this button do?” moment happened during an internal test on randomly chosen web pages, the company said. Claude submitted the tip on July 18 at 11:27 pm through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com, according to police. Tips submitted there can inform real homicide investigations. A fabricated account could send investigators chasing something that never happened. Here’s what Claude Haiku wrote: “I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant.” The agent didn’t provide any description of the person that it didn’t actually see. Neither did it leave any contact details before hitting submit. Haiku did this as part of Anthropic’s internal testing. It had to invent and perform sample tasks on random web pages with live internet access so the company could see how it behaved. There was a list of prohibited actions to go along with the test. Anthropic told the agents not to log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases, or submit “anything destructive.” The instructions did not explicitly rule out form submissions. The spam filter caught this one. Philadelphia police said the report never reached its Real-Time Crime Center for review or distribution to investigators. The department did not explain why it was flagged as spam. All tips go through human review before going out to investigators. That safeguard limited the impact of the incident, the department said, but did not diminish the seriousness of an AI system presenting made-up information as though it came from someone with knowledge of a crime. As it put it in a statement : “Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers.” Anthropic discovered the false tip on September 28 and notified police on October 7, according to the department. Police called the two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident “unacceptable.” It is coordinating with the City Law Department, its Office of Innovation and Technology, and the Mayor’s executive team, the department added. Anthropic described the real-world impact of the incidents in its report as minimal. It has now disabled live internet access across its internal evaluations until it confirms that its safeguards reliably catch this behavior. The company said the transcript suggested Haiku was just trying to produce example content rather than trying to deliberately mislead the cops. But it also admitted that we can’t completely rely on a model’s account of its own reasoning. That leaves its explanation provisional, however reassuring it might sound. An allowlist could offer a tighter boundary for tests like these, limiting agents to approved sites and actions. A live police tip form should hardly be a testing ground. The homicide tip was not the only unwanted submission. Anthropic noted that federal, state, and local government websites also got visits from Claude, which repeatedly tried to fill out forms. Although Anthropic didn’t go into detail, a State Department official said that it got 20 visa applications from a testing model (19 in August, and one in May). None of them were processed, the official added. When an AI gives you fake information about who Beyoncé is married to, it might be irritating but it might only affect your team’s fortunes in a trivia night. The stakes get much higher when we’re dealing with intelligence that can inform law enforcement actions or public policy. In August, the head of the UK’s Police AI center warned law enforcement there to pause plans for AI use in criminal justice work. This came after the UK’s West Midlands Police apologized to members of Parliament over false evidence involving an invented soccer match. The error arose from the use of Microsoft Copilot. Anthropic’s latest incident raises a further concern: AI agents can put invented information into real systems themselves. What would happen if someone deliberately sent agents to flood police tip lines? This time, the false account stayed in spam. The people relying on those tip lines deserve safeguards that hold up when the next submission gets through. “One of the best cybersecurity suites on the planet.” According to CNET. Read their review →

items.title: Zero Trust in Practice: Moving Beyond the Buzzword
items.summary: Zero trust has become one of the most overused terms in security marketing, often applied to products that simply add another layer of network segmentation. This piece looks at what zero trust actually specifies according to its foundational standard, the implementation order that works in practice, and why identity is the dependency most organizations underestimate. What Does Zero Trust Actually Specify, Beyond the Marketing Language? Zero trust gets used loosely enough that it has largely lost precision as a term, applied to everything from a VPN replacement to a full architectural rebuild. That imprecision is a real problem for organizations trying to evaluate vendor claims, since two products both marketed as zero trust solutions can address entirely different parts of the actual model. Organizations working through this evaluation often look at established regional providers as part of their planning. Among them, cybersecurity solutions in Dubai offer a starting point for comparing how different providers translate the zero trust framework into an actual implementation roadmap, which varies considerably depending on an organization’s existing infrastructure. At its core, the specification requires continuous verification of every access request, whether it originates inside or outside the traditional network perimeter, and it removes the assumption that anything on the internal network is inherently trustworthy simply by virtue of its location. Zero trust component What it actually requires Identity verification Every access request authenticated, not just the initial network entry Least privilege access Access scoped to the minimum needed for a specific task Micro segmentation Network divided so lateral movement is contained, not just perimeter defended Continuous monitoring Access patterns evaluated ongoing, not just at login That table names the components. The harder part, and the part most vendor pitches skip, is the order in which an organization actually implements them. What Implementation Order Actually Works, and What Stalls? Organizations that attempt zero trust as a single, comprehensive rollout tend to stall, since the scope quickly exceeds what any team can execute without disrupting normal operations. Organizations that succeed tend to sequence the work, starting with identity infrastructure before touching network segmentation. That sequencing is not arbitrary. Identity is the hard dependency underneath every other component of the model. Microsegmentation without solid identity verification just creates smaller trusted zones rather than removing the underlying trust assumption. Continuous monitoring without reliable identity data produces noise rather than usable signal. Getting identity right first is what makes everything built on top of it actually function as intended. IT Security Guru’s coverage of automated tools in SaaS penetration testing touches a related sequencing question from a different angle: the growing reliance on automation to keep pace with continuous verification demands, which is exactly the kind of tooling that becomes necessary once an organization’s zero trust model matures past the identity foundation stage. Organizations that skip the identity-first ordering often end up with what looks like a zero trust deployment on paper but functions as a rebranded VLAN structure underneath, technically segmented but still relying on implicit trust once a user or device gets past the initial checkpoint. Where Does the NIST Standard Actually Draw the Line? Rather than relying on vendor definitions, it helps to work from the actual specification. NIST Special Publication 800-207 lays out the zero trust architecture in detail, defining the core logical components and the tenets that distinguish a genuine implementation from marketing language attached to conventional network security. The standard makes it clear that zero trust is a set of principles guiding architecture decisions, not a single product or technology you can buy and deploy wholesale. That framing alone rules out a large share of what gets marketed under the term, since a genuine implementation touches identity management, policy enforcement, and monitoring together rather than any one of them in isolation. How Can an Organization Tell Real Progress From a Rebranded VLAN? A few honest checks separate genuine progress toward zero trust from a relabeled version of existing network security. Evaluate access decisions per request based on current context, not grant broad access once a user authenticates at the start of a session. Policy enforcement should apply consistently, whether a request originates inside or outside the traditional network boundary. Monitoring should also detect anomalous access patterns after the fact, not just block unauthorized access at the point of entry. An organization that cannot clearly explain how it makes access decisions on a per-request basis is likely still operating on the old trust model, whatever the marketing materials on its security stack claim. FAQ What is zero trust, in the simplest accurate terms? It is a security model that requires continuous verification of every access request, regardless of whether it originates inside or outside the traditional network perimeter, removing the assumption that internal network location implies trustworthiness. Why does identity have to come before network segmentation in implementation? Identity verification is the dependency the rest of the model relies on. Segmentation and monitoring without reliable identity data produce smaller trusted zones or noisy alerts, rather than genuinely removing implicit trust. How can an organization tell if its zero trust deployment is genuine? Access decisions should be evaluated per request based on current context, not granted broadly after initial login, and policy enforcement should apply consistently regardless of where a request originates. Is zero trust a product an organization can simply buy? No. NIST’s foundational specification describes it as a set of architectural principles, not a single purchasable technology. A genuine implementation brings together identity, policy enforcement, and monitoring rather than relying on any one component alone.
