items.summary_html:
Vega, the pioneer of Agentic Cyber Defense, today announced the appointment of Scott Simkin as Chief Marketing Officer. Simkin joins as Vega II unleashes the best model trained for cyber defense to transform every alert, across all data sources, into a conclusive verdict at the speed of the attack. The platform keeps every lesson and gets faster with every fight, so defenders can finally outpace adversarial AI.

“Once a generation, a company changes how security gets done. For Cyber Defense in the age of AI, that company is Vega,” said Shay Sandler, co-founder and CEO of Vega. “Scott built the stories and execution engine behind the two biggest names in security operations. Now he will help Vega define the post-SIEM era. There is no one I would rather have leading this charge.”

Simkin is one of the industry’s best-known storytellers, having twice helped define a category and drive growth at massive scale. At Palo Alto Networks, he served as Vice President of Marketing for the end-to-end Cortex platform, one of the fastest-growing portfolios spanning security operations, cloud security, and Unit 42 services, with annual revenue approaching $2 billion. Earlier, he helped pioneer the XDR category, which has since replaced EDR as the standard for modern endpoint security. At CrowdStrike, he led product marketing, technical marketing, portfolio positioning, and campaigns across the full Falcon platform. He also launched Falcon Next-Gen SIEM, which CrowdStrike says now exceeds $600 million in annual recurring revenue. Two years after founding, Vega already defends some of the world’s largest banks, healthcare providers, and Fortune 200 enterprises, and Simkin joins to turn that momentum into dominant market leadership.

“For three years, CISOs have asked me the same question about AI in their SOC: isn’t this just an iteration on the SIEM? items.title: Certes wins Frost & Sullivan PQC recognition for decoupling encryption from infrastructure
items.summary: Certes has received Frost & Sullivan’s 2026 Global Enabling Technology Leadership Recognition in post-quantum cryptography (PQC), following an independent evaluation of vendors in the market. The recognition centres on a problem most security teams are now facing: migrating embedded cryptography across legacy applications, cloud environments and critical infrastructure will take years, but “harvest now, decrypt later” attacks mean data intercepted today could be exposed once sufficiently powerful quantum computers arrive. Frost & Sullivan notes that the risk is greatest for data with long regulatory, legal or commercial lifespans, and that protecting it needs to run in parallel with the longer migration effort rather than wait for it to finish. Separating cryptography from the stack At the heart of Certes’ platform is its Cryptographic Abstraction Layer (CAL), which sits between applications and infrastructure and lifts cryptographic protection out of the underlying technology stack. Rather than waiting for each vendor to ship a quantum-safe update and then managing disruptive upgrades, security teams can manage cryptographic change centrally and apply it to data flowing between systems. The platform comprises the Certes Enforcement Point (CEP), which encrypts and decrypts within the data path, and the Certes Policy Manager (CPM), which manages policies and cryptographic controls centrally. Frost & Sullivan singled out its policy-specific key architecture as a key differentiator: each policy-controlled application or data flow can have its own key material, separate rotation schedules and customer-controlled key components. This is combined with quantum-based random number generation and customer-owned keys to support data sovereignty. Certes’ patented Layer 4 payload protection encrypts the payload while preserving original network headers, so routing, QoS, monitoring, SD-WAN and flow visibility tools continue to work without applications being rewritten or networks re-architected. Deployment options span physical appliances, virtual machines on VMware ESXi, KVM, Red Hat and Nutanix AHV, and Windows and Linux client agents. Version 7 extends enforcement closer to workloads and users through expanded agent and cloud deployment options, reducing unprotected segments in the data’s journey. Beyond quantum The report also highlights uses beyond PQC migration. Cryptographic segmentation can separate IT and OT environments and limit lateral movement in flat networks, while a virtual air gap capability can dynamically isolate critical applications, data flows and backups during an active attack while preserving recovery. Certes’ encryption can also stop sensitive data being exposed to internal or external LLMs, giving organisations tighter governance over AI adoption. Ozgun Pelit, Senior Industry Analyst at Frost & Sullivan, said: “Certes stands out in the emerging post-quantum security market through its focus on protecting data independently of the applications and infrastructure around it. Its combination of cryptographic abstraction, crypto-agility and centralized policy enforcement provides organisations with a practical way to reduce near-term quantum risk while navigating what will inevitably be a complex, multi-year migration.” Paul German, CEO at Certes, said: “The next cryptographic revolution could arrive before many organizations have finished implementing the last one. Post-quantum cryptography is only the beginning. As AI and quantum technologies advance, cryptographic change will accelerate, and organisations cannot afford to rebuild their applications, networks and security infrastructure every time it happens.” He added: “In a world where cryptography must constantly evolve, the ability to change it without changing everything else isn’t a luxury. It’s a necessity.” The full Frost & Sullivan report is available HERE

items.title: Google Awarded $250,000 Bounty for a Full-chain Chrome Exploit Found Using GPT-5.6
items.summary: Security researchers earned a $250,000 reward from Google after building a full-chain Chrome exploit with AI agents. The XBOW team says the work took six days and about $40,000 in computing costs, using OpenAI’s publicly available GPT-5.6 Sol model . Google has fixed the flaws. XBOW disclosed the work on October 13, 2026. Its chain linked three bugs to move from JavaScript in a Chrome tab to code execution outside the browser’s renderer sandbox. The company estimated that the issue could affect about one billion users worldwide, while the demonstration targeted Windows. Google Awards $250K for Chrome Exploit A sandbox limits what a compromised web page can do. A full chain joins bugs to cross Chrome’s defenses in sequence. XBOW demonstrated a crafted page launching a program on a test system. It did not report the exploit being used against people. The first flaw was in V8, Chrome’s JavaScript engine. XBOW says a bug in the Maglev compiler let separate JavaScript objects share a changeable number during deoptimization, when V8 moves from optimized code to a less optimized path. Changing the value could mislead optimized code and give the exploit memory access inside V8’s protected region. The second flaw affected animated WebP images. The decoder could use frame details saved from one image while reading changed image data. That mismatch caused an out-of-bounds write and allowed the chain to leave the V8 sandbox. The third flaw was in Crashpad, Chrome’s crash-reporting system. On Windows, Crashpad could retry a failed memory read using a length based on the rest of a page. The code assumed the renderer would not change. XBOW’s exploit changed page access during the retry, causing an oversized read and memory corruption in the handler outside the renderer sandbox. XBOW says its researchers guided the work. They chose targets, split tasks, checked AI results, and prepared backups. The team replaced an early chain after Google said one part was already known. A modular design let it swap in another bug. The company said it developed the final chain from August 2 to August 7. Google’s Chrome Vulnerability Reward Program offers $250,000 for an eligible full-chain exploit that works from web content on an active Chrome release. The rules require a working demonstration and responsible testing. The award recognizes a reported flaw, not a confirmed compromise of users’ devices. Users should keep Chrome up to date and relaunch it when an update is ready. XBOW says Google fixed all three flaws. items.title: Windows SmartScreen Vulnerability Enables Privilege Escalation Attacks
items.summary: Microsoft has released fixes for a Windows SmartScreen vulnerability that allows an attacker with local access to gain higher privileges. Tracked as CVE-2026-85851, the flaw was disclosed on October 13, 2026, and carries a CVSS base score of 7.8. Microsoft rates it Important. The issue involves a use-after-free memory error and affects several Windows 11 releases and Windows Server 2025. According to the supplied Microsoft advisory, successful exploitation lets an attacker move from a low integrity level to a medium integrity level. This is a specific increase in access, not a confirmed path to administrator or SYSTEM privileges. The attacker must already have low privileges on the affected device, but the attack requires no user interaction. The flaw falls under CWE-416, use-after-free . This error occurs when software continues to access memory after that memory has been released. Another operation may reuse the same memory, leaving the original code working with data that no longer belongs to it. Such errors can cause memory corruption, crashes, or other security problems. Microsoft identifies local privilege escalation as the impact for this vulnerability. Its CVSS vector lists low attack complexity, low privileges required, and no user interaction. Those conditions describe an attacker who already has a foothold on the device, not someone exploiting SmartScreen directly over the internet. Windows SmartScreen Vulnerability Microsoft credits researcher yhw with reporting the issue. At publication, the advisory marked it as neither publicly disclosed nor exploited and assessed exploitation as “Exploitation Less Likely.” Those findings do not remove the need to patch, but they do not support describing this flaw as an actively exploited zero-day. Earlier SmartScreen attacks involved different weaknesses. Cyber Security News previously covered SmartScreen bypass attacks delivering malware through CVE-2024-21412 and Water Hydra’s SmartScreen zero-day campaign . Those reports concern bypassing security warnings and should not be confused with the newly disclosed local privilege escalation flaw. Microsoft also disclosed CVE-2026-83504 , a Windows SmartScreen information disclosure flaw rated CVSS 4.7 and classified as a time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition. An attacker who successfully exploits this second flaw could view heap memory from a privileged process. Exploitation requires winning a race condition, which explains its high attack complexity. It also requires local access and low privileges and needs no user interaction. Microsoft credits its Offensive Research & Security Engineering team and reports no exploitation at publication. The supplied material does not establish an exploit chain between the two flaws. For CVE-2026-85851 , the supplied update list covers Windows 11 versions 23H2, 24H2, 25H2, 26H1, and 26H2 across x64 and ARM64 systems. Windows Server 2025, including Server Core, is also listed. The listed fixes are KB5126653 for Windows 11 23H2, KB5127648 for 24H2, 25H2, and 26H2, KB5127646 for 26H1, and KB5126646 for Windows Server 2025. Administrators should match each device to its release and architecture, then verify installation against Microsoft’s update records. The two advisories list different update packages, so check their patch details separately before deploying across affected systems. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.title: Coruna and DarkSword Exploit Kits Can Fully Compromise iPhones From a Single Web Visit
items.summary: Two powerful iPhone exploit kits, Coruna and DarkSword, show how a visit to a malicious or compromised website can put an outdated device at risk. The kits can link several software flaws together to break out of the browser and reach deeper parts of iOS. Depending on the device’s software version and the kit used, an attacker may then steal sensitive information without needing the user to install an app or tap through extra prompts. These are not ordinary malicious webpages. An exploit kit is a set of tools that checks a visitor’s device and selects code designed for its software. Coruna contains five complete exploit chains and 23 exploits targeting iOS 13.0 through 17.2.1. DarkSword uses a six-flaw chain against iOS 18.4 through 18.7. The two kits target different iOS ranges, so the risk depends on the version installed. Researchers from iVerify identified and studied DarkSword with Google and Lookout, and iVerify has also reported on newer variants in the wild. In an investigation published in October 2026, its researchers described a modified strain called P7 DarkSword, which can steal keychain and cryptocurrency wallet data. Coruna and DarkSword Exploit Kits The attack starts when Safari loads a malicious page or content hidden inside a compromised website. The page checks the iPhone’s model and iOS version, then serves code suited to that device. A WebKit or JavaScriptCore flaw can let the code run in the browser. Further flaws help it escape the browser’s safety limits and gain higher system access. That chain matters because the browser normally runs in a restricted area called a sandbox. A sandbox is designed to limit what a webpage can reach. Coruna and DarkSword use additional flaws to break past those limits; the later stages can reach kernel-level access, which gives the attacker much broader control over the device. Earlier Coruna exploit research describes the range of exploits and iOS versions involved. The tools can then collect valuable data. Reporting on DarkSword describes theft of passwords, messages, browsing records, location information and cryptocurrency wallet contents. iVerify’s P7 analysis adds on-device keychain collection and two-way communication with the attacker’s server. That information can put both personal accounts and work access at risk, especially when the phone holds saved credentials or is used to approve sign-ins. From targeted tools to wider criminal use Coruna’s history shows how a powerful exploit can move between different users. Google tracked its use from a surveillance customer to espionage activity against Ukrainian users and later to financially motivated campaigns using fake finance and cryptocurrency websites. The kit’s final payload, called PlasmaLoader, is designed to target cryptocurrency wallets and search Apple Notes for recovery phrases. DarkSword also moved beyond limited use after its source code was leaked publicly in 2026. That made the kit easier for other attackers to obtain and adapt. Separate reporting has described attackers combining DarkSword’s route into a device with Coruna’s wallet-theft tools, a development covered in this DarkSword and Coruna platform report . A public leak does not mean every copy works on every iPhone, but it can make reuse and changes easier. The threat can be difficult to spot. Some implants run inside normal system processes and may remove parts of their activity when finished. Browser or network monitoring can also miss what happens after the exploit code reaches the device. iVerify reported that some DarkSword variants leave useful traces, including Safari history and crash logs, while Coruna artifacts may remain after a reboot or iOS update. Installing the latest iOS update available for the device is the most important step. Updates close known flaws used in these chains; Apple has also issued security fixes for older supported devices. Users should check Settings for Software Update and install the version offered for their model. Lockdown Mode can provide extra protection for people at higher risk, but it is not a replacement for updates. It works best when enabled before opening a malicious page and can limit some features. Users should also avoid signing in through unexpected finance or cryptocurrency pages, even when a site looks familiar. Organizations should track iOS versions across work devices, review which accounts each phone can access and have a plan to isolate a suspected device for investigation. If compromise is suspected, treat credentials stored on that phone as exposed: change them from a trusted device, revoke active sessions where possible and involve the organization’s security team. A loaner phone can help staff keep working while investigators preserve the original device. items.title: Security vendors are racing to govern AI agents. Are they protecting the right thing?
items.summary: BigID and Varonis, two of the larger companies in data security, have both shipped products in the last couple of months aimed at the same problem: AI agents getting to company data. BigID launched AgentIQ on September 21. It lets customers run their data security and compliance work from a prompt or an AI agent, either inside BigID or from assistants like Claude, Copilot, GPT, and Gemini. According to BigID, agents working through AgentIQ inherit the permissions of the person who asked, and every action they take is logged. Varonis announced Agent Intent-Based Access Control in August as part of its Atlas platform. It compares what an agent was told to do with what the agent actually does: the tools it calls, the data it opens, and its reasoning along the way. If the agent drifts from its instructions, Atlas can alert on it, block the action, or quarantine the identity behind it. I think both are well engineered, and both companies are responding to a real problem. Agents now open files, call tools, and pass work to other agents, and most of the access controls companies have in place today were designed for people. Both products control the agent Based on what each company has published, the two products take the same basic approach. They limit what an agent is allowed to do, record what it does, and step in when it does something it wasn’t asked to do. items.title: Hackers Breach Meta GitHub Repositories, Steal Source Code and Data of 1,500 People
items.summary: Hackers used an employee’s stolen credentials to access some of Meta’s GitHub repositories, taking product source code and personal information linked to roughly 1,500 people. Most affected individuals are Meta employees in the United States, according to the company’s disclosure to SecurityWeek. Meta confirmed the breach on October 13, 2026, when it began notifying affected people. The company said it detected the intrusion several weeks earlier, blocked the attackers’ access, and brought in GitHub and law enforcement to support its response. Stolen Credentials Opened Repository Access Meta said attackers entered through stolen employee credentials, not a flaw in a Meta product. The company also said its internal systems were not breached. The disclosed incident involved business data held in GitHub repositories. The report does not explain how the credentials were stolen or identify the attackers. Meta said its investigation with GitHub had not indicated that the group specifically targeted Meta’s data. That assessment remains based on the investigation so far. According to Meta, 99% of the stolen material was business data, consisting of software code related to some products. Personal information accounted for the remaining 1%. Those percentages describe the stolen material, not the share of employees affected. Meta has not named the affected products or detailed the repository contents. The disclosure does not say that attackers changed code, published it, or used it to compromise other systems. Meta told SecurityWeek it mistakenly placed personal information in the repositories, despite company rules that prohibit storing it on GitHub. The company has not disclosed which types of personal information were taken, leaving the full privacy impact unclear. A significant portion of material that appeared to contain personal information was synthetic or anonymized test data, Meta said. The company believes this could make it harder for attackers to separate genuine records from test records. However, that does not remove the need to protect people whose real information was exposed. Meta is notifying regulators and offering affected individuals credit monitoring and dark web monitoring services. These measures form part of its response while it addresses the repository exposure and its handling of personal data.[ securityweek ] Meta Rotates Secrets and Adds Data Checks Meta said it rotated secrets found in the affected repositories and strengthened product security to address risks from the stolen business data. It is also introducing proactive scans to detect user information uploaded by mistake and working with GitHub on additional repository protections. GitHub’s guidance on leaked secrets explains why replacing exposed credentials matters. Removing a secret from source code alone is not enough. Teams must revoke it through its provider and generate a replacement where needed to prevent further use. The incident follows other repository thefts covered by CybersecurityNews, including CrowdSec’s loss of about 170 private GitHub repositories through a compromised former employee account. Separate reporting on hundreds of thousands of active credentials exposed on GitHub highlights the need to revoke leaked keys promptly. Neither report establishes a connection to Meta’s breach. Together, they show why repository security must cover both account access and the data stored inside code projects.

items.title: Attackers Breach European Bank Through Third-Party Gateway and Target WSUS Server
items.summary: A European bank was breached through a poorly secured, third-party gateway before an attacker tried to exploit its Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) infrastructure. The case shows how stolen login details and weak access controls can put a bank’s central software systems at risk without a complex attack chain. The bank’s security team uncovered unauthorized VPN access attempts stretching across several months after spotting unusual activity on its central IT system. Investigators traced the intrusion to an external gateway managed by a third party, where strict authentication had not been properly enforced. Researchers from Unit 42 identified the intrusion and its attempted code execution, but their report does not name any malware family. Published on October 13, 2026, the investigation describes an opportunistic attacker whose noisy actions exposed basic security gaps rather than a confirmed, advanced spying operation. Attackers Breach European Bank The attacker used compromised credentials to sign in to internal systems through the gateway. Unit 42 did not name the appliance vendor or explain how those credentials were first obtained. The confirmed entry point was weak authentication on the externally managed device, not a disclosed gateway software exploit. That distinction matters because valid accounts can give an intruder access without requiring a new vulnerability. Earlier reporting on brute-force attacks against VPNs describes separate incidents involving weak passwords and appliances lacking multifactor authentication, showing why remote access settings deserve close review. Those incidents are not linked to this bank. Once inside, the intruder repeatedly scanned hosts and networks across several protocols, interacting with thousands of systems. Instead of quietly following one narrow path, the attacker searched broadly for more opportunities to gain access. Unit 42 said the volume of scanning and use of common system identifiers showed little effort to stay hidden. Over several months, the attacker also ran repeated password-guessing campaigns against internal systems, with administrator accounts a key focus. These attempts sought additional access while the intruder explored the environment. Separate coverage of automated VPN login attacks illustrates how repeated credential testing can threaten remote access services, although the bank’s reported password guessing occurred internally. The activity extended beyond logins. Automated web requests scraped internal pages and attachments, while the attacker searched operational and network shares. This exposed documentation during the intrusion. However, the report does not give a stolen data volume, identify affected customers, or confirm that customer banking records were taken. WSUS Exploit Attempt Stopped The attacker later targeted a remote code execution vulnerability in WSUS on the bank’s central configuration management server. That server handled software distribution across the organization, making it an attractive place to seek higher privileges and lasting access. Control of such a central service could have widened the incident’s impact. Unit 42 did not disclose the vulnerability’s CVE identifier. Although separate reporting on active WSUS vulnerability exploitation covers CVE-2025-59287, that identifier cannot be assigned to this bank incident from the published evidence. Keeping those cases separate avoids turning a related technical risk into an unsupported finding. Cortex XDR detected the attempt to run unauthorized code and contained the threat before it escalated. Unit 42 reported that the attacker was stopped from establishing persistent access or spreading further through the network. This containment followed earlier scanning, authentication attempts, and access to internal documentation; it did not prevent the initial breach. Responders reviewed endpoint records across thousands of systems and logs from dozens of Windows and Linux servers. They found no additional attacker presence or persistent backdoors. Bank leaders reviewed the exposed documentation and rotated all compromised credentials. The bank also expanded its Cortex XDR and Cortex XSIAM coverage and incident response support. The investigation highlights authentication, timely patching, and endpoint detection as core safeguards. Third-party management did not remove the bank’s exposure to a weak gateway configuration, while containment and follow-up hunting helped limit the damage. For security teams, the lesson is to review vendor-managed access with the same care as internal systems. The report calls for strict identity controls, timely updates, and endpoint monitoring. Checking these controls together is important because a valid login can otherwise turn an outside gateway into internal access. items.title: The Blind Spot in Orbit: Why Space Could Be the Next Infrastructure Crisis
items.summary: Are organisations becoming so reliant on third party space assets that they would face severe disruption if the assets were impacted by a cyber attack? When most people think of space technology, they imagine routine weather forecasts or blue-dot navigation on a smartphone map. But behind those quiet satellite signals lies an invisible digital thread holding modern society together. From crop harvesting schedules to international flight routes and supermarket supply chains, daily life on Earth is deeply dependent on data from space. Yet space security remains the cyber risk that very few in executive boardrooms are addressing. As the space economy surges toward a $1.01 trillion valuation by 2034 , a dangerous blind spot has emerged. Cyber threats to orbital infrastructure are no longer a theoretical hazard—they are happening now. Privatization Outpacing Security Historically, space operations were the exclusive domain of governments operating in strictly air-gapped environments with near-zero tolerance for risk. Today, rapid commercial privatization has slashed launch costs, but speed to market is dangerously outstripping security by design. Commercial operators inherit standard enterprise IT vulnerabilities, complex supply chain risks, unpatched APIs, and operational technology gaps. The systemic disconnect is stark: According to data from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) , space-based systems now support more than 50% of all critical services and infrastructure across modern economies. The European Commission’s latest assessment is that 10% of the EU’s GDP is enabled directly or indirectly by satellite navigation signals . This equates to around €1.88 trillion based on the EU’s GDP for 2025. Yet 85% of organisations aren’t factoring space assets into their cyber risk mitigation strategy, according to the World Economic Forum . Physical Consequences on the Ground Unlike typical corporate breaches, orbital cyber attacks can trigger immediate physical impacts on Earth. Tampering with satellite telemetry can destabilize regional crop yields by altering planting schedules or paralyze commercial aviation by injecting false data into flight-navigation networks. Crucially, these risks are not limited to assets in orbit. Ground-based power substations, telemetry command hubs, and downlink facility infrastructure have become primary cyber-physical targets. A coordinated cyber attack on local energy substations supporting satellite ground operations could sever communication links and ground control just as effectively as an in-orbit compromise. A study commissioned by the European Space Agency (ESA) modeled the impact of a hypothetical 7-day satellite communications outage across ESA member states and Canada. The potential cost reaches up to €20 billion ($21.8 billion) in total economic losses . This includes €19 billion in maritime logistics and port bottlenecks, €558 million in direct aviation losses (canceling ~4,000 transatlantic flights), €352 million in lost connectivity for emergency services and remote communities, and €89.8 million from stalled offshore energy operations. Aging Tech Meets Advanced Threat Actors Geostationary satellites carry mission lifespans of 10 to 15 years, locking critical communications into legacy hardware designed before modern cyber threats existed. Nation-states and cybercriminals are exploiting these gaps; Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 threat intelligence currently tracks multiple state-sponsored groups actively targeting space-sector systems. What Leaders Must Do Now Governments and enterprise boards must recognize space-based timing, navigation, and observation as core national critical infrastructure . Leadership teams should execute four priorities immediately: Map Space Dependencies: Audit third-party services, cloud links, and automated logistics relying on satellite telemetry. Establish Terrestrial Backups: Build manual redundancies—including ground-based radio networks and offline inventory controls—for scenario planning when space signals go dark. Elevate Supply Chain Audits: Evaluate whether key vendors rely on single-point-of-failure commercial satellite constellations or unfortified ground substations. Update Risk Registers: Formally integrate space dependencies into corporate cyber risk registers. Translating these action items into real-world operational resilience requires moving beyond static compliance policies. To protect complex ecosystems—where ground stations, power substations, cloud environments, and orbital data streams converge—organizations need a unified, platformized approach to security that provides continuous visibility across every link in the space supply chain. In the modern threat landscape, business resilience, national sovereignty, and space security are inseparable. It is time for leaders to look up before an orbital breach brings ground operations to a standstill.

items.title: Gears of War: E-Day Hit by DDoS Attack, Causing Login Failures and Disconnects
items.summary: Gear of War: E-Day players faced login failures, sudden disconnects, and other online service problems after distributed denial-of-service attacks targeted the game’s online services. The official Gears Community account confirmed the cause on X, linking the disruption to DDoS activity and ending speculation about the source of the failures. The Gears Community reported attacks on its online services that caused intermittent disconnects, login issues, and other disruptions, but did not identify the attackers, disclose traffic figures, or specify affected services, limiting details about the attack’s scale and method. A separate update from the same account said the login issue had been resolved and that the team would continue closely monitoring services. Earlier messaging had flagged extended login times and said the issue was improving. The updates show progress toward recovery, but the login fix should not be read as proof that every reported service problem had ended. Gears of War: E-Day Hit by DDoS Attack Players may experience delayed or failed logins, intermittent disconnections, and difficulty reconnecting, symptoms confirmed by the Gears Community during the online service disruption. The available statement does not establish that the attacker accessed player accounts or stole personal information. It describes an attack against service availability. Reporting the incident as a confirmed data breach would go beyond the evidence released by the Gears Community team. A DDoS attack uses multiple machines to overwhelm a target with traffic or requests. The aim is to make a system or network unavailable to legitimate users. Compromised devices can form a botnet, allowing attackers to send traffic from many sources at once, according to CISA’s DDoS response guidance. This can exhaust network capacity or system resources, preventing the system from handling normal requests. However, the Gears update does not identify a botnet, a traffic flood type, or an attack rate. There is no published basis in that statement for assigning the incident to a known group or connecting it to another campaign. Gaming infrastructure has faced similar availability threats before. Cybersecurity News previously covered DDoS malware targeting Valve Source Engine game servers , with several supported attack methods. That report provides useful background on game-server threats. However, it does not link to the E-Day disruption. Another report examined a 3.15-billion-packets-per-second attack against a Minecraft server . The case shows why packet volume matters alongside bandwidth when assessing attacks. No comparable measurements have been shared in the available Gears statement. CISA recommends confirming DDoS activity through network monitoring and traffic analysis, then applying measures such as traffic filtering and rate limits. These are general defensive steps, not confirmed details of the Gears team’s response. Official updates confirm the reported cause, player impact, and login recovery, but leave the attack’s scale and technical handling undisclosed. The team’s stated recovery approach still includes monitoring after the service disruption. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. Integrate TI Feeds with data from 16K SOCs .

There is no published basis in that statement for assigning the incident to a known group or connecting it to another campaign.

Gaming infrastructure has faced similar availability threats before. Cybersecurity News previously covered DDoS malware targeting Valve Source Engine game servers, with several supported attack methods. That report provides useful background on game-server threats. However, it does not link to the E-Day disruption.

Another report examined a 3.15-billion-packets-per-second attack against a Minecraft server. The case shows why packet volume matters alongside bandwidth when assessing attacks. No comparable measurements have been shared in the available Gears statement.

CISA recommends confirming DDoS activity through network monitoring and traffic analysis, then applying measures such as traffic filtering and rate limits. These are general defensive steps, not confirmed details of the Gears team’s response.

Official updates confirm the reported cause, player impact, and login recovery, but leave the attack’s scale and technical handling undisclosed. The team’s stated recovery approach still includes monitoring after the service disruption.

items.title: Multiple Google Chrome Flaws Could Enable Memory Corruption and Code Execution Attacks
items.summary: Google released a Chrome security update that addresses 37 vulnerabilities, including seven critical flaws that raise concerns about memory corruption and possible code execution . Published on October 13, 2026, the update covers Windows, Mac, and Linux, with fixes spanning graphics, PDF handling, media processing, networking, and other browser components. According to Google’s Stable Channel Update for Desktop, the patched versions are 155.0.8059.79/.80 for Windows and Mac, and 155.0.8059.79 for Linux. The release includes seven critical, 29 high, and one medium-severity security fixes. Google says it will continue distributing updates over the coming days and weeks. The critical vulnerabilities include CVE-2026-110152, a buffer overflow in ANGLE, Chrome’s graphics translation layer. Zhenpeng “Leo” Lin at depthfirst reported the issue on September 30. Buffer overflows can corrupt memory when software writes beyond the space reserved for data, potentially creating opportunities for attackers to change program behavior. The remaining six critical entries are use-after-free flaws. CVE-2026-110149 affects Browser, CVE-2026-110136 affects PDF, CVE-2026-110161 affects Network, and CVE-2026-110165 affects Core. Multiple Google Chrome Vulnerabilities Google also patched CVE-2026-110148 in SVG and CVE-2026-110151 in Media. These findings involve Google researchers and Xinyang Ge. A use-after-free vulnerability occurs when software continues accessing memory after releasing it. Depending on the bug, attackers may influence that memory’s contents, causing crashes, corrupting data, or potentially running malicious code. However, the flaw category alone does not enable an attack against every affected component. Cybersecurity News previously covered Chrome’s update fixing 247 vulnerabilities , including four critical use-after-free issues. The latest release continues that focus on memory safety across multiple browser features rather than a single isolated component. Among the high-severity vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-110169 affects V8, Chrome’s JavaScript and WebAssembly engine. Rapid7’s vulnerability record states that a crafted HTML page could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code inside Chrome’s sandbox in versions before 155.0.8059.79. That limitation matters. Code execution inside the sandbox does not, by itself, prove an attacker can take control of the entire operating system. items.title: A Little More Logic in Splunk: Introducing SPL2’s if Command
items.summary: A quick use case for the new execution flow control feature If you have spent enough time writing SPL (10y here!), you have probably run into a familiar situation: you want to process events differently depending on what they contain. In a typical SPL pipeline, commands are executed sequentially, and filtering commands such as where and search can reduce the number of events passed to subsequent commands. Maybe you want to enrich events conditionally, or apply different transformations based on a field value. In classic SPL, you can often get the job done with eval, if(), case(). That works, but what if you want to control which block of code gets executed based on a field’s value, just as you would in a procedural programming language ? Enter SPL2’s if command. How does it work? The SPL2 if command was announced for Splunk Cloud Platform version 10.5.2605 on June 29, 2026, but I only became aware of it after seeing this LinkedIn post from Mikael Bjerkeland : SPL vs. SPL2: what actually changes? One important distinction: SPL already has an if() function . You do not need SPL2 to write conditional expressions. In classic SPL, you might use: | eval severity=if(status>=500, "high", "medium") The SPL above evaluates a condition and returns one of two values. For several conditions, you might use case()function. This is present in pretty much any modern piped language, including KQL . SPL2's if command works differently. Instead of using conditional logic only to calculate a value via eval, it lets you define different processing paths directly in your search. In other words: you can control which SPL2 statements or code blocks are executed based on a condition. It is a small feature, but one that can make certain searches more powerful. A real use case: to enrich or not to enrich? If you have ever worked with events containing network IP addresses, you probably know about the challenges of enriching them with geolocation. The problem becomes more significant in a large enterprise environment, where network traffic comes from all over the globe. In Splunk there's a command called iplocation which allows users to enrich the IP address value with its corresponding geolocation data (country, latitude, etc). This has become important enough that many vendors now include this enrichment in their logs. That's the case for Azure/Entra Sign In logs. The logs contain a field called location that holds a two-letter country code linked to the IP origin. However, for whatever reason, not every IP address gets enriched, as you can see below: 30-min worth of sign-in events sorted by most prevalent countries So, what's the solution here? Enrich it yourself, right? The issue is that if you decide to fill the gap (location = Unknown) with enriched data returning from the iplocation command, you need to do it for every single IP address, not only for the unknown ones. In SPL, that would look like this: In this case, iplocation is executed for every single IP value, no matter what! As you can imagine, looking up the geolocation of every IP address can become expensive, depending on the use case (hunting, reporting, etc.) and the event volume (or lookback period). The query may end up running much more slowly than necessary. The SPL2 solution With the if command, users can run iplocation only on events where the location field is empty (condition). Based on the example, the SPL2 code equivalent would look like this: SPL2 query leveraging the 'if' command to selectively use the 'iplocation' command A few notes here: This is a common demand, especially when pivoting to ASN hunting to reveal threat actor infrastructure from a specific location. The iplocation command doesn't produce a two-letter country code, but you can enrich or normalize the result later using public lists . If you leverage Data Engineering or Data Pipelines, it's worth enriching critical data sources such as Entra ID at ingestion time. Closing: is that a big deal? I haven’t had much time to explore this further, but I’m sure I’ll come across other use cases. For now, I wanted to share this with the community and hear what others think. That’s likely not the best example, but perhaps better than the one in the reference docs which can be easily done using SPL's eval… A few more interesting examples: Renaming a field based on a condition (doable with SPL’s {field}=value trick) Setting _time bin based on a field value To be transparent, I rarely use SPL2 , and I suspect many detection engineers and threat hunters are in the same boat. However, some of its features can be particularly useful in specific scenarios. There are pros and cons to using it that deserve a deeper discussion, so perhaps I’ll explore those in a future article. Don’t forget to subscribe and follow me to get notified about new stories! A Little More Logic in Splunk: Introducing SPL2’s if Command was originally published in Detect FYI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
items.summary_html:
A quick use case for the new execution flow control feature

If you have spent enough time writing SPL (10y here!), you have probably run into a familiar situation: you want to process events differently depending on what they contain.

In a typical SPL pipeline, commands are executed sequentially, and filtering commands such as where and search can reduce the number of events passed to subsequent commands.

Maybe you want to enrich events conditionally, or apply different transformations based on a field value. In classic SPL, you can often get the job done with eval, if(), case().

That works, but what if you want to control which block of code gets executed based on a field’s value, just as you would in a procedural programming language?

Enter SPL2’s if command.

How does it work?

The SPL2 if command was announced for Splunk Cloud Platform version 10.5.2605 on June 29, 2026, but I only became aware of it after seeing this LinkedIn post from Mikael Bjerkeland:

SPL vs. SPL2: what actually changes?

One important distinction: SPL already has an if() function. You do not need SPL2 to write conditional expressions.

In classic SPL, you might use:

| eval severity=if(status>=500, "high", "medium")

The SPL above evaluates a condition and returns one of two values. For several conditions, you might use case()function. This is present in pretty much any modern piped language, including KQL.

SPL2's if command works differently. Instead of using conditional logic only to calculate a value via eval, it lets you define different processing paths directly in your search.

In other words: you can control which SPL2 statements or code blocks are executed based on a condition.

It is a small feature, but one that can make certain searches more powerful.

A real use case: to enrich or not to enrich?

If you have ever worked with events containing network IP addresses, you probably know about the challenges of enriching them with geolocation.

The problem becomes more significant in a large enterprise environment, where network traffic comes from all over the globe.

In Splunk there's a command called iplocation which allows users to enrich the IP address value with its corresponding geolocation data (country, latitude, etc).

This has become important enough that many vendors now include this enrichment in their logs. That's the case for Azure/Entra Sign In logs.

The logs contain a field called location that holds a two-letter country code linked to the IP origin.

However, for whatever reason, not every IP address gets enriched, as you can see below:

30-min worth of sign-in events sorted by most prevalent countries

So, what's the solution here? Enrich it yourself, right?

The issue is that if you decide to fill the gap (location = Unknown) with enriched data returning from the iplocation command, you need to do it for every single IP address, not only for the unknown ones.

In SPL, that would look like this:

In this case, iplocation is executed for every single IP value, no matter what!

As you can imagine, looking up the geolocation of every IP address can become expensive, depending on the use case (hunting, reporting, etc.) and the event volume (or lookback period). The query may end up running much more slowly than necessary.

The SPL2 solution

With the if command, users can run iplocation only on events where the location field is empty (condition).

Based on the example, the SPL2 code equivalent would look like this:

SPL2 query leveraging the 'if' command to selectively use the 'iplocation' command

A few notes here:

  • This is a common demand, especially when pivoting to ASN hunting to reveal threat actor infrastructure from a specific location.
  • The iplocation command doesn't produce a two-letter country code, but you can enrich or normalize the result later using public lists.
  • If you leverage Data Engineering or Data Pipelines, it's worth enriching critical data sources such as Entra ID at ingestion time.
Closing: is that a big deal?

I haven’t had much time to explore this further, but I’m sure I’ll come across other use cases. For now, I wanted to share this with the community and hear what others think.

That’s likely not the best example, but perhaps better than the one in the reference docs which can be easily done using SPL's eval…

A few more interesting examples:

Renaming a field based on a condition (doable with SPL’s {field}=value trick)Setting _time bin based on a field value

To be transparent, I rarely use SPL2, and I suspect many detection engineers and threat hunters are in the same boat. However, some of its features can be particularly useful in specific scenarios.

There are pros and cons to using it that deserve a deeper discussion, so perhaps I’ll explore those in a future article.

Don’t forget to subscribe and follow me to get notified about new stories!

items.title: Critical Vulnerabilities Discovered in Google Chrome and Arm GPU Drivers
items.summary: Florian Schweitzer, Security Researcher at Certitude Consulting, has identified two serious vulnerabilities in products from Google and Arm that affect the same attack vector in the GPU software stack used by modern web browsers and mobile devices (CVE-2026-9034 and CVE-2026-93374). The issue can be triggered via JavaScript and could enable a sandbox escape. Such vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to compromise a user’s device after they visit a website. The discovery comes at a time of significant changes in vulnerability research, driven by the increasing use of artificial intelligence. The starting point for Schweitzer’s research was a deliberate decision not to compete with the enormous computing resources already being used to identify vulnerabilities in Chrome. “My strategy was simple: If you can’t compete with Google’s computing resources, you shouldn’t even try. I wanted to find attack surfaces that are difficult to integrate into a fuzzer or a fully automated AI workflow: real devices, stateful behavior, and boundaries between systems,” Schweitzer explained. Nevertheless, Schweitzer made extensive use of AI to generate WebGPU workloads, create automated test harnesses and device instrumentation, modify and compile Chromium, process crash data, and assist with reverse engineering the proprietary GPU driver. Rather than treating the model’s conclusions as definitive answers, he followed a process inspired by Austrian philosopher Karl Popper: formulating competing hypotheses, turning them into experiments, and attempting to falsify them as early and cost-effectively as possible. “The economics become interesting when the cost of failure decreases. If a hypothesis that would previously have taken several weeks to test can now be tested and discarded within a few hours, security researchers can conduct significantly more experiments. The competitive advantage increasingly lies in deciding which questions are worth asking, which evidence can be trusted, and which results warrant another hour of investigation,” said Marc Nimmerrichter, Managing Partner at Certitude Consulting. Critical Chrome Vulnerabilities Compared: 2025 and 2026 Certitude’s analysis of Google’s public Chrome Stable security releases shows that only four critical Chrome vulnerabilities were fixed in 2025. Three of these were reported by external security researchers, while one was attributed to Google. As of September 17, 2026, the same public data lists 179 critical vulnerabilities fixed in 2026: 145 attributed to Google and 34 to external researchers. External researchers have therefore already contributed more than ten times as many critical findings as in the previous year. At the same time, the number of critical findings attributed internally to Google has increased from one in 2025 to 145 in 2026. This shift coincides with Google’s rapid expansion of AI use in security research. In July, the Chrome Security Team described this as a “massive shift in the software security industry” and explained that large language models enable automated vulnerability discovery on a scale beyond traditional human research. Google states that it now uses AI throughout the entire vulnerability lifecycle, including vulnerability discovery, reproduction, triage, and remediation. The first vulnerability reported by Schweitzer, CVE-2026-9034, affects the Arm Mali GPU userspace driver. According to the public security advisory, an unprivileged process executing valid GPU operations “via WebGL or WebGPU” could access previously freed memory. The vulnerability affects several generations of Arm GPU drivers, including the 5th Gen GPU architecture, which provides graphics and compute capabilities for a wide range of consumer devices, including smartphones, tablets, TVs, and wearables. The second vulnerability, CVE-2026-93374, affects Google Chrome. Google classifies it as critical and describes it as a “use after free in Dawn,” Chromium’s implementation of WebGPU. The public CVE description identifies the issue as remotely exploitable via a crafted HTML page and as a potential sandbox escape: “Use after free in Dawn in Google Chrome on Android prior to 153.0.8010.52 allowed a remote attacker to potentially execute arbitrary code outside the sandbox via a crafted HTML page. (Chromium security severity: Critical)” Potential Sandbox Escape The Chrome sandbox is a key security boundary designed to restrict access to the underlying operating system by exposed browser components responsible for rendering websites. Vulnerabilities that can bypass this boundary are therefore particularly dangerous. Exploit code can be delivered via a link to a website. Google credits Florian Schweitzer with reporting the Chrome vulnerability on April 8, 2026. Arm also publicly names Schweitzer of Certitude Consulting as the discoverer of CVE-2026-9034. Detailed technical information is intentionally being withheld during the coordinated disclosure process to avoid providing information that could enable exploitation before affected systems are adequately protected. Further details will be published at an appropriate time. Public References Arm Security Advisory: CVE-2026-9034, September 8, 2026 https://support.arm.com/documentation/111552/1-0/?lang=en NIST NVD: CVE-2026-9034 https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2026-9034 Google Chrome Security Announcement: CVE-2026-93374, September 17, 2026 https://chromereleases.googleblog.com/2026/09/stable-channel-update-for-desktop_0194356994.html NIST NVD: CVE-2026-93374 https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2026-93374

items.title: Microsoft Windows Shell 0-Day Vulnerability Actively Exploited in Attacks
items.summary: Microsoft has patched an actively exploited Windows Shell zero-day vulnerability that allows attackers to bypass Mark of the Web protections. Tracked as CVE-2026-96951, the flaw was addressed in the October 2026 Patch Tuesday updates . It carries a CVSS score of 8.8 and is rated Important by Microsoft. The vulnerability was not publicly disclosed before the update, but Microsoft confirmed that exploitation had already occurred. Its “Exploitation Detected” assessment signals a confirmed attack rather than a possible future threat. Microsoft’s Exploitability Index advises customers to give applicable updates in this category the highest priority. Windows Shell 0-Day Exploited The flaw involves command injection, where Windows Shell fails to properly handle special elements used in a command. Microsoft describes the outcome as a security feature bypass available to an unauthorized attacker over a network. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to evade Mark of the Web defenses. Mark of the Web identifies files that come from the internet and helps Windows apply warnings or other protective checks. Bypassing this protection can remove an important barrier between a downloaded file and a user opening dangerous content. However, the reported impact is a security bypass, not a standalone remote code execution flaw. Attackers can deliver a specially crafted file through email or instant messaging and use social engineering to persuade the target to open it. Exploitation requires user action. This means the flaw should not be treated as a zero-click attack, despite its network-based delivery path. Earlier reporting on Windows LNK Stomping attacks described another way attackers bypassed Mark of the Web through Windows shortcuts. Separately, a WinZip Mark of the Web vulnerability showed how archive extraction could lose internet-origin tags. These are separate vulnerabilities, not confirmed techniques used in the current attacks. The supplied Microsoft advisory credits Riku Bamba and Yuya Chudo of Fujitsu Limited, Benoit Sevens using Claude with Anthropic, and researcher yhw. It does not identify the attackers, their targets, the malicious file format, or the scale of exploitation. Those missing details limit conclusions about the campaign and its reach. Security teams should prioritize applicable Windows updates and check Microsoft’s Security Update Guide for affected products. Testing and deploying the fix quickly is especially important because exploitation is confirmed. Users should remain cautious with unexpected attachments, since this attack depends on persuading someone to interact with attacker-controlled content. An EDR alert reveals an attack. The flaw involves command injection, where Windows Shell fails to properly handle special elements used in a command. Microsoft describes the outcome as a security feature bypass available to an unauthorized attacker over a network. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to evade Mark of the Web defenses.

Mark of the Web identifies files that come from the internet and helps Windows apply warnings or other protective checks. Bypassing this protection can remove an important barrier between a downloaded file and a user opening dangerous content. However, the reported impact is a security bypass, not a standalone remote code execution flaw.

These are separate vulnerabilities, not confirmed techniques used in the current attacks.

It does not identify the attackers, their targets, the malicious file format, or the scale of exploitation. Those missing details limit conclusions about the campaign and its reach.

items.title: OpenAI Engineer Arrested for Planting Spyware Device in an Executive Conference Room
items.summary: An OpenAI engineer has been arrested for allegedly hiding an audio recording device in an executive conference room at the company’s San Francisco offices. Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, was arrested on October 9, 2026, and appeared in federal court on October 13, according to the U.S. Department of Justice . Prosecutors charged him with using or attempting to use a device to intercept spoken communications. Although described as a spyware device in the headline, the hardware was a hidden audio recorder. The public announcement does not describe malware installed on OpenAI computers. OpenAI Engineer Arrested for Planting Spyware According to the complaint, OpenAI staff discovered the first device around September 30. It was plugged into a USB port behind a television, wrapped in toilet paper, and contained encrypted data. OpenAI determined that it had been installed around September 28. We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices. We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re… — OpenAI Newsroom (@OpenAINewsroom) October 13, 2026 The room hosted highly confidential discussions about research, product plans, business opportunities, government engagements, and technical progress. Prosecutors allege that Alfozan, who joined OpenAI in July 2025, had no authority to enter the room or attend those meetings. Office CCTV allegedly showed him near the room on several dates before the discovery. Footage from October 5 reportedly showed him entering the room and looking behind the television. Investigators also examined searches made through a productivity tool. Before September 28, Alfozan allegedly asked about building addresses, room calendars, meeting capacities, leadership locations, and meetings with outside partners. The complaint describes related prompts from a chatbot account associated with his spouse. Authorities said that account shared several identifiers and attributes with Alfozan’s account. Between September 24 and September 30, it requested help with continuous audio recording, Wi-Fi connectivity, live listening, remote access, concealment, and SD card encryption. Prompts submitted on September 27 and September 28 allegedly referenced the first recorder’s custom header and unique MAC address. These details form part of the evidence linking the account activity to the recovered hardware. However, requests about remote access do not establish that recordings were transmitted outside OpenAI. On October 5, security staff also found a similar recorder inside a bag Alfozan allegedly left unattended elsewhere in the office. The bag contained his wallet and identification. The case concerns alleged physical eavesdropping, not a confirmed network breach. The Justice Department announcement does not identify a foreign recipient or establish that confidential recordings reached another party. Separately, Cybersecurity News has covered OpenAI’s response to AI reasoning extraction and researchers reaching internal repositories through a forum security flaw . Those reports concern different security paths and are not evidence of a connection to this case. The FBI is investigating. Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Parker is prosecuting, with support from National Security Division attorney Kate Tagert. According to the Northern District of California announcement , Alfozan faces up to five years in prison, a $250,000 fine, and three years of supervised release if convicted. The complaint describes related prompts from a chatbot account associated with his spouse. Authorities said that account shared several identifiers and attributes with Alfozan’s account. items.title: Podman Desktop 1.30 Release
items.summary: Podman Desktop 1.30 Release Podman Desktop 1.30 is now available. Click here to download it ! This release includes new features, bug fixes, and continues the Svelte 5 migration: Bulk container stop : Select multiple running containers and stop them in one click. Warning-level preflight checks : Preflight checks on Windows can now warn instead of block. No more console flashes on Windows : Machine autostart no longer pops up a Command Prompt window. Docker contexts as connections : Each Docker context is now surfaced as its own container connection. Extension API additions : Searchable routes in the command palette and display names for configuration properties. Release details ​ Bulk container stop ​ You can now select multiple containers from the list and stop them all with a single action. Warning severity for preflight checks ​ Preflight checks during onboarding previously only had two outcomes: pass or fail. The API now supports a warning severity. A check can flag a potential issue with a ⚠️ icon without blocking the setup. On Windows, a new BIOS virtualization firmware check uses this: if hardware virtualization is not enabled in the BIOS and no hypervisor is present, the check reports a warning instead of a hard failure, so you can still proceed with the Podman installation. No more console window flashes on Windows ​ On Windows, autostarting a Podman machine at launch no longer causes a Command Prompt window to briefly flash on screen ( #19318 ). Docker contexts as container connections ​ If you work with Docker alongside Podman, Podman Desktop now registers a separate container connection for each configured Docker context. Whether you have a local daemon, a remote host, or multiple Docker Desktop contexts, they all appear individually on the dashboard without manual switching. Extension API improvements ​ Two additions for extension authors: Searchable routes in the command palette : Extensions can now pass a searchEntry option to navigation.register() to make their pages discoverable from the command palette ( #18550 ). Configuration display names : Extension manifests can now declare a displayName on configuration properties. When present, the Settings UI shows this label instead of the raw property key ( #19186 , #19203 ). Other improvements ​ Keyboard shortcut validation utils : New keyboard utilities for validating keyboard shortcuts ( #19314 ). CI telemetry detection : Telemetry is now automatically disabled when a CI environment is detected ( #19266 ). FileInput disabled state and error display : The FileInput component can now be disabled and display validation errors ( #19300 ). Table row onClick API : The Table component now supports an onClick handler on rows ( #18893 ). ButtonRow component : A new ButtonRow UI component standardizes button layout in dialogs and forms ( #18724 ). Button aria-pressed toggle support : Buttons can now expose a pressed prop for accessible toggle behavior ( #18591 ). Themed image support in Icon : The Icon component now supports themed images that adapt to light/dark modes ( #18558 ). Cancel long press on pointer movement : Long press gestures are now properly cancelled when the pointer moves away ( #18569 ). Expandable settings navigation sections : Settings navigation now supports expandable sections with children for better organization ( #19125 ). Navigation item pinning (backend) : The backend now supports pinning navigation items to the top of the sidebar ( #18464 ). Network menu context contributions : Extensions can now contribute menu actions to the network context menu ( #18601 ). Declarative env:/file: configuration defaults : Configuration properties now support env: and file: prefixes for dynamic default values ( #18797 ). Infra container detection : Podman Desktop now detects and labels infrastructure containers ( #18892 ). Startup update dialog improvements : The dismiss buttons in the startup update dialog are now grouped under a "Later" dropdown ( #19194 ). Managed configuration for provider updates : A new managed configuration controls whether provider update notifications are shown ( #17878 ). 5M downloads banner on website : A celebratory banner marks the 5 million downloads milestone ( #18533 ). Svelte 5 migration : Over 100 renderer components migrated to Svelte 5 runes by @gastoner and @0xKalasi , covering Preferences, Extensions, Containers, Volumes, Compose, Kubernetes resources, PVCs, and Icons. Replaced got with native fetch in image-registry ( #18523 ). Removed win-ca dependency ( #18187 ). Extracted DockerDaemonMonitor from the Docker extension ( #18524 ). Switched ESLint from parserOptions.project to projectService ( #19265 ). Bundled express instead of externalizing it in Vite ( #19239 ). Used discriminated unions in getMatchingConnectionFromProvider ( #14840 ). Bumped Podman v5 to 5.8.9 and Podman v6 to 6.1.4, addressing CVE-2026-94603 (checkpoint image sandboxing bypass). Notable bug fixes ​ Windows console flash : Background process spawning on Windows no longer flashes a console window ( #19318 ). High-contrast navbar focus : The focus outline on selected navbar items is now visible in high-contrast themes ( #19323 ). Rosetta configuration : The Podman extension now always writes an explicit Rosetta value in containers.conf , preventing silent misconfigurations ( #19238 ). Remote Podman connections : Connections that have no Identity field are now registered correctly ( #19147 ). Zstd decompression bombs : Streaming zstd layer decompression now rejects decompression bombs ( #19166 ). Atomic configuration writes : Storage and configuration files now use atomic writes and serialization, preventing corruption on concurrent access ( #19071 ). UTF-8 log streaming : Multi-byte UTF-8 characters split across stream chunks are now preserved correctly in container logs ( #17994 ). WSL error surfacing : WSL errors are now surfaced directly instead of showing misleading notifications ( #17936 ). Accurate memory usage : The dashboard now uses memAvailable for accurate Podman memory usage reporting ( #18418 ). Container command display : The full container command is now shown, not only its first argument ( #18561 ). Typeahead cleanup : The Typeahead input delay timeout is now properly cleared on component destruction ( #19223 ). Slider styling : The preferences slider track now shows a proper two-tone fill gradient ( #19158 ). Network name ordering : Network views now show the network name before the ID ( #18917 ). Lima empty configuration values : Empty Lima configuration values are now treated as unset ( #18639 ). Registry path spaces : Spaces in registry configuration paths are now supported on Podman ( #18542 ). Hyper-V cleanup during migration : Hyper-V VMs are now cleaned up during migration data reset ( #18791 ). Welcome page overlay : The resize handle no longer appears above the welcome overlay ( #18998 ). Long error messages : Long unbreakable error messages now wrap correctly in the UI ( #19301 ). Tooltip after menu close : Tooltips no longer reappear after a menu closes ( #18864 ). Dashboard socket liveness on Linux : The Podman tile on the dashboard now correctly updates socket liveness on Linux ( #18580 ). Toggle Timestamps accessibility : The Toggle Timestamps button in container logs now has proper accessibility attributes ( #18627 ). Sentence case for tab labels : Tab labels now use consistent sentence case ( #18885 ). App navigation resize glitch : The sidebar navigation no longer glitches when resizing ( #18593 ). Task Manager deep-linking : Clicking "see more" on a failed connection lifecycle task now navigates to the actual connection page instead of the generic Resources list ( #19345 ). Experimental feature feedback dialog : The dialog was never shown at startup because it fired before the renderer was ready. It now waits for extensions to finish loading ( #18562 ). Flatpak StartupWMClass mismatch : The StartupWMClass in the Flatpak desktop entry now matches the actual Electron window class, fixing broken task manager icon linking on KDE Plasma/Wayland ( #19403 ). Extension README loading : Extension READMEs are now fetched from the main process instead of the renderer, fixing CSP errors that prevented README display for uninstalled extensions ( #19472 ). JS exception pop-ups on quit : Closing the main window no longer triggers JavaScript exception pop-ups from streams trying to send events to the destroyed window ( #19328 ). Webview file server directory boundary : The webview file server now enforces proper directory boundaries using path.relative , preventing path traversal to sibling extension directories ( #19613 ). Known issues ​ WSL v3.0.1 breaks podman run : Windows users who have updated to WSL v3.0.1 may see a crun: controller 'pids' is not available error when running containers. This is an upstream Podman issue . As a workaround, you can either pass --cgroups=disabled to podman run , or add cgroup_manager="cgroupfs" under [engine] in your containers.conf file. Community thank you ​ Thank you to everyone who contributed to this release: atirna in feat(ui): add ButtonRow component cblecker in refactor(main): extract macOS login minimize preference helper DevShiba in feat(extensions): support menu context contribution for networks GauravR31 in fix: prevent creation of extension file watcher on non-existent folder hamedrabah in fix(renderer): show network name before ID hugosmoreira in feat(preferences): render explicit configuration display names jmdlrg in feat(ui): add pressed prop to Button for aria-pressed toggle support joaogabriel15 in feat(renderer): add bulk stop action for containers luoy16002-svg in fix(podman): support spaces in registry configuration paths manrods in refactor: remove temp-file-service IPC maskjelly in feat(renderer): let FileInput be disabled and show an error MFA-G in fix(logs): preserve multi-byte UTF-8 characters split across stream chunks Mohammed-Thaha in fix(renderer): improve Toggle Timestamps button accessibility MsfPablo in fix(Images): match Load/Import/Save modal icons to toolbar pacocartones in fix(lima): treat empty configuration values as unset RealJasonHu in fix(renderer): keep resize handle below welcome overlay sAchin-680 in feat(telemetry): disable telemetry when a CI environment is detected SlothLady in feat: Add Tap & Go to ADOPTERS.md SoniaSandler in fix(extensions): load extensions README from main turkeryildirim in fix(flatpak): correct StartupWMClass to match window class Community meeting ​ If you would like to discuss any of the new features, issues or other topics, please join us at the monthly community meeting that takes place every 4th Thursday of the month . Here are the meeting details . Final notes ​ The complete list of issues fixed in this release is available here . Get the latest release from the Downloads section of the website. Visit the GitHub repository to report issues or contribute.
