Podman Desktop 1.30 Release

Podman Desktop 1.30 is now available. Click here to download it!

This release includes new features, bug fixes, and continues the Svelte 5 migration:

  • Bulk container stop: Select multiple running containers and stop them in one click.
  • Warning-level preflight checks: Preflight checks on Windows can now warn instead of block.
  • No more console flashes on Windows: Machine autostart no longer pops up a Command Prompt window.
  • Docker contexts as connections: Each Docker context is now surfaced as its own container connection.
  • Extension API additions: Searchable routes in the command palette and display names for configuration properties.
Release details​ Bulk container stop​

You can now select multiple containers from the list and stop them all with a single action.

Warning severity for preflight checks​

Preflight checks during onboarding previously only had two outcomes: pass or fail. The API now supports a warning severity. A check can flag a potential issue with a ⚠️ icon without blocking the setup.

On Windows, a new BIOS virtualization firmware check uses this: if hardware virtualization is not enabled in the BIOS and no hypervisor is present, the check reports a warning instead of a hard failure, so you can still proceed with the Podman installation.

No more console window flashes on Windows​

On Windows, autostarting a Podman machine at launch no longer causes a Command Prompt window to briefly flash on screen (#19318).

Docker contexts as container connections​

If you work with Docker alongside Podman, Podman Desktop now registers a separate container connection for each configured Docker context. Whether you have a local daemon, a remote host, or multiple Docker Desktop contexts, they all appear individually on the dashboard without manual switching.

Extension API improvements​

Two additions for extension authors:

  • Searchable routes in the command palette: Extensions can now pass a searchEntry option to navigation.register() to make their pages discoverable from the command palette (#18550).
  • Configuration display names: Extension manifests can now declare a displayName on configuration properties. When present, the Settings UI shows this label instead of the raw property key (#19186, #19203).
Other improvements​
  • Keyboard shortcut validation utils: New keyboard utilities for validating keyboard shortcuts (#19314).
  • CI telemetry detection: Telemetry is now automatically disabled when a CI environment is detected (#19266).
  • FileInput disabled state and error display: The FileInput component can now be disabled and display validation errors (#19300).
  • Table row onClick API: The Table component now supports an onClick handler on rows (#18893).
  • ButtonRow component: A new ButtonRow UI component standardizes button layout in dialogs and forms (#18724).
  • Button aria-pressed toggle support: Buttons can now expose a pressed prop for accessible toggle behavior (#18591).
  • Themed image support in Icon: The Icon component now supports themed images that adapt to light/dark modes (#18558).
  • Cancel long press on pointer movement: Long press gestures are now properly cancelled when the pointer moves away (#18569).
  • Expandable settings navigation sections: Settings navigation now supports expandable sections with children for better organization (#19125).
  • Navigation item pinning (backend): The backend now supports pinning navigation items to the top of the sidebar (#18464).
  • Network menu context contributions: Extensions can now contribute menu actions to the network context menu (#18601).
  • Declarative env:/file: configuration defaults: Configuration properties now support env: and file: prefixes for dynamic default values (#18797).
  • Infra container detection: Podman Desktop now detects and labels infrastructure containers (#18892).
  • Startup update dialog improvements: The dismiss buttons in the startup update dialog are now grouped under a "Later" dropdown (#19194).
  • Managed configuration for provider updates: A new managed configuration controls whether provider update notifications are shown (#17878).
  • 5M downloads banner on website: A celebratory banner marks the 5 million downloads milestone (#18533).
  • Svelte 5 migration: Over 100 renderer components migrated to Svelte 5 runes by @gastoner and @0xKalasi, covering Preferences, Extensions, Containers, Volumes, Compose, Kubernetes resources, PVCs, and Icons.
  • Replaced got with native fetch in image-registry (#18523).
  • Removed win-ca dependency (#18187).
  • Extracted DockerDaemonMonitor from the Docker extension (#18524).
  • Switched ESLint from parserOptions.project to projectService (#19265).
  • Bundled express instead of externalizing it in Vite (#19239).
  • Used discriminated unions in getMatchingConnectionFromProvider (#14840).
  • Bumped Podman v5 to 5.8.9 and Podman v6 to 6.1.4, addressing CVE-2026-94603 (checkpoint image sandboxing bypass).
Notable bug fixes​
  • Windows console flash: Background process spawning on Windows no longer flashes a console window (#19318).
  • High-contrast navbar focus: The focus outline on selected navbar items is now visible in high-contrast themes (#19323).
  • Rosetta configuration: The Podman extension now always writes an explicit Rosetta value in containers.conf, preventing silent misconfigurations (#19238).
  • Remote Podman connections: Connections that have no Identity field are now registered correctly (#19147).
  • Zstd decompression bombs: Streaming zstd layer decompression now rejects decompression bombs (#19166).
  • Atomic configuration writes: Storage and configuration files now use atomic writes and serialization, preventing corruption on concurrent access (#19071).
  • UTF-8 log streaming: Multi-byte UTF-8 characters split across stream chunks are now preserved correctly in container logs (#17994).
  • WSL error surfacing: WSL errors are now surfaced directly instead of showing misleading notifications (#17936).
  • Accurate memory usage: The dashboard now uses memAvailable for accurate Podman memory usage reporting (#18418).
  • Container command display: The full container command is now shown, not only its first argument (#18561).
  • Typeahead cleanup: The Typeahead input delay timeout is now properly cleared on component destruction (#19223).
  • Slider styling: The preferences slider track now shows a proper two-tone fill gradient (#19158).
  • Network name ordering: Network views now show the network name before the ID (#18917).
  • Lima empty configuration values: Empty Lima configuration values are now treated as unset (#18639).
  • Registry path spaces: Spaces in registry configuration paths are now supported on Podman (#18542).
  • Hyper-V cleanup during migration: Hyper-V VMs are now cleaned up during migration data reset (#18791).
  • Welcome page overlay: The resize handle no longer appears above the welcome overlay (#18998).
  • Long error messages: Long unbreakable error messages now wrap correctly in the UI (#19301).
  • Tooltip after menu close: Tooltips no longer reappear after a menu closes (#18864).
  • Dashboard socket liveness on Linux: The Podman tile on the dashboard now correctly updates socket liveness on Linux (#18580).
  • Toggle Timestamps accessibility: The Toggle Timestamps button in container logs now has proper accessibility attributes (#18627).
  • Sentence case for tab labels: Tab labels now use consistent sentence case (#18885).
  • App navigation resize glitch: The sidebar navigation no longer glitches when resizing (#18593).
  • Task Manager deep-linking: Clicking "see more" on a failed connection lifecycle task now navigates to the actual connection page instead of the generic Resources list (#19345).
  • Experimental feature feedback dialog: The dialog was never shown at startup because it fired before the renderer was ready. It now waits for extensions to finish loading (#18562).
  • Flatpak StartupWMClass mismatch: The StartupWMClass in the Flatpak desktop entry now matches the actual Electron window class, fixing broken task manager icon linking on KDE Plasma/Wayland (#19403).
  • Extension README loading: Extension READMEs are now fetched from the main process instead of the renderer, fixing CSP errors that prevented README display for uninstalled extensions (#19472).
  • JS exception pop-ups on quit: Closing the main window no longer triggers JavaScript exception pop-ups from streams trying to send events to the destroyed window (#19328).
  • Webview file server directory boundary: The webview file server now enforces proper directory boundaries using path.relative, preventing path traversal to sibling extension directories (#19613).
Known issues​
  • WSL v3.0.1 breaks podman run: Windows users who have updated to WSL v3.0.1 may see a crun: controller 'pids' is not available error when running containers. This is an upstream Podman issue. As a workaround, you can either pass --cgroups=disabled to podman run, or add cgroup_manager="cgroupfs" under [engine] in your containers.conf file.
Community thank you​

Thank you to everyone who contributed to this release:

  • atirna in feat(ui): add ButtonRow component
  • cblecker in refactor(main): extract macOS login minimize preference helper
  • DevShiba in feat(extensions): support menu context contribution for networks
  • GauravR31 in fix: prevent creation of extension file watcher on non-existent folder
  • hamedrabah in fix(renderer): show network name before ID
  • hugosmoreira in feat(preferences): render explicit configuration display names
  • jmdlrg in feat(ui): add pressed prop to Button for aria-pressed toggle support

items.title: How attackers maintained persistence in AWS after stealing credentials
items.summary: In the cloud, attackers don’t need to break in. They just need a working set of keys. Several AWS customers learned this the hard way when threat actors used compromised IAM credentials to deploy a rapid cryptomining campaign across EC2 and ECS environments. The incident didn’t rely on vulnerabilities or sophisticated exploitation; it simply relied on valid credentials and overly permissive access. Below is a clear breakdown of what happened, what matters, and how organizations can strengthen their defenses using a Zero Standing Privilege (ZSP) approach. What happened during the AWS cyberattack When an attack of this scale occurs, it’s important to understand how attackers gained access and what they did with it. How the attackers gained initial access According to reporting from Dark Reading , as well as AWS’s own analysis, attackers used stolen IAM credentials to authenticate into customer environments and immediately begin provisioning cryptomining workloads. The campaign was active across multiple AWS customers, who were directly notified. AWS also confirmed this was not the result of a flaw in its infrastructure. The privileges attached to the compromised identity permitted every action the attackers took. Once inside, the attackers: Targeted EC2 and ECS resources to spin up mining infrastructure Used automation to deploy workloads within about 10 minutes of initial access Leveraged AWS APIs to create new roles, extending their control Enabled persistence by modifying instance attributes to make resources harder to terminate This combination of legitimate access and rapid provisioning made the campaign highly effective and very difficult to stop in its early stages. For full details, you can read the AWS security blog here . How the attackers stayed in control After gaining access, the attackers created two new IAM roles using the victim’s own permissions to achieve their goals and persistence: A service-linked role for Auto Scaling groups A Lambda execution role, with AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole attached These roles gave them flexibility to deploy and manage resources in ways that blended into normal cloud operations. They also set DisableApiTermination=true on EC2 instances, which forces defenders to manually re-enable termination before cleanup. This slows incident responders and disrupts automated remediation workflows. On top of that, the attackers attempted to launch as many EC2 instances and ECS tasks as each victim’s quota allowed. It’s a simple technique: push the environment to its compute limits, maximize mining output, and generate profit before alarms start ringing. Compromised credentials are still the easiest way in This attack chain is not surprising to anyone working in cloud security. In many environments: IAM permissions are broad Long-lived access keys still exist Role creation is not guarded AI agents and NHIs inherit long-standing privileged credentials There is little friction between authentication and high-impact actions When a compromised identity can create new roles, deploy compute resources, and modify protection settings without additional checks, attackers don’t need zero-days. They just need opportunity. This is exactly the kind of scenario where a Zero Standing Privileges strategy provides real value. Why Zero Standing Privileges are the key to preventing credential attack Zero Standing Privileges (ZSP) reduces the risk of credential misuse by ensuring that no human or non-human identity keeps permanent access to sensitive or high-impact permissions. How ZSP removes the risk of long-lived access If the credentials in the AWS incident had been tied to temporary, tightly scoped permissions instead of broad, standing access to create roles and launch resources, the attackers’ options would have been dramatically limited. Since the AWS attack, however, the risks of standing access have only increased as AI agents become more common. Agents, and the non-human identities (NHIs) they use to interface with systems, are often provisioned with broad, long-lived access to enable them to perform tasks across various systems. All of this creates more unmanaged risk from standing access. In fact, 1Password research found that 73% of technical workers report visibility gaps in which AI agents use credentials at their company, and 86% of respondents reported credential-related issues with NHIs. To manage the risks that led to the AWS breach, teams need to implement ZSP with agentic and NHI access risks in mind. ZSP manages the risk of standing access by ensuring that: Access is Just-in-Time Privileges are scoped to the exact task Access expires automatically Sensitive roles require additional validation or approval How 1Password Privileged Access helps implement ZSP in AWS ZSP is a powerful strategy, but difficult to enforce manually. 1Password Privileged Access automates the operational layer, making least privilege practical for real engineering teams. Just-in-time access flows 1Password Privileged Access ensures that scoped access to cloud environments, K8s, databases, or SaaS platforms is provisioned on request and removed when the session ends. This means a compromised identity cannot silently elevate itself, create roles, or deploy infrastructure without triggering controls. Dynamic Guardrails Instead of relying on static IAM roles, which age poorly and are always available for abuse, 1Password Privileged Access creates Dynamic Guardrails that factor in who's requesting access, what they need, and the risk of that action. Policies adapt as your environment scales. This accomplishes two important outcomes: Attackers cannot rely on pre-existing roles to escalate Admin teams no longer need to pre-build and maintain dozens of role variations Continuous monitoring and anomaly detection Within 1Password Privileged Access, every request, approval, and access event gets logged automatically. AI-generated session summaries give auditors and compliance teams instant answers. Moreover, Autonomous Anomaly Detection would have flagged activity such as: High-risk access requests, approvals of previously rejected requests, and sudden requests from inactive users Repetitive or suspicious automated actions, to ensure that automation doesn’t become a security vulnerability AI agent controls When agents require access to perform a task, 1Password Privileged Access gives each agent a distinct identity and a role scoped for its specific task. It also validates declared intent against actual actions in real time so that if an agent deviates from its stated purpose, access is restricted or revoked before the action executes. Regardless, access is deprovisioned when the task is complete, meaning agents can take on work without the access surface expanding alongside them. All of this reduces the blast radius of compromised credentials and limits how much damage attackers can do before they’re stopped. Taking the next step toward smarter access controls The AWS incident is a reminder of a simple truth: identity is the primary attack surface in cloud environments. Compromised credentials, combined with broad standing privileges, give attackers everything they need to operate inside your infrastructure. A Zero Standing Privilege approach minimizes this risk by ensuring access is temporary, scoped, and closely governed. 1Password Privileged Access provides the automation needed to make that practical in real-world environments. items.summary_html:
In the cloud, attackers don’t need to break in. They just need a working set of keys.

Several AWS customers learned this the hard way when threat actors used compromised IAM credentials to deploy a rapid cryptomining campaign across EC2 and ECS environments. The incident didn’t rely on vulnerabilities or sophisticated exploitation; it simply relied on valid credentials and overly permissive access.

Below is a clear breakdown of what happened, what matters, and how organizations can strengthen their defenses using a Zero Standing Privilege (ZSP) approach.

What happened during the AWS cyberattack

When an attack of this scale occurs, it’s important to understand how attackers gained access and what they did with it.

How the attackers gained initial access

According to reporting from Dark Reading, as well as AWS’s own analysis, attackers used stolen IAM credentials to authenticate into customer environments and immediately begin provisioning cryptomining workloads. The campaign was active across multiple AWS customers, who were directly notified.

AWS also confirmed this was not the result of a flaw in its infrastructure. The privileges attached to the compromised identity permitted every action the attackers took.

Once inside, the attackers:

  • Targeted EC2 and ECS resources to spin up mining infrastructure

  • Used automation to deploy workloads within about 10 minutes of initial access

  • Leveraged AWS APIs to create new roles, extending their control

  • Enabled persistence by modifying instance attributes to make resources harder to terminate

This combination of legitimate access and rapid provisioning made the campaign highly effective and very difficult to stop in its early stages.

For full details, you can read the AWS security blog here.

How the attackers stayed in control

After gaining access, the attackers created two new IAM roles using the victim’s own permissions to achieve their goals and persistence:

  1. A service-linked role for Auto Scaling groups

  2. A Lambda execution role, with AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole attached

These roles gave them flexibility to deploy and manage resources in ways that blended into normal cloud operations.

They also set DisableApiTermination=true on EC2 instances, which forces defenders to manually re-enable termination before cleanup. This slows incident responders and disrupts automated remediation workflows.

On top of that, the attackers attempted to launch as many EC2 instances and ECS tasks as each victim’s quota allowed. It’s a simple technique: push the environment to its compute limits, maximize mining output, and generate profit before alarms start ringing.

Compromised credentials are still the easiest way in

This attack chain is not surprising to anyone working in cloud security. In many environments:

  • IAM permissions are broad

  • Long-lived access keys still exist

  • Role creation is not guarded

  • AI agents and NHIs inherit long-standing privileged credentials

  • There is little friction between authentication and high-impact actions

When a compromised identity can create new roles, deploy compute resources, and modify protection settings without additional checks, attackers don’t need zero-days. They just need opportunity.

This is exactly the kind of scenario where a Zero Standing Privileges strategy provides real value.

Why Zero Standing Privileges are the key to preventing credential attack

Zero Standing Privileges (ZSP) reduces the risk of credential misuse by ensuring that no human or non-human identity keeps permanent access to sensitive or high-impact permissions.

How ZSP removes the risk of long-lived access

If the credentials in the AWS incident had been tied to temporary, tightly scoped permissions instead of broad, standing access to create roles and launch resources, the attackers’ options would have been dramatically limited.

Since the AWS attack, however, the risks of standing access have only increased as AI agents become more common.

Agents, and the non-human identities (NHIs) they use to interface with systems, are often provisioned with broad, long-lived access to enable them to perform tasks across various systems. All of this creates more unmanaged risk from standing access. In fact, 1Password research found that 73% of technical workers report visibility gaps in which AI agents use credentials at their company, and 86% of respondents reported credential-related issues with NHIs. To manage the risks that led to the AWS breach, teams need to implement ZSP with agentic and NHI access risks in mind.

ZSP manages the risk of standing access by ensuring that:

  • Access is Just-in-Time

  • Privileges are scoped to the exact task

  • Access expires automatically

  • Sensitive roles require additional validation or approval

How 1Password Privileged Access helps implement ZSP in AWS

ZSP is a powerful strategy, but difficult to enforce manually. 1Password Privileged Access automates the operational layer, making least privilege practical for real engineering teams.

Just-in-time access flows

1Password Privileged Access ensures that scoped access to cloud environments, K8s, databases, or SaaS platforms is provisioned on request and removed when the session ends.

This means a compromised identity cannot silently elevate itself, create roles, or deploy infrastructure without triggering controls.

Dynamic Guardrails

Instead of relying on static IAM roles, which age poorly and are always available for abuse, 1Password Privileged Access creates Dynamic Guardrails that factor in who's requesting access, what they need, and the risk of that action. Policies adapt as your environment scales.

This accomplishes two important outcomes:

  • Attackers cannot rely on pre-existing roles to escalate

  • Admin teams no longer need to pre-build and maintain dozens of role variations

Continuous monitoring and anomaly detection

Within 1Password Privileged Access, every request, approval, and access event gets logged automatically. AI-generated session summaries give auditors and compliance teams instant answers.

Moreover, Autonomous Anomaly Detection would have flagged activity such as:

  • High-risk access requests, approvals of previously rejected requests, and sudden requests from inactive users

  • Repetitive or suspicious automated actions, to ensure that automation doesn’t become a security vulnerability

AI agent controls

When agents require access to perform a task, 1Password Privileged Access gives each agent a distinct identity and a role scoped for its specific task. It also validates declared intent against actual actions in real time so that if an agent deviates from its stated purpose, access is restricted or revoked before the action executes.

Regardless, access is deprovisioned when the task is complete, meaning agents can take on work without the access surface expanding alongside them.

All of this reduces the blast radius of compromised credentials and limits how much damage attackers can do before they’re stopped.

Taking the next step toward smarter access controls

The AWS incident is a reminder of a simple truth: identity is the primary attack surface in cloud environments. Compromised credentials, combined with broad standing privileges, give attackers everything they need to operate inside your infrastructure.

A Zero Standing Privilege approach minimizes this risk by ensuring access is temporary, scoped, and closely governed. 1Password Privileged Access provides the automation needed to make that practical in real-world environments.

items.title: Better HTTP/1 connection reuse
items.summary: The Go Blog Better HTTP/1 connection reuse Nicholas Husin and Damien Neil 14 October 2026 Take a look at the following function: func getStatus(url string) (int, error) { resp, err := http.Get(url) if err != nil { return 0, err } defer resp.Body.Close() return resp.StatusCode, nil } It sends a GET request to url and returns the HTTP status code. Using HTTP/1 ( GODEBUG=http2client=0 ), calling this function 100 times against index.golang.org takes ~710 milliseconds on Go 1.26 on my machine. On Go 1.27, the same program takes ~150 milliseconds. That is almost 5 times faster! How is such a drastic performance difference possible? The cost of establishing HTTP connections To understand the difference, consider what happens on the network when we make an HTTP request. Go’s net/http package supports HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1, and HTTP/2. All three run over TCP, and usually over TLS when talking to HTTPS endpoints. Making a request over a new connection looks something like this: TCP handshake (1 RTT) : the client sends a SYN packet, the server replies with SYN-ACK , and the client replies with ACK . Because the client can send the first TLS message alongside that final ACK , establishing the TCP connection takes 1 round-trip time (RTT). TLS handshake (2 RTT) : next, a TLS handshake exchanges encryption keys and verifies the server’s identity; using TLS 1.2, this takes 2 RTT. HTTP request : with the keys exchanged, HTTP requests can finally be sent after a total of 3 RTT. These round trips (plus some CPU time spent on TLS handshakes) add up quickly. In cross-region communications, one-way latencies often reach or exceed the 50 ms (100 ms RTT) shown in the diagram above. Compared to the 300 ms spent just setting up the connection, the HTTP request itself can be cheap to serve, taking only a little over 1 RTT when bandwidth is plentiful or the HTTP response is small. Even in more favorable conditions, opening a new connection can still be expensive. Our opening benchmark queries index.golang.org , which is distributed worldwide and supports TLS 1.3. This means that latency is relatively low, and the TLS handshake can actually finish in just 1 RTT. Even so, the performance difference is still very noticeable. Connection reuse To avoid paying this setup cost on every request, HTTP clients and servers try to reuse existing connections across multiple requests when possible. The mechanics of this differ based on the HTTP version: HTTP/1.0 : while not part of the official specification, clients and servers often opt into connection reuse by sending a Connection: keep-alive header. Reuse continues until either endpoint omits the header or sends a Connection: close header. HTTP/1.1 : connections are persistent by default, and can be reused for subsequent requests and responses unless either side declares otherwise by sending a Connection: close header. HTTP/2 : multiple requests and responses can be multiplexed over a single TCP connection. When connection reuse fails In HTTP/1 (both HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1), multiple requests and responses on the same connection are sent sequentially on the wire. If two GET requests are sent to index.golang.org over the same TCP connection, the responses arrive as a single stream of bytes: As shown in the diagram, net/http.Get reads and parses the status line and headers from the byte stream to populate net/http.Response , then returns immediately. The response body remains unread on the connection and is consumed only as the caller reads from net/http.Response.Body . Because responses are sent back-to-back on the same stream, net/http can only find the start of the next response after the current response body has been read to the very end (as determined by the Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding header). Now look back at our example program, where we never read resp.Body : func getStatus(url string) (int, error) { resp, err := http.Get(url) if err != nil { return 0, err } defer resp.Body.Close() return resp.StatusCode, nil } Through Go 1.26, when resp.Body.Close is called, net/http sees that there is still an unread response body. Realizing that it cannot reuse the connection, it abandons the existing connection and creates new connections for its next requests, causing it to repeatedly incur the cost of establishing new connections. (HTTP/2 does not have this problem. Because it multiplexes streams of frames over a single connection rather than sending responses strictly back-to-back, an unread response body on one stream does not block other requests from sharing the connection.) Where failed connection reuse hurts This subtlety of HTTP/1 connection reuse can cause silent performance degradation in seemingly innocuous code. As in our opening example, a client might only care about an API response’s status code. However, the API endpoint it is talking to might send bodies that provide more detailed but ultimately unused information, such as {"success": true, "message": "update processed"} . This will unfortunately cause connection reuse to fail. Even programs that do read the response body can run into this issue if they stop just short of the end of the body. For example, encoding/json.Decoder stops reading as soon as it sees the closing } of a JSON object. If a server sends a JSON response terminated with a newline, decoding the JSON object will leave the newline still unread. The connection cannot be reused for a new request until that newline is consumed. Thus, a healthy connection might end up being abandoned, even though it was only a single byte away from being reusable. The manual solution The unread body problem has been a long-standing sharp edge. Over the years, many Go developers came up with their own workarounds. Most commonly, this is done by draining the response body prior to closing it: func getStatus(url string) (int, error) { resp, err := http.Get(url) if err != nil { return 0, err } drainAndCloseBody(resp.Body) return resp.StatusCode, nil } func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) { io.Copy(io.Discard, body) // Drain the response body before closing it. body.Close() } While this works for small responses, if the unread body is large, establishing a new TCP connection can be faster than downloading and discarding the rest of the body. A better approach is to cap the number of bytes we are willing to drain: func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) { io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB. body.Close() } However, a server might send a response body that trickles in slowly, so we also need to cap the time we spend draining: func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) { drainDone := make(chan struct{}, 1) go func() { io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB. drainDone <- struct{}{} }() // Only spend at most 50 ms trying to drain the response body. select { case <-drainDone: case <-time.After(50 * time.Millisecond): // If we reach the 50 ms timeout, body.Close will run and interrupt the // io.CopyN, preventing goroutine leaks. } body.Close() } Of course, we also do not want to block for up to 50 milliseconds when closing a response body. Instead, we can drain the body asynchronously in the background and let it race against subsequent requests: func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) { drainDone := make(chan struct{}, 1) go func() { io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB. drainDone <- struct{}{} }() go func() { // Only spend at most 50 ms trying to drain the response body. select { case <-drainDone: // If the drain can finish before a new request is sent, the // connection will be reused; otherwise, a new connection is // created, and the current connection will be put in a pool of // idle connections, potentially being reused for another future // request. case <-time.After(50 * time.Millisecond): // If we reach the 50 ms timeout, body.Close will run and interrupt // the io.CopyN, preventing goroutine leaks. } body.Close() }() } As we can see, draining response bodies safely is surprisingly tricky and cumbersome. Worse, as the practice of draining response bodies spread, some nuances were often lost. This has led to misunderstandings such as attempting to drain response bodies for HTTP/2 connections, when doing so is unnecessary. The current state and conclusion Starting in Go 1.27, net/http.Transport automatically does everything we have implemented in the code above: it will asynchronously drain an unread HTTP/1 response body for up to 50 ms or 256 KB. It also implements additional optimizations; for example, when a response contains the Connection: close header, draining the body is guaranteed to be wasted work, and it therefore skips doing so. Note that this behavior might evolve in future versions of Go, as other possible enhancements become apparent. As a general best practice, we now recommend that users simply close their HTTP bodies once they no longer need them, like in our original example: func getStatus(url string) (int, error) { resp, err := http.Get(url) if err != nil { return 0, err } defer resp.Body.Close() return resp.StatusCode, nil } Go is all about simplicity. items.summary_html:
The Go Blog Better HTTP/1 connection reuse

Nicholas Husin and Damien Neil
14 October 2026

Take a look at the following function:

func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
    resp, err := http.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    return resp.StatusCode, nil
}

It sends a GET request to url and returns the HTTP status code.

Using HTTP/1 (GODEBUG=http2client=0), calling this function 100 times against index.golang.org takes ~710 milliseconds on Go 1.26 on my machine. On Go 1.27, the same program takes ~150 milliseconds.

That is almost 5 times faster! How is such a drastic performance difference possible?

The cost of establishing HTTP connections

To understand the difference, consider what happens on the network when we make an HTTP request.

Go’s net/http package supports HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1, and HTTP/2. All three run over TCP, and usually over TLS when talking to HTTPS endpoints. Making a request over a new connection looks something like this:

  1. TCP handshake (1 RTT): the client sends a SYN packet, the server replies with SYN-ACK, and the client replies with ACK. Because the client can send the first TLS message alongside that final ACK, establishing the TCP connection takes 1 round-trip time (RTT).
  2. TLS handshake (2 RTT): next, a TLS handshake exchanges encryption keys and verifies the server’s identity; using TLS 1.2, this takes 2 RTT.
  3. HTTP request: with the keys exchanged, HTTP requests can finally be sent after a total of 3 RTT.

These round trips (plus some CPU time spent on TLS handshakes) add up quickly. In cross-region communications, one-way latencies often reach or exceed the 50 ms (100 ms RTT) shown in the diagram above. Compared to the 300 ms spent just setting up the connection, the HTTP request itself can be cheap to serve, taking only a little over 1 RTT when bandwidth is plentiful or the HTTP response is small.

Even in more favorable conditions, opening a new connection can still be expensive. Our opening benchmark queries index.golang.org, which is distributed worldwide and supports TLS 1.3. This means that latency is relatively low, and the TLS handshake can actually finish in just 1 RTT. Even so, the performance difference is still very noticeable.

Connection reuse

To avoid paying this setup cost on every request, HTTP clients and servers try to reuse existing connections across multiple requests when possible. The mechanics of this differ based on the HTTP version:

  • HTTP/1.0: while not part of the official specification, clients and servers often opt into connection reuse by sending a Connection: keep-alive header. Reuse continues until either endpoint omits the header or sends a Connection: close header.
  • HTTP/1.1: connections are persistent by default, and can be reused for subsequent requests and responses unless either side declares otherwise by sending a Connection: close header.
  • HTTP/2: multiple requests and responses can be multiplexed over a single TCP connection.
When connection reuse fails

In HTTP/1 (both HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1), multiple requests and responses on the same connection are sent sequentially on the wire. If two GET requests are sent to index.golang.org over the same TCP connection, the responses arrive as a single stream of bytes:

As shown in the diagram, net/http.Get reads and parses the status line and headers from the byte stream to populate net/http.Response, then returns immediately. The response body remains unread on the connection and is consumed only as the caller reads from net/http.Response.Body.

Because responses are sent back-to-back on the same stream, net/http can only find the start of the next response after the current response body has been read to the very end (as determined by the Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding header).

Now look back at our example program, where we never read resp.Body:

func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
    resp, err := http.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    return resp.StatusCode, nil
}

Through Go 1.26, when resp.Body.Close is called, net/http sees that there is still an unread response body. Realizing that it cannot reuse the connection, it abandons the existing connection and creates new connections for its next requests, causing it to repeatedly incur the cost of establishing new connections.

(HTTP/2 does not have this problem. Because it multiplexes streams of frames over a single connection rather than sending responses strictly back-to-back, an unread response body on one stream does not block other requests from sharing the connection.)

Where failed connection reuse hurts

This subtlety of HTTP/1 connection reuse can cause silent performance degradation in seemingly innocuous code.

As in our opening example, a client might only care about an API response’s status code. However, the API endpoint it is talking to might send bodies that provide more detailed but ultimately unused information, such as {"success": true, "message": "update processed"}. This will unfortunately cause connection reuse to fail.

Even programs that do read the response body can run into this issue if they stop just short of the end of the body. For example, encoding/json.Decoder stops reading as soon as it sees the closing } of a JSON object. If a server sends a JSON response terminated with a newline, decoding the JSON object will leave the newline still unread. The connection cannot be reused for a new request until that newline is consumed. Thus, a healthy connection might end up being abandoned, even though it was only a single byte away from being reusable.

The manual solution

The unread body problem has been a long-standing sharp edge. Over the years, many Go developers came up with their own workarounds. Most commonly, this is done by draining the response body prior to closing it:

func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
    resp, err := http.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    drainAndCloseBody(resp.Body)
    return resp.StatusCode, nil
}

func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
    io.Copy(io.Discard, body) // Drain the response body before closing it.
    body.Close()
}

While this works for small responses, if the unread body is large, establishing a new TCP connection can be faster than downloading and discarding the rest of the body. A better approach is to cap the number of bytes we are willing to drain:

func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
    io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB.
    body.Close()
}

However, a server might send a response body that trickles in slowly, so we also need to cap the time we spend draining:

func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
    drainDone := make(chan struct{}, 1)
    go func() {
        io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB.
        drainDone <- struct{}{}
    }()
    // Only spend at most 50 ms trying to drain the response body.
    select {
    case <-drainDone:
    case <-time.After(50 * time.Millisecond):
        // If we reach the 50 ms timeout, body.Close will run and interrupt the
        // io.CopyN, preventing goroutine leaks.
    }
    body.Close()
}

Of course, we also do not want to block for up to 50 milliseconds when closing a response body. Instead, we can drain the body asynchronously in the background and let it race against subsequent requests:

func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
    drainDone := make(chan struct{}, 1)
    go func() {
        io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB.
        drainDone <- struct{}{}
    }()
    go func() {
        // Only spend at most 50 ms trying to drain the response body.
        select {
        case <-drainDone:
            // If the drain can finish before a new request is sent, the
            // connection will be reused; otherwise, a new connection is
            // created, and the current connection will be put in a pool of
            // idle connections, potentially being reused for another future
            // request.
        case <-time.After(50 * time.Millisecond):
            // If we reach the 50 ms timeout, body.Close will run and interrupt
            // the io.CopyN, preventing goroutine leaks.
        }
        body.Close()
    }()
}

As we can see, draining response bodies safely is surprisingly tricky and cumbersome. Worse, as the practice of draining response bodies spread, some nuances were often lost. This has led to misunderstandings such as attempting to drain response bodies for HTTP/2 connections, when doing so is unnecessary.

The current state and conclusion

Starting in Go 1.27, net/http.Transport automatically does everything we have implemented in the code above: it will asynchronously drain an unread HTTP/1 response body for up to 50 ms or 256 KB. It also implements additional optimizations; for example, when a response contains the Connection: close header, draining the body is guaranteed to be wasted work, and it therefore skips doing so. Note that this behavior might evolve in future versions of Go, as other possible enhancements become apparent.

As a general best practice, we now recommend that users simply close their HTTP bodies once they no longer need them, like in our original example:

func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
    resp, err := http.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    return resp.StatusCode, nil
}

Go is all about simplicity. Let your code stay clean and simple, and let net/http deal with the complexities on your behalf.
